items.title: Product modulo 1,000,000,007
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: Read n, 1 <= n <= 1000, then n integers, each from 0 to 10^9. Print their product modulo 1000000007. Multiply in a 64-bit type and reduce after every step. Run it here. Compiler Explorer compiles it with gcc 16.2, -O2 -std=c++23, and the page checks the output.

items.title: Sum until the input ends
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: Read integers until the input ends, with no count given first. Each is between -10^12 and 10^12, and there are at most 10^5 of them. Print their sum. Loop on while (cin >> x). Run it here. Compiler Explorer compiles it with gcc 16.2, -O2 -std=c++23, and the page checks the output.

questions.prompt: With a 4-byte unsigned int, x holds 2 and y holds 3. What does printing x-y output?
questions.why: Unsigned arithmetic wraps around modulo 2^32. The true result is -1, which wraps to 2^32-1 = 4294967295.

ref.label: learncpp.com 4.5 Unsigned integers, and why to avoid them

questions.prompt: A 32-bit signed int holds 2147483647. The program adds 1 to it. What does C++ say happens?
questions.why: Signed integer overflow is undefined behavior. A given compiler may print a wrapped value, but nothing is guaranteed.

ref.label: learncpp.com 4.4 Signed integers

questions.prompt: Which type is guaranteed to be an 8-byte signed integer, from about -9.2*10^18 to 9.2*10^18?
questions.why: Lesson 4.6 lists std::int64_t as 8 bytes and signed. std::size_t and std::uint64_t are unsigned, and std::int32_t is 4 bytes.

ref.label: learncpp.com 4.6 Fixed-width integers and size_t

questions.prompt: Read n, 1 <= n <= 10^5, then n integers, each from 1 to 10^18. Print the sum of their squares modulo 1000000007.
questions.why: x*x overflows 64 bits when x is near 10^18. Reduce x modulo 1000000007 first. The square is then below 1.1*10^18 and fits in a 64-bit signed integer.

ref.label: learncpp.com 4.6 Fixed-width integers and size_t

questions.prompt: A 1-byte unsigned integer holds 255. You add 25 and store the result back in it. What value does it hold?
questions.why: A 1-byte unsigned integer holds 0 to 255 and wraps modulo 256. 280 wraps to 280-256 = 24.

ref.label: learncpp.com 4.5 Unsigned integers, and why to avoid them

items.title: Reverse the words of a line
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: Read one line of up to 10^5 characters: words of lowercase letters separated by one or more spaces. Print the words in reverse order, separated by single spaces. Use getline and a std::string. Run it here. Compiler Explorer compiles it with gcc 16.2, -O2 -std=c++23, and the page checks the output.

questions.prompt: A function reads a std::vector<int> of 10^5 elements and is called 10^5 times. Which parameter avoids a copy on each call and stops the function from changing the vector?
questions.why: Pass by const reference avoids the copy and forbids changes through the reference. Pass by value copies all 10^5 elements on every call.

ref.label: learncpp.com 12.6 Pass by const lvalue reference

questions.prompt: What is std::string_view?
questions.back: A read-only view of an existing string, added in C++17. It reads a C-style string, a std::string, or another std::string_view without making a copy.
questions.why: Copying a std::string is slow. A view gives read access to the same characters without the copy.

ref.label: learncpp.com 5.8 Introduction to std::string_view

questions.prompt: Read one string s of 1 to 2*10^5 lowercase letters. Print its run-length encoding on one line: for each maximal run of equal letters, the letter and then the run length. For example, aaabcc prints a3b1c2.
questions.why: Walk the string with an index i. Advance a second index j while s[j] equals s[i], append s[i] and j-i, and continue from j.

ref.label: learncpp.com 5.7 Introduction to std::string

questions.prompt: Which call reads a whole line of text, spaces included, into a std::string name, skipping leading whitespace left by an earlier cin >> read?
questions.why: operator>> stops at the first space. std::getline reads to the end of the line, and std::cin >> std::ws first skips the newline left in the buffer.

ref.label: learncpp.com 5.7 Introduction to std::string

items.title: Rank by score, then by name
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: Read n, 1 <= n <= 10^5, then n lines each holding a name (lowercase letters) and a score (0 to 10^9). Print the names one per line, highest score first, and names in alphabetical order when scores tie. Use a struct and std::sort with a lambda. Run it here. Compiler Explorer compiles it with gcc 16.2, -O2 -std=c++23, and the page checks the output.

questions.prompt: x is an int set to 1. A lambda f is defined that captures x by value, with [x], and returns x. Then x is set to 5. What does f() return?
questions.why: A capture by value makes a copy of x when the lambda is created. Later changes to the outer x do not reach the copy, so f() returns 1.

ref.label: learncpp.com 20.7 Lambda captures

questions.prompt: A comparator passed to std::sort returns a.score >= b.score. What is wrong with it?
choices: Nothing. It sorts by score in descending order.
It returns true for two equal elements, which a comparator must never do, so the behavior is undefined.
std::sort cannot take a lambda as its comparator.
questions.why: A comparator must return false for equal objects. Using >= breaks that rule and gives undefined behavior. Use > for descending order.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Custom Comparators and Coordinate Compression: Comparators

questions.prompt: Read n, 1 <= n <= 10^5, then n words of lowercase letters. Print the words one per line, shortest first. Words of equal length go in alphabetical order. Use std::sort with a lambda.
questions.why: The lambda compares lengths first and falls back to string comparison when the lengths are equal.

ref.label: learncpp.com 20.6 Introduction to lambdas (anonymous functions)

questions.prompt: Lambda captures: what is the difference between [x] and [&x]?
questions.back: [x] gives the lambda its own copy of x, made when the lambda is created, and the copy is const unless the lambda is mutable. [&x] refers to the original x, so the lambda sees later changes and can modify it.
questions.why: Capture by value clones the variable into the lambda object. Capture by reference binds to the outer variable.

ref.label: learncpp.com 20.7 Lambda captures

Run it here. Compiler Explorer compiles it with gcc 16.2, -O2 -std=c++23, and the page checks the output.

items.minutesBasis: Proposed

items.title: Range sums with prefix sums
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: Read n and q, each up to 2*10^5, then n integers (absolute value up to 10^9), then q queries l r with 1 <= l <= r <= n. Print the sum of elements l to r for each query, one per line. Build the prefix sums once, with std::partial_sum or a loop, in 64-bit integers. Run it here. Compiler Explorer compiles it with gcc 16.2, -O2 -std=c++23, and the page checks the output.

questions.prompt: Call std::unique on the vector {1, 1, 2, 1, 1}, with no sort first, then erase the leftover tail. How many elements remain?
questions.why: std::unique removes all but the first element of each group of consecutive equal elements. The groups are 1 1, 2, and 1 1, so {1, 2, 1} remains.

ref.label: cppreference: std::unique

questions.prompt: Start from the sorted vector {1, 2, 2, 3}. A do-while loop calls std::next_permutation until it returns false. How many arrangements does the loop body see?
questions.why: next_permutation steps through distinct arrangements in lexicographic order. There are 24/2 = 12 distinct arrangements of 1, 2, 2, 3, since swapping the two 2s gives the same arrangement.

ref.label: cppreference: std::next_permutation

questions.prompt: What does std::vector<int> v{ 10 } contain?
questions.why: A braced list matches the list constructor first, so v holds the single value 10. std::vector<int> v(10) makes ten zeros.

ref.label: learncpp.com 16.2 Introduction to std::vector and list constructors

questions.prompt: std::vector: cost of v[i], of push_back, and of insert at the front
questions.back: v[i] is O(1). Insertion or removal at the end is amortized O(1). Insertion or removal elsewhere is O(n), linear in the distance to the end.
questions.why: A vector stores its elements contiguously, so inserting before the end shifts every later element.

ref.label: cppreference: std::vector

questions.prompt: Read n, 1 <= n <= 10^5, then n integers. Print the next arrangement in lexicographic order on one line. If the input is already the last arrangement, print the first one, which is the sorted order.
questions.why: std::next_permutation does both cases. When no next arrangement exists, it returns false and leaves the range sorted, which is the first arrangement.

ref.label: cppreference: std::next_permutation

questions.prompt: s is a std::set<int> with 10^5 elements. Which call finds the smallest element at least x in O(log n) time?
questions.why: The member s.lower_bound(x) is logarithmic in the size of the set. Set iterators move one step at a time, so the free functions walk the set in linear time.

ref.label: cppreference: std::set::lower_bound

questions.prompt: A std::multiset<int> ms holds {1, 2, 2, 2, 3}. After ms.erase(2), what is ms.size()?
questions.why: erase with a value removes every copy of that value, which leaves {1, 3}. To remove one copy, call ms.erase(ms.find(2)).

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sorted Sets: Multisets

questions.prompt: m is a std::map<std::string, int> that has no key "cow". The program evaluates m["cow"] == 0. What else happens?
choices: The key "cow" is inserted with value 0, so m.size() grows by 1
questions.why: operator[] inserts a missing key with a default-constructed value, which is 0 for int. Use m.count(key) or m.find(key) to test without inserting.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sets & Maps: Maps

questions.prompt: Read q, 1 <= q <= 2*10^5, then q operations. "+ x" adds x. "- x" removes one copy of x if there is one. "?" prints the largest value minus the smallest, or -1 if nothing is stored. Values are between -10^9 and 10^9. Use std::multiset.
questions.why: A multiset keeps duplicates in sorted order. Remove one copy with erase(find(x)), and read the ends with begin() and rbegin().

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sorted Sets: Multisets

questions.prompt: std::set and std::map: cost of insert, erase, and find
questions.back: Logarithmic in the size of the container. Both keep keys sorted and are usually red-black trees.
questions.why: A balanced search tree has height O(log n), and each operation walks one path from the root.

ref.label: cppreference: std::set

items.what: Submit on CSES until it is accepted. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Push 5, 1, and 4 into a std::priority_queue<int>. Pop once. What does top() return?
questions.why: By default a priority_queue gives the largest element first. The pop removes 5, so top() is 4.

ref.label: cppreference: std::priority_queue

questions.prompt: Which declaration makes top() return the smallest int?
questions.why: The default comparator std::less puts the largest element on top. std::greater<int> makes the smallest appear as top().

ref.label: cppreference: std::priority_queue

questions.prompt: std::deque: cost of push_front, push_back, and dq[i]
questions.back: O(1) for insertion or removal at either end, and O(1) random access. Insertion or removal in the middle is O(n).
questions.why: A deque grows at both ends without shifting its elements, unlike a vector.

ref.label: cppreference: std::deque

questions.prompt: People 1 to n stand in a circle. Starting from person 1, count k people around the circle and remove the k-th. Continue counting from the next person until everyone is removed. Read n and k, 1 <= n, k <= 2000, and print the removal order on one line. Use a std::deque.
questions.why: Rotate the deque k-1 times by moving the front to the back, then pop the front. Each rotation step is O(1) on a deque.

ref.label: cppreference: std::deque

questions.prompt: std::stack: what order does it give, and where do push and pop act?
questions.back: Last in, first out. push, pop, and top act on the back of the underlying container, which is the top of the stack.
questions.why: A stack is an adapter that exposes only the back of its container.

ref.label: cppreference: std::stack

units.title: Refresher: complexity
units.why: Plan, Phase 0: you have not coded or competed in over a year, so Phase 0 opens with a refresher before placement. Complexity from Saad's Algorithms Part 1, before the contest template and stress test in the next unit.

items.title: Saad, Mastering critical SKILLS in Algorithms using C++: Part 1, section 4: Complexity Analysis, 5 lectures, 46 min
items.minutesBasis: The section's lecture lengths on Udemy, read 9 Nov 2026
items.what: Watch the section and do its quiz. Then write down the largest n that O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), and O(2^n) handle in one second at about 10^8 simple operations.

links.label: Saad, Mastering critical SKILLS in Data Structures using C++, section 3: Asymptotic Complexity, 4 lectures, 46 min

questions.prompt: i runs from 1 to n. For each i, j runs from i to n. How many times does the inner body run when n = 10?
questions.why: The inner loop runs n, n-1, down to 1 times. The total is n(n+1)/2 = 55, which is O(n^2).

ref.label: USACO Guide, Time Complexity: Complexity Calculations

questions.prompt: i starts at 1 and doubles after each pass. The loop runs while i < 1000. How many passes does it make?
questions.why: i takes the values 1, 2, 4, up to 512, which is 10 values. A doubling loop up to n runs about log2(n) times.

ref.label: Saad, Mastering critical SKILLS in Algorithms using C++: Part 1, section 4: Complexity Analysis, 5 lectures, 46 min

questions.prompt: n is at most 2*10^5. By the USACO Guide table, which is the slowest of these complexities that is safe?
questions.why: The table allows O(n log n) up to n = 5*10^5 and O(n sqrt n) only up to 7*10^4. O(n^2) is safe only to 7500.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Time Complexity: Common Complexities and Constraints

questions.prompt: At the conservative 10^8 simple operations a second, how many seconds does an O(n^2) loop take for n = 10^5?
questions.why: n^2 = 10^10 operations. 10^10 / 10^8 = 100 seconds, far over a 2 second limit.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Time Complexity

questions.prompt: How many triples i < j < k can you choose from 10 elements?
questions.why: This is C(10,3) = 120. Iterating over all subsets of size k is O(n^k), so all triples is O(n^3).

ref.label: USACO Guide, Time Complexity: Common Complexities and Constraints

questions.prompt: Which code is O(n^2 + m)?
choices: A loop over n with a loop over n inside it, followed by a separate loop over m
A loop over n with a loop over m inside it
A loop over n followed by a loop over m
A loop over m with a loop over m inside it, followed by a loop over n
questions.why: Separate blocks add, and nested loops multiply. n*n plus m gives O(n^2 + m), and neither term is lower order than the other.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Time Complexity: Complexity Calculations

questions.prompt: The formal definition of f(n) = O(g(n))
questions.back: There exist positive constants c and n0 such that f(n) <= c*g(n) for every n >= n0.
questions.why: Big O is an upper bound that ignores constant factors and small n.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Time Complexity: Formal Definition of Big O notation

questions.prompt: n starts at 100. While n > 0, the loop sets n to n/3 with integer division. How many passes does it make?
questions.why: n goes 100, 33, 11, 3, 1, then 0. That is 5 passes. Dividing by a constant each pass gives O(log n).

ref.label: Saad, Mastering critical SKILLS in Algorithms using C++: Part 1, section 4: Complexity Analysis, 5 lectures, 46 min

questions.prompt: By the USACO Guide table, the largest n for O(n factorial) and for O(2^n * n)
questions.back: About n <= 10 for O(n factorial) and n <= 20 for O(2^n * n).
questions.why: These bounds keep the operation count near 10^8, the conservative count the grader handles in a second.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Time Complexity: Common Complexities and Constraints

questions.prompt: Binary search on a sorted array and insertion into a sorted set are both O(log n). Which runs faster in practice?
choices: Neither. Equal complexity means equal time.
questions.why: Big O ignores the constant factor. The guide names binary search as noticeably faster than set insertion.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Time Complexity: Constant Factor

questions.prompt: f(n) returns at once when n = 0. Otherwise it calls f(n-1) twice. How many calls does f(10) make in total, counting the first?
questions.why: Calls double at each level: 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^10 = 2^11 minus 1 = 2047. Two-way branching recursion is O(2^n).

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to DP: Without Dynamic Programming

items.title: A stress-test script
items.what: Write a brute force, a random input generator, and a loop that runs both against your solution and stops on the first difference. Done when it finds a bug you planted.

questions.prompt: Which g++ option replaces each STL container with a debug version, so an out-of-range v[i] stops with an error?
questions.why: -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG turns on debug mode for the standard library containers. The guide shows v[-1] on an empty vector reported in place of a segmentation fault.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Debugging C++: -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG

questions.prompt: What does && do in g++ name.cpp -o name && ./name?
choices: It runs ./name only if the compile succeeds
It runs both commands at the same time
It pipes the compiler output into ./name
questions.why: && runs the second command only when the first one finishes successfully.

ref.label: USACO Guide, C++ With the Command Line: Basics of Compiling & Running

questions.prompt: Which command runs ./name with standard input from inp.txt and standard output to out.txt?
questions.why: < redirects standard input from a file and > redirects standard output to a file. They can be used together.

ref.label: USACO Guide, C++ With the Command Line: Redirecting Input & Output

questions.prompt: What does -fsanitize=undefined do, and how do you make it stop at the first error?
questions.back: It reports undefined behavior at run time, such as signed integer overflow and an array index out of bounds, to standard error. By default the program keeps running. Add -fno-sanitize-recover to exit at the first error.
questions.why: The sanitizer instruments the program. The guide shows it catching an array out of bounds and an integer overflow.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Debugging C++: -fsanitize=undefined

questions.prompt: Which warning option does the How to Debug checklist pair with -Wall to catch shadowed variables?
questions.why: The checklist says compiling with -Wall -Wshadow should detect shadowed, unused, or uninitialized variables.

ref.label: USACO Guide, How to Debug: Wrong Answer (or Runtime Error)

questions.prompt: Stress testing: what are the parts, and when does the loop stop?
questions.back: Your solution, a slower solution you trust, and a generator of small random inputs. Run both solutions on each generated input and stop at the first input where their outputs differ.
questions.why: That input is a small failing case you can trace by hand.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Basic Debugging: Stress Testing

questions.prompt: A solution reads many test cases from one input. It passes each case alone but fails when they run together. What does the How to Debug checklist tell you to check?
choices: That every data structure is cleared between test cases
That cin is replaced with scanf
That endl is used in place of a newline character
questions.why: Leftover data from one test case corrupts the next. The checklist warns this can show up only when a test case follows a smaller one.

ref.label: USACO Guide, How to Debug: Wrong Answer (or Runtime Error)

questions.prompt: What does adding -g to -fsanitize=address give you?
choices: The source line where the error occurred
questions.why: -g adds debugging information based on line numbers, so the address sanitizer report names the line.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Debugging C++: -fsanitize=address

questions.prompt: What does -Wconversion warn about?
choices: Implicit conversions that may alter a value
Variables used before they are set
Local variables that hide other variables
questions.why: -Wconversion flags implicit conversions that may change a value, such as a long long stored into an int.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Debugging C++: -Wconversion

questions.prompt: Which item is on the How to Debug checklist for Time Limit Exceeded?
choices: Unnecessary copying of data, fixed in C++ by passing variables by reference
Using long long in place of int
questions.why: The TLE list asks about infinite loops, the algorithm complexity, leftover debug output, and needless copying.

ref.label: USACO Guide, How to Debug: Time Limit Exceeded

questions.prompt: What is the minimum number of moves to solve the Tower of Hanoi with 10 disks?
questions.why: Moving n disks takes n-1 disks aside, one move for the largest, and n-1 disks back on top. That gives 2^n minus 1 moves, which is 1023 for n = 10.

ref.label: CSES 2165: Tower of Hanoi

questions.prompt: The reflected Gray code of n is n XOR (n >> 1). What is the code for n = 13, as a decimal number?
questions.why: 13 is 1101 in binary and 13 >> 1 is 0110. Their XOR is 1011, which is 11. Consecutive codes differ in one bit.

ref.label: cp-algorithms: Gray code

questions.prompt: Read n, 1 <= n <= 15. Print every string of n bits with no two adjacent 1s, one per line, in lexicographic order.
questions.why: Recurse on the next position. Try 0 first, then 1 only if the previous bit is not 1. Trying 0 before 1 gives lexicographic order.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Complete Search with Recursion: Generating Subsets Recursively

questions.prompt: What must every recursive function have to stop?
questions.back: A recursive termination condition: a case where the function returns without calling itself. Without it, the recursion runs until the call stack runs out of memory.
questions.why: Each call takes stack space, so a recursion that never stops overflows the stack.

ref.label: learncpp.com 20.3 Recursion

questions.prompt: In the optimal Tower of Hanoi solution with 3 disks, how many moves does the smallest disk make?
questions.why: The optimal solution has 7 moves, and the smallest disk moves on every other one: moves 1, 3, 5, and 7. That is 4 moves, which is 2^(n-1).

ref.label: CSES 2165: Tower of Hanoi

items.title: CSES 1618: Trailing Zeros
items.what: Submit on CSES until it is accepted. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

links.label: Saad, Mastering critical SKILLS in Algorithms using C++: Part 1, section 6: Searching: Binary Search, 21 lectures, 161 min

questions.prompt: How many trailing zeros does 100 factorial have?
questions.why: Each trailing zero needs a factor 10 = 2*5, and factors of 2 outnumber factors of 5. floor(100/5) + floor(100/25) = 20 + 4 = 24.

ref.label: CSES 1618: Trailing Zeros

questions.prompt: How many trailing zeros does 1000 factorial have?

ref.label: CSES 1618: Trailing Zeros

questions.prompt: Legendre's formula: the power of a prime p in n factorial
questions.back: floor(n/p) + floor(n/p^2) + floor(n/p^3) + ..., stopping when p^i exceeds n.
questions.why: Every p-th factor of n factorial adds one factor of p, every p^2-th adds another, and so on.

ref.label: cp-algorithms: Finding Power of Factorial Divisor, Prime k

questions.prompt: The number of trailing zeros of n factorial is the power of 10 in it. Why is it enough to count factors of 5?
choices: 10 = 2*5, the answer is the smaller of the powers of 2 and 5, and 2 appears at least as often as 5
Factors of 2 never appear in n factorial
Every multiple of 5 is a multiple of 10
questions.why: For a composite k, the power of k in n factorial is the minimum over its prime factors of the prime power divided by its exponent. For 10 that is min(power of 2, power of 5), which is the power of 5.

ref.label: cp-algorithms: Finding Power of Factorial Divisor, Composite k

items.title: Saad, Mastering critical SKILLS in Algorithms using C++: Part 2, section 1: Dynamic Programming (DP) - Intro, 4 lectures, 42 min
items.minutesBasis: The section's lecture lengths on Udemy, read 9 Nov 2026
items.what: Watch the section. It is the bridge to Gold's DP units, which come later.

questions.prompt: In how many ordered ways can you throw a die one or more times so the outcomes sum to 6?
questions.why: Let dp[s] be the ways to reach sum s. dp[0] = 1 and dp[s] is the sum of dp[s-1] through dp[s-6]. This gives 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 for s = 1 to 6.

ref.label: CSES 1633: Dice Combinations

questions.prompt: fib(k) returns k when k <= 1, and fib(k-1) + fib(k-2) otherwise, with no memo. How many calls does fib(10) make in total, counting the first?
questions.why: The call count C(k) = 1 + C(k-1) + C(k-2) with C(0) = C(1) = 1 gives 177 for k = 10. The same values are computed many times, which is what memoization removes.

ref.label: Saad, Mastering critical SKILLS in Algorithms using C++: Part 2, section 1: Dynamic Programming (DP) - Intro, 4 lectures, 42 min

questions.prompt: Frog 1 by plain recursion on jumps of 1 or 2 is O(2^N). What makes the dynamic programming version O(N)?
choices: It computes the best cost to each stone once and reuses it
It sorts the stones by height
It only allows jumps of length 1
questions.why: The recursion reaches the same stone along many jump sequences. Caching the best cost per stone computes each state once.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to DP: Example, Frog 1

questions.prompt: Push DP versus pull DP
questions.back: Push DP updates future states from the current state. Pull DP computes the current state from past states.
questions.why: Both fill the same table. They differ only in the direction of the update.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to DP: With Dynamic Programming

questions.prompt: State the three exponent laws for a product of powers, a power of a power, and a negative exponent.
questions.back: a^m * a^n = a^(m+n). (a^m)^n = a^(mn). a^(-n) = 1/a^n for a not 0.
questions.why: Each law counts the factors of a. A negative exponent undoes multiplication by a, so it divides.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 1.6, Exponents, p. 28

questions.prompt: What does a^(m/n) mean for a positive base a?
questions.back: The nth root of a, raised to the mth power. It equals the nth root of a^m.
questions.why: Raising a^(1/n) to the nth power must give a by the power of a power law, so a^(1/n) is the nth root.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 1.7, Fractional Exponents, p. 37

questions.prompt: What happens to each term inside parentheses when you subtract the whole group, as in a-(b-c)?
questions.back: Every term changes sign: a-(b-c) = a-b+c.
questions.why: Subtracting a group is adding -1 times it, and the distributive property sends -1 to every term.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 2.3, Distribution, Subtraction, and Factoring, p. 62

questions.prompt: Describe the elimination method for a system of two linear equations.
questions.back: Multiply one or both equations so that one variable has opposite coefficients. Add the equations to remove that variable, solve for the other, then substitute back.
questions.why: Adding two true equations gives a true equation, and the chosen multipliers make one variable cancel.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 5.3, Elimination, p. 131

questions.prompt: When does the system ax+by=c, dx+ey=f have exactly one solution?
questions.back: When ae-bd is not 0, so the two lines have different slopes. If ae = bd the lines are parallel (no solution) or the same line (infinitely many).
questions.why: Two lines in the plane meet in exactly one point unless they are parallel or coincide.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 5.1, Introduction to Two-Variable Linear Equations, p. 123

items.title: Alcumus, Algebra: Distance in the Plane, Midpoint of a Segment, Graphing Lines, and Graphing Multiple Lines

questions.prompt: What is the slope of the line through (x1, y1) and (x2, y2)?
questions.back: (y2-y1)/(x2-x1), for x1 not equal to x2.
questions.why: Slope is rise over run between any two points of the line.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 8.2, Introduction to Graphing Linear Equations, p. 215

questions.prompt: How do the slopes of two parallel lines compare, and of two perpendicular lines?
questions.back: Parallel lines have equal slopes. Perpendicular lines (neither vertical) have slopes whose product is -1.
questions.why: Rotating a line by 90 degrees sends the direction (1, m) to (-m, 1), whose slope is -1/m.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 8.6, Comparing Lines, p. 238

questions.prompt: In the bucket-pouring example, milk is poured from bucket i, holding m_i, into bucket j, with capacity c_j and amount m_j. How much moves?
choices: The smaller of m_i and c_j minus m_j
The larger of m_i and c_j minus m_j
questions.why: The pour stops when bucket i is empty or bucket j is full, whichever comes first.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Simulation: Example 2

questions.prompt: Read n and k, then n lines each with a bucket capacity c and its starting amount m. Then read k pours, each "i j": pour from bucket i into bucket j until i is empty or j is full. Print the final amounts, one per line. Amounts are at most 10^9.
questions.why: Simulate each pour in order. The amount moved is the smaller of m_i and c_j minus m_j.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Simulation: Example 2

questions.prompt: In the CSES Number Spiral, what number is in row 1, column 4?
questions.why: Layer 4 is even, so it runs down column 4 from (1,4) after layer 3 ends at 9. The cell (1,4) holds 10.

ref.label: CSES 1071: Number Spiral

questions.prompt: A Bronze statement asks for the end result of a described process. What does the guide say is usually enough?
questions.why: In Bronze, when a problem asks for the end result of a process or when something occurs, simulating it directly is usually enough.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Simulation

items.what: Submit on CSES until it is accepted. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: In how many ways can two knights be placed on a 9 by 9 board so they do not attack each other?
questions.why: There are C(81,2) = 3240 placements. Each 2 by 3 or 3 by 2 box holds 2 attacking pairs, and there are 2*(k-1)(k-2) = 112 boxes, so 224 attack. 3240 minus 224 = 3016.

ref.label: CSES 1072: Two Knights

questions.prompt: Maximum Distance asks for the largest squared distance between two of n integer points. Why keep the running maximum as an integer squared distance?
choices: Squared distances between integer points are integers, so integer math is exact. A floating-point distance squared later can round wrong.
Integers use less memory than doubles
sqrt is not in the C++ standard library
questions.why: The guide shows a solution that stores the distance as a double and prints 12 where the answer is 13. Stay with integers when you can.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Basic Complete Search: Solution, Maximum Distance

questions.prompt: A loop checks every pair of 50 points, with j starting at i+1. How many pairs does it check?
questions.why: Starting j at i+1 counts each unordered pair once: C(50,2) = 1225.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Basic Complete Search: Solution, Maximum Distance

questions.prompt: Read n, 3 <= n <= 100, then n integers between -10^6 and 10^6. Print how many index triples i < j < k have a_i + a_j + a_k = 0.
questions.why: With n <= 100 there are under 2*10^5 triples, so checking every one is fast. Start each inner loop after the outer index so each triple counts once.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Basic Complete Search

questions.prompt: How many triples i < j < k does a complete search over 20 elements check?
questions.why: C(20,3) = 1140. All triples is O(n^3).

ref.label: USACO Guide, Time Complexity: Common Complexities and Constraints

questions.prompt: Apple Division tries every split of n = 20 apples by looping over all bitmasks. How many masks is that?
questions.why: Masks run from 0 to 2^n minus 1, so there are 2^20 = 1048576.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Complete Search with Recursion: Generating Subsets with Bitmasks

questions.prompt: How many different strings can be made from the letters of aabac?
questions.why: 5 letters with a repeated 3 times: 120/6 = 20, which is 5 factorial over 3 factorial.

ref.label: CSES 1622: Creating Strings

questions.prompt: Chessboard and Queens: how many ways are there to choose 8 of the 64 squares, the count a naive search would check?
questions.why: C(64,8) = 4426165368, over 4 billion. Placing one queen per row with a permutation cuts it to 8 factorial = 40320.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Complete Search with Recursion: Solution, Chessboard & Queens

questions.prompt: Read n and S, 1 <= n <= 20, then n integers between -10^6 and 10^6. Print how many subsets have sum exactly S. The empty subset counts and has sum 0.
questions.why: Loop mask from 0 to 2^n minus 1. Bit i of mask set means element i is in the subset. Total work is O(n 2^n).

ref.label: USACO Guide, Complete Search with Recursion: Generating Subsets with Bitmasks

questions.prompt: Why does the guide call next_permutation in a do-while loop and not a while loop?
choices: A while loop would move past the first permutation before processing it
next_permutation must be called at least twice
A while loop cannot call a function
questions.why: The range starts sorted, which is the first permutation. do-while processes it before the first call changes it.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Complete Search with Recursion: Permutations

questions.prompt: Backtracking
questions.back: Start from an empty solution and extend it one step at a time, recursing through every way the solution can be built. Undo each step after the recursive call returns.
questions.why: Chessboard and Queens places a queen, recurses, then removes the queen and tries the next square.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Complete Search with Recursion: Backtracking

items.title: CSES 1621: Distinct Numbers
items.what: Submit on CSES until it is accepted. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: A vector of pairs holds (2,5), (1,9), and (2,3). What order does sort give?
questions.why: Pairs sort by first element and use the second element to break ties.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sorting: (Dynamic) Arrays of Pairs & Tuples

questions.prompt: Which indices does sort(v.begin() + 1, v.begin() + 4) sort?
questions.why: The range is half open, [1, 4), so index 4 is not included.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sorting: Dynamic Arrays

questions.prompt: What is [5, 1, 4, 2, 8] after one pass of bubble sort?
questions.why: One pass swaps each adjacent pair that is out of order, left to right: 5 moves right until it meets 8.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sorting: Sorting Methods

questions.prompt: Read n, 2 <= n <= 2*10^5, then n integers between -10^9 and 10^9. Print the smallest difference between any two of them.
questions.why: After sorting, the closest pair is adjacent. Check the n-1 adjacent differences. The largest difference reaches 2*10^9, so use long long.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sorting

questions.prompt: Sort 1000 distinct numbers by repeatedly finding the minimum of the remaining ones, at k-1 comparisons for k numbers. How many comparisons in total?
questions.why: 999 + 998 + ... + 1 = 999*1000/2 = 499500. This O(n^2) sort always suffices in Bronze.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sorting: Problems

items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Sets & Maps, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

items.title: CSES 1640: Sum of Two Values
items.what: Submit on CSES until it is accepted. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Insert 3, 1, 3, 2, and 1 into a std::set<int>. What is its size?
questions.why: A set stores each value once, so it holds {1, 2, 3}.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sets & Maps: Sorted Sets

questions.prompt: Why can an unordered_set solution to Distinct Numbers fail one test?
choices: A test built against the hash function makes it run in Theta(N^2) time
unordered_set keeps elements in sorted order
questions.why: Hashing is O(1) expected only under assumptions about the hash. An anti-hash test breaks them. Switch to set or use a custom hash.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sets & Maps: Method 2, Hashset

questions.prompt: Read n and x, 1 <= n <= 2*10^5, then n integers a_1 to a_n, all between -10^9 and 10^9. Print how many index pairs i < j have a_i + a_j = x.
questions.why: Scan left to right with a map from value to count. For each a, add the count of x-a seen so far, then record a. The answer can reach about 2*10^10, so use long long.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sets & Maps: Maps

questions.prompt: m is a std::map. What does m.count(key) return?
choices: 1 if the key is present, 0 if not
The value stored at the key
The number of entries in the map
The position of the key in sorted order
questions.why: Keys in a map are unique, so count is 1 or 0. It checks for a key without inserting it.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sets & Maps: Maps

questions.prompt: Which of these uses hashing?
questions.why: C++ has sorted versions, std::set and std::map, and hashed versions, std::unordered_set and std::unordered_map.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sets & Maps: Introduction

questions.prompt: std::set versus std::unordered_set: cost per operation
questions.back: std::set: O(log N) worst case, with elements kept in sorted order. std::unordered_set: O(1) expected, but proportional to N in the worst case.
questions.why: A sorted set is a balanced tree. A hashset depends on its hash function spreading elements across buckets.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Sets & Maps: Sets

items.title: USACO Guide: Casework, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Sleepy Cow Herding: cows stand at positions 1, 2, and 10. What is the maximum number of moves before they are consecutive?
questions.why: The maximum is the largest gap between adjacent cows minus 1. The gaps are 1 and 8, so the answer is 7.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Casework: Solution, Sleepy Cow Herding

questions.prompt: Sleepy Cow Herding: cows stand at positions 3, 5, and 9. What is the minimum number of moves?
questions.why: Cows 3 and 5 have exactly one empty spot between them, so moving 9 into position 4 finishes in 1 move.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Casework: Solution, Sleepy Cow Herding

questions.prompt: Casework
questions.back: Split the problem into cases that can each be solved separately, often by drawing many cases and looking for ones that share a method.
questions.why: Sleepy Cow Herding splits the minimum into three cases: already consecutive, one gap of exactly one spot, and everything else.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Casework

questions.prompt: In Sleepy Cow Herding, why is the maximum number of moves always finite?
choices: Every move shrinks the distance between the two end cows by at least one
Each cow moves at most once
questions.why: The span between the endpoints strictly decreases, so the game must end.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Casework: Solution, Sleepy Cow Herding

items.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Greedy Algorithms
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Greedy Algorithms, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

items.title: CSES 1092: Two Sets
items.what: Submit on CSES until it is accepted. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: What is a greedy algorithm?
choices: One that makes the choice that looks best at each step and never takes a choice back
One that backtracks to find the best answer
One that sorts the input first
questions.why: A greedy algorithm builds the final solution directly from locally best choices, which usually makes it fast.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Greedy Algorithms

questions.prompt: For how many n from 1 to 20 can the numbers 1 to n be split into two sets of equal sum?
questions.why: A split needs n(n+1)/2 to be even, which holds when n mod 4 is 0 or 3, and then a split always exists. That is 10 values of n.

ref.label: CSES 1092: Two Sets

questions.prompt: What do competitive programmers mean by Proof by AC?
choices: Coding an easy greedy and submitting it to see whether it passes
A formal proof that the greedy is optimal
A stress test against a brute force
questions.why: Whether a greedy is correct is often unclear. If it is easy to code, one option is to submit it and see.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Greedy Algorithms: Solution, Mad Scientist

questions.prompt: Mad Scientist: A = HGHGGHHG and B = HHHHHHHH. Each flip toggles a contiguous range of A. What is the fewest flips to turn A into B?
questions.why: The greedy flips each maximal run of mismatches. A differs from B at position 2, at positions 4 and 5, and at position 8. That is 3 runs.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Greedy Algorithms: Solution, Mad Scientist

items.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Graphs
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Graphs, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: An undirected graph has nodes 1 to 6 and edges 1-2, 2-3, and 4-5. How many connected components does it have?
questions.why: The components are {1, 2, 3}, {4, 5}, and {6}. A node with no edges is its own component.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Graphs: Introduction

questions.prompt: An undirected graph on 8 nodes is read as 7 edges, and each edge is added to the adjacency lists of both ends. How many entries do the lists hold in total?
questions.why: Each undirected edge appears twice, once in each endpoint list, so 2*7 = 14.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Graphs: Constructing Adjacency Lists

questions.prompt: Which is NOT true of a tree with n nodes?
choices: There is exactly one simple path between any two nodes
questions.why: A tree is connected and has no cycles. It follows that it has n-1 edges and a unique path between any two nodes.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Graphs: Check Your Understanding

questions.prompt: Livestock Lineup has C cows and N constraints. What does the intended brute force over all orderings cost?
questions.why: It checks all C factorial orderings against N constraints. Treating the constraints as a graph of chains solves it in O(C).

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Graphs: Livestock Lineup

items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Rectangle Geometry, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Fence Painting: one interval [3, 5] and another [4, 8] are painted. What total length is painted?
questions.why: Add the lengths and subtract the overlap: 2 + 4 minus (min(5,8) minus max(3,4)) = 6 minus 1 = 5.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Rectangle Geometry: Example, Fence Painting

questions.prompt: Rectangle a has bottom left (1,1) and top right (5,4). Rectangle b has bottom left (3,2) and top right (7,6). What is the area of their intersection?
questions.why: Width = min(5,7) minus max(1,3) = 2 and length = min(4,6) minus max(1,2) = 2, so the area is 4.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Rectangle Geometry: Finding area of intersection

questions.prompt: Read two rectangles, each as x1 y1 x2 y2 with (x1, y1) bottom left and (x2, y2) top right, coordinates between -10^9 and 10^9. Print the total area covered by at least one of them.
questions.why: Union area = area a + area b minus intersection. The intersection width and length are min of the right sides minus max of the left sides, and count only if both are positive. Areas reach 4*10^18, so use long long.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Rectangle Geometry: Finding area of intersection

questions.prompt: Two axis-parallel rectangles a and b are given by bottom left bl and top right tr. When do they NOT intersect?
choices: When tr_a.y <= bl_b.y or bl_a.y >= tr_b.y, or when bl_a.x >= tr_b.x or tr_a.x <= bl_b.x
Only when one is inside the other
questions.why: They miss each other only if one lies fully above or below the other, or fully left or right of it.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Rectangle Geometry: Checking if two rectangles intersect

questions.prompt: Fence Painting: intervals [0, 10] and [2, 5] are painted. What total length is painted?
questions.why: The overlap is min(10,5) minus max(0,2) = 3. So 10 + 3 minus 3 = 10, since [2, 5] lies inside [0, 10].

ref.label: USACO Guide, Rectangle Geometry: Example, Fence Painting

questions.prompt: How many bit strings of length 10 are there, modulo 10^9+7?

questions.prompt: Photoshoot 2: the cows stand in order 1 2 3 4 5 and must end as 3 1 4 2 5. One modification moves one cow anywhere to its left. What is the fewest modifications?

questions.prompt: How to approach an ad hoc problem
questions.back: Draw many small cases. Write down every observation that seems useful. Do not get stuck on one idea unless you see a whole solution. Try many perspectives, such as formulas or a picture.
questions.why: Ad hoc problems have no standard method, so progress comes from observations on small cases.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Ad Hoc Problems: Introduction

questions.prompt: How many bit strings of length 40 are there, modulo 10^9+7?
questions.why: 2^40 = 1099511627776, and its remainder modulo 1000000007 is 511620083. Reduce after each doubling to stay in range.

ref.label: CSES 1617: Bit Strings

items.title: CSES 1646: Static Range Sum Queries
items.what: Submit on CSES until it is accepted. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: arr = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2], 1-indexed. What is the sum of arr[3] through arr[6]?
questions.why: prefix = [0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 23, 25]. The sum is prefix[6] minus prefix[2] = 23 minus 4 = 19.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Prefix Sums: Explanation

questions.prompt: With prefix[0] = 0 and prefix[k] = arr[1] + ... + arr[k], which gives arr[L] + ... + arr[R]?
questions.why: prefix[R] holds everything up to R. Subtract everything before L, which is prefix[L-1].

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Prefix Sums: Explanation

questions.prompt: Read n and x, 1 <= n <= 2*10^5, then n integers between -10^9 and 10^9. Print how many subarrays have sum exactly x.
questions.why: A subarray (l, r] has sum p[r] minus p[l]. Scan r left to right, add the count of earlier prefix sums equal to p[r] minus x, then record p[r]. Start with prefix sum 0 recorded once.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Prefix Sums

questions.prompt: N = Q = 10^5 and each range sum query loops over up to N elements. How many operations is that in the worst case?
questions.why: O(NQ) = 10^10, which will exceed the time limit. Prefix sums cut it to O(N + Q).

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Prefix Sums: Explanation

questions.prompt: Which operations can prefix sums handle besides addition?
questions.back: Any invertible operation, such as bitwise XOR: the XOR of a range is p[R] XOR p[L-1].
questions.why: The query subtracts the prefix before L, so the operation needs an inverse. XOR is its own inverse.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Prefix Sums: Introduction

questions.prompt: A = [2, 5, 7, 1, 4] has prefix sums P = [2, 7, 14, 15, 19], 1-indexed. What is the sum of A[2] through A[4]?
questions.why: P[4] minus P[1] = 15 minus 2 = 13, which matches 5 + 7 + 1.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Prefix Sums: Explanation

items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: More on Prefix Sums, problems

items.title: CSES 1652: Forest Queries
items.what: Submit on CSES until it is accepted. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: The grid has rows 1 2 3, 4 5 6, and 7 8 9. Using 2D prefix sums, what is the sum of the submatrix in rows 2 to 3 and columns 2 to 3?
questions.why: prefix[3][3] minus prefix[1][3] minus prefix[3][1] + prefix[1][1] = 45 minus 6 minus 12 + 1 = 28, which matches 5 + 6 + 8 + 9.

ref.label: USACO Guide, More on Prefix Sums: 2D Prefix Sums

questions.prompt: Read n and q, 1 <= n, q <= 2*10^5, then q updates "l r v": add v to every element from l to r, 1-indexed. All elements start at 0 and |v| <= 10^9. Print the final array on one line.
questions.why: Add v at d[l] and subtract it at d[r+1]. The prefix sums of d give the final array in O(n + q). Values reach 2*10^14, so use long long.

ref.label: USACO Guide, More on Prefix Sums: Difference Arrays

questions.prompt: Read n, 1 <= n <= 2*10^5, then n integers between -10^9 and 10^9. Print the largest sum of a nonempty contiguous subarray.
questions.why: For each right end r, the best sum ending there is p[r] minus the smallest earlier prefix sum. Keep a running minimum. If all values are negative, the answer is the largest single value.

ref.label: USACO Guide, More on Prefix Sums: Max Subarray Sum

questions.prompt: Which recurrence builds the 2D prefix sum array?
choices: prefix[i][j] = prefix[i-1][j] + prefix[i][j-1] minus prefix[i-1][j-1] + arr[i][j]
questions.why: Adding the cell above and the cell to the left counts prefix[i-1][j-1] twice, so subtract it once.

ref.label: USACO Guide, More on Prefix Sums: 2D Prefix Sums

questions.prompt: An array of 5 zeros gets +2 on positions 1 to 3 and +3 on positions 2 to 5, using a difference array. What is the final value at position 4?
questions.why: d gets +2 at 1, -2 at 4, +3 at 2, and -3 at 6. The prefix sum at 4 is 2 + 3 minus 2 = 3.

ref.label: USACO Guide, More on Prefix Sums: Difference Arrays

questions.prompt: Ferris Wheel: children weigh 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, each gondola holds at most two children, and the weight limit is 7. What is the fewest gondolas?
questions.why: Sort and pair the lightest with the heaviest that fits: 1 with 6, 2 with 5, 3 with 4. That is 3 gondolas.

ref.label: CSES 1090: Ferris Wheel

questions.prompt: Read n and x, 1 <= n <= 2*10^5, then n integers between -10^9 and 10^9. Print how many index pairs i < j have a_i + a_j <= x.
questions.why: Sort. With l at the start and r at the end, if a[l] + a[r] <= x then every index from l+1 to r pairs with l, so add r minus l and move l. Otherwise move r left. O(n log n) for the sort.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Two Pointers: Two Pointers

questions.prompt: Which statement about two pointers is false?
choices: It is only useful on a sorted array
With both pointers moving one way, it runs in O(N)
It uses O(1) extra space besides the array
A sliding window is a two pointers variant
questions.why: The array need not be sorted. A sliding window over a subarray works on unsorted data.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Two Pointers: Sliding Window

questions.prompt: Books: reading times are 2, 2, 3, 1, 1, 4 and there are 5 free minutes. What is the most consecutive books you can read?
questions.why: A sliding window finds 3, 1, 1 with total 5 and length 3. No window of length 4 has total at most 5.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Two Pointers: Sliding Window

items.what: Submit on CSES until it is accepted. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: v = [1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 8] is sorted. What is upper_bound(v, 3) minus lower_bound(v, 3), as indices?
questions.why: lower_bound finds the first element not less than 3, at index 1. upper_bound finds the first element greater than 3, at index 4. The difference counts the 3s.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Binary Search on a Sorted Array: Implementation (With Built-in Functions)

questions.prompt: Read n and q, 1 <= n, q <= 10^5, then n haybale positions between 0 and 10^9, then q queries "a b". For each query print how many haybales lie in [a, b].
questions.why: Sort the positions once. For each query, upper_bound(b) minus lower_bound(a) counts the positions in range in O(log n).

ref.label: USACO Guide, Binary Search on a Sorted Array: Example, Counting Haybales

questions.prompt: On a sorted range, what does std::lower_bound(first, last, x) return?
choices: An iterator to the first element not less than x
An iterator to the first element greater than x
An iterator to the last element less than x
questions.why: lower_bound gives the first position where x could be inserted while keeping order. upper_bound gives the first element greater than x.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Binary Search on a Sorted Array: Implementation (With Built-in Functions)

items.title: CSES 1074: Stick Lengths
items.what: Submit on CSES until it is accepted. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Binary search starts with 10^9 candidate values and halves them each step. How many steps does it take in the worst case to reach one value?
questions.why: Each step halves the range, so it takes ceil(log2(10^9)) = 30 steps.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Binary Search

questions.prompt: Read t, 1 <= t <= 10^5, then t integers x, each from 0 to 10^18. For each, print the largest integer r with r*r <= x. Use binary search on r.
questions.why: r*r <= x is true for small r and false after some point, so it is monotonic. Search r in [0, 10^9] and round mid up to avoid an infinite loop. 10^9 squared fits in long long.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Binary Search: Finding The Maximum x Such That f(x) = true

questions.prompt: lo can be negative. Why can mid = (lo + hi) / 2 break a firstTrue loop?
choices: Integer division rounds toward zero, so for a negative odd sum it rounds up, not down
questions.why: For lo + hi = -3, C++ gives -1, not -2. The loop can then fail to shrink. The guide lists this as a common mistake.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Binary Search: Mistake 2, Not Accounting for Negative Bounds

questions.prompt: Maximum Median: arr = [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 8, 8] and k = 5 increments. What is the largest possible median?
questions.why: Raising the median to x costs the sum of max(0, x minus arr[i]) over the upper half 4, 5, 5, 6, 8, 8. x = 6 costs 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. x = 7 costs 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8, over 5.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Binary Search: Example, Maximum Median

questions.why: Ending earliest leaves the most room. Any event that fits after a later-ending choice also fits after the earlier-ending one.

questions.prompt: Coins are 1, 3, and 4. How many coins does the greedy rule, largest coin that fits first, use to make 6?

questions.prompt: Knapsack with capacity 4: A weighs 3 with value 18, and B and C each weigh 2 with value 10. What does greedy by value per weight get, and what is optimal?
choices: Greedy gets 18. The optimum is 20 with B and C.
questions.why: A has the best ratio, 6, and then nothing else fits. B and C together give 20. Knapsack needs dynamic programming.

items.title: CSES 1091: Concert Tickets
items.what: Submit on CSES until it is accepted. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Customers stay (1, 4), (2, 5), and (5, 7), as arrival and departure days. A room frees up only if its departure is strictly before the arrival. How many rooms are needed?
questions.why: Sort by arrival. (1,4) and (2,5) need two rooms. At arrival 5 the earliest departure, 4, is before it, so (5,7) reuses that room. The heap never exceeds 2.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Priority Queues: Solution

questions.prompt: When does the guide say to prefer a priority queue over a sorted set?
choices: Whenever it can do the job, since it is simpler and faster
questions.why: A priority queue supports insert, max, and pop max in O(log N) with a better constant factor than a set.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Priority Queues: Introduction

questions.prompt: Read n and k, 1 <= k <= n <= 2*10^5, then n integers. After each one is read, print the k-th largest value read so far, or -1 if fewer than k have been read.
questions.why: Keep a min-heap of the k largest values. Push each value and pop when the size passes k. The top is then the k-th largest.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Priority Queues: Implementation

questions.prompt: Priority queue operations and their cost
questions.back: Insert an element, read the highest-priority element, and remove it, each in O(log N). In C++ std::priority_queue is a max-heap by default.
questions.why: A binary heap keeps the top element at the root and restores order along one path.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Priority Queues: Introduction

questions.prompt: Push 7, 3, 9, and 1 into a min-heap. Pop twice. What is the top?
questions.why: The pops remove 1 and then 3. The smallest remaining value is 7.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Priority Queues: Implementation

questions.prompt: Building Roads: 7 cities and roads 1-2, 2-3, 4-5, and 6-7. How many new roads are needed to connect every city?
questions.why: There are C = 3 components: {1,2,3}, {4,5}, and {6,7}. Each new road joins at most two components, so C minus 1 = 2 roads.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Graph Traversal: Solution, Building Roads

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between DFS and BFS?
choices: BFS visits nodes in order of distance from the start. DFS follows one path and backtracks only when it must.
DFS is recursive and BFS is iterative.
DFS visits nodes in order of distance from the start.
questions.why: Either can be written recursively or iteratively. The difference is the visit order.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Graph Traversal: BFS

questions.prompt: Read n and m, 1 <= n <= 10^5 and 0 <= m <= 2*10^5, then m undirected edges. Print YES if the nodes can be colored with two colors so every edge joins different colors, otherwise NO.
questions.why: Run BFS or DFS from each uncolored node. Give each new neighbor the opposite color, and answer NO if an edge joins two nodes of the same color.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Graph Traversal: Solution, Building Teams

questions.prompt: A recursive DFS on a path of 10^6 nodes crashes locally but passes on the judge. Why?
choices: Each recursive call uses the call stack, which is limited to a few megabytes by default
The judge runs a different algorithm
questions.why: Deep recursion overflows the default stack. Raise the stack size or use an iterative traversal.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Graph Traversal: An Issue With Deep Recursion

questions.prompt: Which structures do iterative DFS and BFS use?
choices: A stack for DFS and a queue for BFS
A queue for DFS and a stack for BFS
questions.why: A stack takes the newest node first, which goes deep. A queue takes the oldest first, which goes level by level.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Graph Traversal: Queues

questions.prompt: The grid rows are ##.#, #..#, and .##. How many connected regions of . cells are there, moving up, down, left, and right?
questions.why: The three . cells in rows 1 and 2 near the middle connect. The . at the left of row 3 and the . at the right of row 3 are each alone. That is 3.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Flood Fill: Introduction

questions.prompt: Read n and m, 1 <= n, m <= 1000, then n rows of m characters, . for floor and # for wall. Print the size of the largest room, a group of floor cells connected up, down, left, or right. Print 0 if there is no floor.
questions.why: Flood fill each unvisited floor cell and count the cells reached. An iterative BFS avoids deep recursion on a 1000 by 1000 grid.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Flood Fill: Example, Counting Rooms

questions.prompt: In flood fill on a grid, what are the neighbors of a cell?
choices: The cells directly adjacent in the four cardinal directions
Every cell in the same row or column
The cells listed in the input as edges
questions.why: A grid is an implicit graph. Its edges are not given, and each cell connects to its four direct neighbors.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Flood Fill: Introduction

questions.prompt: What can go wrong with a recursive flood fill on a 4000 by 4000 grid?
choices: Stack overflow, or memory over 256 MB
questions.why: Recursion depth can reach the number of cells. Non-recursive versions generally use less memory.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Flood Fill: Example, Counting Rooms

questions.prompt: A tree has 50 nodes. How many edges does it have?
questions.why: A connected graph is a tree if and only if it has N-1 edges, so 49.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Tree Algorithms

questions.prompt: Read n, 1 <= n <= 2*10^5, then n-1 edges of a tree. Root it at node 1 and print the depth of every node, 1 to n, on one line. The root has depth 0.
questions.why: Traverse from the root. A node depth is its parent depth plus 1. BFS avoids deep recursion on a long path.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Tree Algorithms

questions.prompt: Subtree sizes need each child finished before its parent. Which traversal order is that?
questions.why: Postorder visits all children before processing the current node, so the children sizes are ready.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Tree Algorithms: Tree Traversal Order

questions.prompt: Why is void dfs(int v, int p, vector<vector<int>>& adj) linear time on a tree while the same header without & is not?
choices: Without &, adj is copied in O(n) on every call
The & removes the need for p
questions.why: Passing by reference copies a reference in O(1). By value copies the whole list each call, O(n^2) in total.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Tree Algorithms

items.what: Submit on CSES until it is accepted. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: A functional graph has successors 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 4, 4 to 2, and 5 to 1. Start at node 5 and follow 10 edges. Where do you end?
questions.why: The walk goes 1, 2, 3, 4, then cycles 2, 3, 4 with length 3. After 4 steps you are at 4, and 6 more steps is two full cycles, so 4.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Functional Graphs: K-th Successor

questions.prompt: What is a functional graph?
choices: A directed graph where every node has exactly one outgoing edge
questions.why: It is also called a successor graph. Each component is a cycle with trees hanging into it.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Functional Graphs: Introduction

questions.prompt: Successors: 1 to 2, 2 to 1, 3 to 3, 4 to 5, 5 to 6, 6 to 4, 7 to 4, and 8 to 7. How many cycles does the graph have?
questions.why: The cycles are {1, 2}, {3} as a self-loop, and {4, 5, 6}. Nodes 7 and 8 lead into the third cycle.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Functional Graphs: Count Cycles

questions.prompt: What are the time and extra memory of Floyd's cycle detection on a functional graph?
choices: O(N log N) time and O(N) memory
questions.why: Two pointers move at speeds 1 and 2. They meet inside the cycle in O(N) steps, and only the two positions are stored.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Functional Graphs: Floyd's Algorithm

questions.prompt: How fast can binary jumping find the k-th successor after preprocessing?
questions.why: Precompute the 2^j-th successor of every node, then follow the set bits of k.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Introduction to Functional Graphs: K-th Successor

items.title: CSES 1146: Counting Bits
items.what: Submit on CSES until it is accepted. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: What is 12 & 10?
questions.why: 12 is 1100 and 10 is 1010. AND keeps bits set in both: 1000 = 8.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Intro to Bitwise Operators

questions.prompt: What is 12 ^ 10?
questions.why: XOR keeps bits set in exactly one: 1100 XOR 1010 = 0110 = 6.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Intro to Bitwise Operators: XOR Operation

questions.prompt: What is 1 << 10?
questions.why: 1 << x is 2^x, a number with only bit x set. 2^10 = 1024.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Complete Search with Recursion: Generating Subsets with Bitmasks

questions.prompt: Two numbers a and b have a & b = 8 and a ^ b = 6. What is a + b?
questions.why: a + b = 2*(a & b) + (a ^ b). XOR is the sum without carries and AND marks the carries. 2*8 + 6 = 22.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Intro to Bitwise Operators: Solution, Take a Guess

questions.prompt: Read n, an odd number up to 2*10^5, then n integers from 0 to 10^18. Every value appears an even number of times except one. Print that value.
questions.why: XOR all the values. x ^ x = 0, so every value with an even count cancels and the odd one out remains.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Intro to Bitwise Operators: XOR Operation

questions.prompt: How many one bits are there in total in the binary forms of 1 through 20?
questions.why: Sum the popcounts: 1 to 7 give 12, 8 to 15 give 20, and 16 to 20 give 10. The total is 42.

ref.label: CSES 1146: Counting Bits

questions.prompt: The property of XOR that makes prefix XOR work
questions.back: XOR is its own inverse: x ^ x = 0. So the XOR of a range is p[R] ^ p[L-1].
questions.why: Applying the same XOR twice cancels it, so the prefix before L drops out.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Intro to Bitwise Operators: XOR Operation

questions.prompt: What does mask & (1 << x) test?
choices: Whether bit x of mask is set
Whether mask is a power of two
questions.why: AND with a number that has only bit x set is nonzero exactly when bit x of mask is 1.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Complete Search with Recursion: Generating Subsets with Bitmasks

questions.why: The XOR of 1 to 7 is 0, since bits pair off. XOR with 8 gives 8.

ref.label: USACO Guide, Intro to Bitwise Operators: XOR Operation

questions.prompt: State the commutative and associative properties of addition.
questions.back: Commutative: a+b = b+a. Associative: (a+b)+c = a+(b+c).
questions.why: Order and grouping do not change a sum, which is what lets you add a long list in any convenient order.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 1.2, Addition, p. 4

questions.prompt: How does Prealgebra define subtraction in terms of addition?
questions.back: a-b = a+(-b). Subtracting b is adding the negation of b.
questions.why: This definition lets every property of addition apply to subtraction.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 1.5, Subtraction, p. 24

questions.prompt: How is division defined in terms of multiplication?
questions.back: a/b = a * (1/b) for b not 0. Dividing by b is multiplying by its reciprocal.
questions.why: The reciprocal 1/b is the number whose product with b is 1, so multiplying by it undoes multiplying by b.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 1.7, Division, p. 38

questions.prompt: Using the distributive property and the definition of negation, prove that (-a)(-b) = ab.
rubric: Shows (-a)b = -(ab) because ab + (-a)b = (a+(-a))b = 0 * b = 0.
Shows 0 * b = 0 from the distributive property.
Applies the same argument to (-a)(-b) + (-a)b = (-a)(-b+b) = 0.
Concludes (-a)(-b) is the negation of (-a)b = -(ab), so it equals ab.
questions.why: The product is forced once the distributive property must hold for negative numbers.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 1.4, Negation, p. 17

questions.prompt: Why is a^0 = 1 for every nonzero a?
questions.back: Because a^n / a^n = a^(n-n) = a^0 must equal 1 for the exponent laws to keep working.
questions.why: Defining a^0 = 1 is the only choice that keeps a^m * a^n = a^(m+n) true when n = 0.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 2.3, Zero as an Exponent, p. 73

questions.prompt: What does a negative exponent mean?
questions.back: a^(-n) = 1/a^n for a not 0.
questions.why: The product a^n * a^(-n) must be a^0 = 1, so a^(-n) is the reciprocal of a^n.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 2.4, Negative Exponents, p. 76

questions.prompt: Expand (ab)^n and (a^m)^n.
questions.back: (ab)^n = a^n b^n. (a^m)^n = a^(mn).
questions.why: Write out the n factors and regroup them by commutativity and associativity.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 2.2, Higher Exponents, p. 63

questions.prompt: State the divisibility tests for 3, 9, 4, and 8.
questions.back: 3 or 9: the digit sum is divisible by 3 or 9. 4: the last two digits form a multiple of 4. 8: the last three digits form a multiple of 8.
questions.why: Every power of 10 leaves remainder 1 on division by 3 or 9. 100 is a multiple of 4 and 1000 is a multiple of 8.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 3.2, Divisibility Tests, p. 97

questions.prompt: How do you find the least common multiple from prime factorizations?
questions.back: Take each prime to the highest power it has in any of the numbers, and multiply.
questions.why: A common multiple must contain each prime at least as often as every number does, and the highest power is the least that works.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 3.5, Least Common Multiple, p. 120

questions.prompt: How do you find the greatest common divisor from prime factorizations?
questions.back: Take each prime to the lowest power it has in all of the numbers, and multiply.
questions.why: A common divisor can use each prime no more often than the number with the fewest copies.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 3.7, Greatest Common Divisor, p. 134

questions.prompt: Prove that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
rubric: Assumes there are finitely many primes p1, ..., pk.
Forms N = p1 * p2 * ... * pk + 1.
Notes N leaves remainder 1 on division by each pi, so no pi divides N.
Notes N > 1 has some prime factor, which is not on the list, a contradiction.
questions.why: This is Euclid's argument. The key step is that N has a prime factor that is not any of the listed primes.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 3.3, Prime Numbers, p. 105

questions.prompt: How do you divide by a fraction?
questions.back: Multiply by its reciprocal: (a/b) / (c/d) = (a/b) * (d/c).
questions.why: Dividing by c/d is multiplying by the number whose product with c/d is 1, which is d/c.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 4.3, Dividing by a Fraction, p. 162

questions.prompt: How can you compare a/b and c/d with positive denominators without decimals?
questions.back: Compare ad and bc. a/b < c/d exactly when ad < bc.
questions.why: Multiplying both fractions by the positive number bd keeps the order and clears the denominators.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 4.6, Comparing Fractions, p. 177

questions.prompt: Write a/b + c/d as one fraction.
questions.back: (ad+bc)/(bd). The least common denominator gives a simpler form when b and d share factors.
questions.why: Rewrite each fraction over the common denominator bd, then add the numerators.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 4.7, Adding and Subtracting Fractions, p. 181

questions.prompt: What is the one rule behind every step of solving a linear equation?
questions.back: Do the same thing to both sides: add, subtract, multiply, or divide by a nonzero number.
questions.why: Equal quantities stay equal under the same operation, so each step keeps every solution.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 5.2, Solving Linear Equations I, p. 209

questions.prompt: What happens to an inequality when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number?
questions.back: The inequality reverses: if a < b and c < 0 then ac > bc.
questions.why: Negation flips the order of numbers on the number line.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 5.5, Inequalities, p. 230

questions.prompt: Prove that if a < b then -a > -b.
rubric: Starts from a < b, meaning b-a is positive.
Rewrites (-a)-(-b) as b-a.
Concludes (-a)-(-b) is positive, so -a > -b.
questions.why: The difference that measures the order is the same number in both statements, so the order flips.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 5.5, Inequalities, p. 230

questions.prompt: Which fractions in lowest terms have terminating decimals?
questions.back: Exactly those whose denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5.
questions.why: A terminating decimal is a fraction over a power of 10, and 10 = 2 * 5.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 6.3, Decimals and Fractions, p. 263

questions.prompt: How do you write a repeating decimal such as 0.272727... as a fraction?
questions.back: Let x be the decimal. Multiply by 10^k where k is the period length, subtract x, and solve. 0.272727... = 27/99 = 3/11.
questions.why: Shifting by a full period lines up the repeating tails, so they cancel on subtraction.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 6.4, Repeating Decimals, p. 267

questions.prompt: Prove that 0.999... (nines forever) equals 1.
rubric: Computes 10x = 9.999....
Subtracts to get 9x = 9, since the repeating tails cancel.
Concludes x = 1.
questions.why: The subtraction removes the infinite tail exactly, which leaves a linear equation.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 6.4, Repeating Decimals, p. 267

questions.prompt: If a ratio of red to blue is a:b, what fraction of the total is red?
questions.why: The ratio splits the whole into a+b equal parts, and a of them are red.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 7.1, What is a Ratio?, p. 281

questions.prompt: How do you convert units with a conversion factor?
questions.back: Multiply by a fraction equal to 1, such as (12 inches)/(1 foot), arranged so the unwanted unit cancels.
questions.why: Multiplying by 1 does not change the quantity, only the unit it is written in.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 7.4, Conversions, p. 296

questions.prompt: How do you find the average speed of a whole trip?
questions.back: Total distance divided by total time. It is not the average of the speeds in general.
questions.why: Speed is a rate, and averaging rates must weight each by the time spent at it.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 7.5, Speed, p. 302

questions.prompt: What does p percent mean?
questions.back: p/100. So p percent of x is (p/100)x.
questions.why: Percent means per hundred.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 8.1, What is a Percent?, p. 320

questions.prompt: A price rises by p percent and then falls by p percent. What is the net change?
questions.back: The price is multiplied by (1+p/100)(1-p/100) = 1-(p/100)^2, a net decrease.
questions.why: Successive percent changes multiply, and the decrease applies to the larger price.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 8.3, Percent Increase and Decrease, p. 337

items.title: Alcumus, Prealgebra: Integer Square Roots and Non-integer Square Roots
items.minutesBasis: 10 minutes a topic, proposed
items.what: In the Prealgebra course, work Integer Square Roots and Non-integer Square Roots until each shows mastered on your progress report. A topic you mastered earlier counts. Tick this when all 2 are mastered.

questions.prompt: State the product rule for square roots.
questions.back: sqrt(a) * sqrt(b) = sqrt(ab) for nonnegative a and b.
questions.why: Both sides are nonnegative and both square to ab.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 9.3, Arithmetic with Square Roots, p. 363

questions.prompt: How do you put sqrt(n) in simplest radical form?
questions.back: Write n = k^2 m with m having no square factor greater than 1. Then sqrt(n) = k sqrt(m).
questions.why: The product rule splits off the perfect square factor.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 9.2, Square Roots of Non-square Integers, p. 358

questions.prompt: Prove that sqrt(2) is irrational.
rubric: Assumes sqrt(2) = p/q with integers p, q in lowest terms.
Squares to get p^2 = 2q^2, so p^2 is even and therefore p is even.
Writes p = 2r to get q^2 = 2r^2, so q is even.
Concludes p and q share the factor 2, contradicting lowest terms.
questions.why: The contradiction comes from both p and q being even.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 9.2, Square Roots of Non-square Integers, p. 358

items.title: Alcumus, Prealgebra: Angle Basics, Parallel Lines and Triangles, and Angles in a Polygon
items.minutesBasis: 10 minutes a topic, proposed

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the interior angles of a convex polygon with n sides?
questions.back: (n-2) * 180 degrees.
questions.why: Diagonals from one vertex cut the polygon into n-2 triangles, each with angle sum 180 degrees.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 10.3, Angles in Polygons, p. 397

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the exterior angles of a convex polygon, one at each vertex?
questions.back: 360 degrees, for every number of sides.
questions.why: Walking around the polygon you turn through one full rotation.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 10.3, Angles in Polygons, p. 397

questions.prompt: A line crosses two parallel lines. Which angle pairs are equal and which are supplementary?
questions.back: Corresponding angles and alternate interior angles are equal. Same-side interior angles are supplementary.
questions.why: These are the angle facts that characterize parallel lines.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 10.2, Parallel Lines, p. 392

questions.prompt: Prove that the angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees.
rubric: Draws the line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side.
Identifies two pairs of alternate interior angles that are equal.
Notes the three angles at that vertex form a straight angle of 180 degrees.
Concludes the triangle's three angles sum to 180 degrees.
questions.why: The parallel line moves the two far angles to the vertex, where all three lie along a line.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 10.3, Angles in Polygons, p. 397

questions.prompt: Give the area formulas for a triangle and a trapezoid.
questions.back: Triangle: bh/2. Trapezoid: h(b1+b2)/2, where b1 and b2 are the parallel sides.
questions.why: A triangle is half a parallelogram. A trapezoid splits into two triangles of height h.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 11.2, Area, p. 422

questions.prompt: Give the circumference and area of a circle of radius r.
questions.back: Circumference 2 pi r. Area pi r^2.
questions.why: Pi is defined as circumference over diameter, and the area formula follows from slicing the disk.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 11.3, Circles, p. 432
