items.title: Alcumus, Prealgebra: The Pythagorean Theorem, Special Right Triangles, and Quadrilaterals
items.minutesBasis: 10 minutes a topic, proposed
items.what: In the Prealgebra course, work The Pythagorean Theorem, Special Right Triangles, and Quadrilaterals until each shows mastered on your progress report. A topic you mastered earlier counts. Tick this when all 3 are mastered.

questions.prompt: State the Pythagorean theorem.
questions.back: In a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c, a^2+b^2 = c^2.
questions.why: It is the defining relation of right triangles and its converse also holds.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 12.1, The Pythagorean Theorem, p. 442

questions.prompt: Give the side ratios of a 45-45-90 triangle and a 30-60-90 triangle.
questions.back: 45-45-90: 1 : 1 : sqrt(2). 30-60-90: 1 : sqrt(3) : 2, with the short leg opposite 30 degrees.
questions.why: The first is half a square. The second is half an equilateral triangle.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 12.2, Some Special Triangles, p. 451

questions.prompt: Is every square a rectangle and a rhombus?
questions.back: Yes. A square has four right angles, which makes it a rectangle, and four equal sides, which makes it a rhombus.
questions.why: Each quadrilateral type is defined by a property, and a square has both.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 12.3, Types of Quadrilaterals, p. 457

questions.prompt: Prove the Pythagorean theorem by rearranging four copies of a right triangle in a square of side a+b.
rubric: Places four copies of the triangle with legs a, b inside a square of side a+b, leaving a tilted square of side c.
Explains why the inner figure is a square: its angles are 180 degrees minus the two acute angles, which is 90 degrees.
Equates areas: (a+b)^2 = 4(ab/2) + c^2.
Expands and simplifies to a^2+b^2 = c^2.
questions.why: The two ways of counting the big square's area give the identity.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 12.1, The Pythagorean Theorem, p. 442

questions.prompt: Define the mean, median, and mode of a list of numbers.
questions.back: Mean: the sum divided by the count. Median: the middle value when sorted, or the mean of the two middle values. Mode: the most frequent value.
questions.why: These are the three basic measures of center.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 13.1, Basic Statistics, p. 476

questions.prompt: Which measure of center is pulled by one extreme value, the mean or the median?
questions.back: The mean. The median does not move when the largest value grows.
questions.why: The mean uses every value's size, while the median uses only the order.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 13.2, Limits of Basic Statistics, p. 486

questions.prompt: How many integers are there from a to b inclusive?
questions.why: Subtract a-1 from each to get the list 1 to b-a+1.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 14.1, Counting with Addition and Subtraction, p. 510

questions.prompt: State the multiplication principle.
questions.back: If one choice can be made in m ways and then a second in n ways regardless of the first, the pair can be made in mn ways.
questions.why: Each of the m first choices pairs with each of the n second choices.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 14.2, The Multiplication Principle, p. 519

questions.prompt: How many unordered pairs can be chosen from n items?
questions.why: There are n(n-1) ordered pairs, and each unordered pair is counted twice.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 14.4, Counting Pairs, p. 530

questions.prompt: When does working backwards help?
questions.back: When the problem gives the final result of a sequence of steps and asks for the start. Undo each step in reverse order.
questions.why: Each step has an inverse, so the start is the end with every step undone.

ref.label: Prealgebra, section 15.4, Work Backwards, p. 560

questions.why: Small cases suggest a rule but do not prove it.

questions.prompt: What does factoring an expression such as 6x+9 mean?
questions.back: Writing it as a product: 6x+9 = 3(2x+3). Factoring is the distributive property in reverse.
questions.why: Distribution multiplies out a factor and factoring pulls a common factor back out.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 2.3, Distribution, Subtraction, and Factoring, p. 62

questions.prompt: What is the goal of each step when solving a one-variable linear equation?
questions.back: Isolate the variable by undoing operations in reverse order, doing the same to both sides.
questions.why: Inverse operations peel away what was done to the variable.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 3.1, Solving Linear Equations I, p. 77

questions.prompt: When an equation has the variable in a denominator, what must you check after solving?
questions.back: That no solution makes a denominator zero. Such a value is extraneous and must be rejected.
questions.why: Multiplying both sides by an expression that can be zero may add solutions that were not there.

questions.prompt: How do you solve a formula such as A = P(1+rt) for one variable, say r?

questions.back: Solve one equation for one variable, substitute that expression into the other equation, solve, then back substitute.
questions.why: Substitution reduces the number of variables by one.

questions.prompt: How many equations do you usually need to find the values of n unknowns?

questions.back: Both equal xy/100.

questions.prompt: The ratio a:b equals 3:5 and a+b = 40. How do you find a?

questions.why: A ratio fixes the parts up to one common multiplier.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that y is directly proportional to x?
questions.back: y = kx for a constant k. The ratio y/x is constant.
questions.why: Doubling x doubles y.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 7.1, Direct Proportion, p. 187

questions.prompt: What does it mean that y is inversely proportional to x?
questions.back: y = k/x for a constant k. The product xy is constant.
questions.why: Doubling x halves y.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 7.2, Inverse Proportion, p. 190

questions.prompt: Two workers can finish a job alone in a hours and b hours. How long together?
questions.back: ab/(a+b) hours, because their rates 1/a and 1/b add.
questions.why: Rates of work add, and time is the reciprocal of the combined rate.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 7.4, Rate Problems, p. 197

questions.prompt: Give the slope-intercept form of a line and the meaning of each constant.

questions.prompt: When graphing y < mx+b, how do you draw the boundary line and pick the side?
questions.back: Draw the line dashed because it is not included, and shade the side containing a test point that satisfies the inequality.
questions.why: A strict inequality excludes the boundary, and one test point decides the whole half-plane.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 9.4, Graphing Inequalities, p. 269

questions.prompt: Where does a linear expression ax+by reach its maximum over a bounded region cut out by linear inequalities?
questions.back: At a vertex of the region.
questions.why: The level lines of ax+by are parallel, and the last one that touches a polygon touches a corner.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 9.5, Optimization, p. 272

questions.prompt: How do you factor x^2+bx+c over the integers?
questions.back: Find integers r and s with r+s = b and rs = c. Then x^2+bx+c = (x+r)(x+s).
questions.why: Expanding (x+r)(x+s) gives x^2+(r+s)x+rs.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 10.2, Factoring Quadratics I, p. 293

questions.prompt: For ax^2+bx+c = 0 with roots r and s, what are r+s and rs?
questions.back: r+s = -b/a and rs = c/a.
questions.why: Expand a(x-r)(x-s) and match coefficients.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 10.4, Sums and Products of Roots of a Quadratic, p. 307

questions.prompt: Prove that the roots r and s of ax^2+bx+c = 0 (a not 0) satisfy r+s = -b/a and rs = c/a.
rubric: Writes ax^2+bx+c = a(x-r)(x-s).
Expands the right side to ax^2-a(r+s)x+ars.
Matches the x coefficients: b = -a(r+s).
Matches the constants: c = ars, and divides by a.
questions.why: Two polynomials equal for all x have equal coefficients.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 10.4, Sums and Products of Roots of a Quadratic, p. 307

questions.prompt: Expand (a+b)^2 and (a-b)^2.
questions.why: Distribute and combine the two equal cross terms.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 11.1, Squares of Binomials, p. 324

questions.prompt: Factor a^3+b^3 and a^3-b^3.
questions.why: Multiplying out each right side cancels the middle terms.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 11.3, Sum and Difference of Cubes, p. 339

questions.prompt: State Simon's Favorite Factoring Trick for xy+ax+by.
questions.back: xy+ax+by+ab = (x+b)(y+a), so add ab to both sides of an equation like xy+ax+by = c.
questions.why: Completing the product turns a two-variable equation into a factored one, which suits integer solutions.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 11.5, Simon’s Favorite Factoring Trick, p. 348

questions.prompt: How do you rationalize the denominator of 1/(a+sqrt(b))?
questions.back: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate a-sqrt(b). The denominator becomes a^2-b.
questions.why: The difference of squares removes the square root.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 11.4, Rationalizing Denominators, p. 344

questions.prompt: What are i^1, i^2, i^3, i^4, and how do higher powers behave?

questions.why: i^4 = (i^2)^2 = 1, so every fourth power returns to 1.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 12.2, Imaginary Numbers, p. 358

questions.prompt: What is (a+bi)(a-bi)?

questions.prompt: Complete the square in x^2+bx.
questions.why: Expanding (x+b/2)^2 gives x^2+bx+b^2/4.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 13.2, Completing the Square, p. 379

questions.prompt: State the quadratic formula and the role of the discriminant.
questions.back: x = (-b ± sqrt(b^2-4ac))/(2a). The discriminant b^2-4ac is positive for two real roots, zero for one, negative for two nonreal roots.
questions.why: The formula is the result of completing the square, and the sign under the root decides whether a real root exists.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 13.3, The Quadratic Formula, p. 385

questions.prompt: Derive the quadratic formula from ax^2+bx+c = 0 with a not 0.
rubric: Divides by a to get x^2+(b/a)x+c/a = 0.
Completes the square: (x+b/(2a))^2 = (b^2-4ac)/(4a^2).
Takes square roots with both signs.
Solves for x to get x = (-b ± sqrt(b^2-4ac))/(2a).
questions.why: Completing the square turns the quadratic into a square equal to a constant.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 13.3, The Quadratic Formula, p. 385

questions.prompt: How do you solve a quadratic inequality such as (x-1)(x-4) < 0?
questions.back: Find the roots, split the number line there, and test the sign on each interval. Here the answer is 1 < x < 4.
questions.why: A product changes sign only where a factor is zero.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 15.1, Quadratic Inequalities, p. 425

questions.prompt: State the trivial inequality.
questions.back: x^2 ≥ 0 for every real x, with equality only at x = 0.
questions.why: A square of a real number is never negative.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 15.3, The Trivial Inequality, p. 435

questions.prompt: Prove that (a+b)/2 ≥ sqrt(ab) for nonnegative a and b, and say when equality holds.
rubric: Applies the trivial inequality to sqrt(a)-sqrt(b).
Expands (sqrt(a)-sqrt(b))^2 ≥ 0 to a+b-2sqrt(ab) ≥ 0.
Rearranges to (a+b)/2 ≥ sqrt(ab).
States equality holds exactly when a = b.
questions.why: The two-variable AM-GM inequality is the trivial inequality in disguise.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 15.3, The Trivial Inequality, p. 435

questions.prompt: What is the minimum value of ax^2+bx+c when a > 0?
questions.back: c-b^2/(4a), reached at x = -b/(2a).
questions.why: The square term in the completed-square form is at least 0.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 15.4, Quadratic Optimization, p. 439

questions.prompt: What makes a relation a function?
questions.back: Each input has exactly one output.
questions.why: A function is a rule that assigns one output to every input in its domain.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 16.1, The Machine, p. 451

questions.prompt: What is the composition f(g(x)), and is it the same as g(f(x))?
questions.back: Apply g first, then f. It is usually different from g(f(x)).
questions.why: Order matters: with f(x) = x+1 and g(x) = 2x, f(g(x)) = 2x+1 but g(f(x)) = 2x+2.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 16.3, Composition, p. 464

questions.prompt: What does the inverse function f^(-1) do?
questions.back: It undoes f: f^(-1)(f(x)) = x and f(f^(-1)(y)) = y.
questions.why: An inverse exists only when f never sends two inputs to the same output.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 16.4, Inverse Functions, p. 467

questions.prompt: How is the graph of y = f(x-h)+k related to the graph of y = f(x)?
questions.back: Shifted h units right and k units up.
questions.why: The point (x, y) on y = f(x) moves to (x+h, y+k).

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 17.2, Transformations, p. 491

questions.prompt: How do the graphs of y = f(-x) and y = -f(x) relate to y = f(x)?
questions.back: y = f(-x) is the reflection over the y-axis. y = -f(x) is the reflection over the x-axis.
questions.why: Negating the input flips left and right, negating the output flips up and down.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 17.2, Transformations, p. 491

questions.prompt: How is the graph of f^(-1) related to the graph of f?
questions.back: It is the reflection over the line y = x.
questions.why: If (a, b) is on f then (b, a) is on f^(-1).

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 17.3, Inverse Functions Revisited, p. 502

questions.prompt: What is the degree of the product of a degree m polynomial and a degree n polynomial?
questions.back: m+n.
questions.why: The leading terms multiply to a nonzero term of degree m+n, and no other product reaches that degree.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 18.2, Multiplication, p. 516

questions.prompt: What can you say about the degree of the sum of two polynomials?
questions.back: It is at most the larger of the two degrees, and it can be smaller when the leading terms cancel.
questions.why: Adding never creates a higher power.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 18.1, Addition and Subtraction, p. 513

questions.prompt: Define log_b(a).
questions.back: The exponent c with b^c = a, for b > 0, b not 1, and a > 0.
questions.why: A logarithm answers what power of the base gives the number.

questions.prompt: Define the floor of x and give the inequality it satisfies.
questions.back: The floor of x is the greatest integer at most x. It satisfies x-1 < floor(x) ≤ x.
questions.why: The nearest integer at or below x is less than 1 away from x.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 20.3, Floor and Ceiling, p. 569

questions.prompt: Write |x| as a piecewise function.
questions.back: |x| = x if x ≥ 0, and |x| = -x if x < 0.
questions.why: Absolute value is distance from 0, which is never negative.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 20.2, Absolute Value, p. 562

questions.prompt: Where does a rational function p(x)/q(x) in lowest terms have vertical asymptotes?
questions.back: At the zeros of q(x).
questions.why: Near such a point the denominator approaches 0 while the numerator does not.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 20.4, Rational Functions, p. 573

items.minutesBasis: 10 minutes a topic, proposed

questions.prompt: What is the sum of an arithmetic series?
questions.back: The number of terms times the average of the first and last terms: n(a1+an)/2.
questions.why: Pairing the first and last, second and second to last, and so on gives equal sums.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 21.2, Arithmetic Series, p. 594

questions.prompt: Give the sum of a finite and an infinite geometric series with first term a and ratio r.
questions.back: Finite, n terms: a(1-r^n)/(1-r) for r not 1. Infinite: a/(1-r) when |r| < 1.
questions.why: Multiplying the sum by r shifts it by one term, so subtracting cancels all but two terms.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 21.4, Geometric Series, p. 605

questions.prompt: Write 1/(k(k+1)) as a difference that telescopes.
questions.why: Over a common denominator, 1/k-1/(k+1) = 1/(k(k+1)). Summing cancels every middle term.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 21.5, Telescoping, p. 617

questions.prompt: Prove that a+ar+...+ar^(n-1) = a(1-r^n)/(1-r) for r not 1.
rubric: Names the sum S.
Writes rS = ar+ar^2+...+ar^n.
Subtracts to get S-rS = a-ar^n, since the middle terms cancel.
Divides by 1-r, which is not 0.
questions.why: Multiplying by r shifts the series one place, so the difference has only two terms.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 21.4, Geometric Series, p. 605

questions.prompt: What is the risk in squaring both sides of an equation, and what must you do?
questions.back: Squaring can add extraneous solutions, because a = -b also gives a^2 = b^2. Check every candidate in the original equation.
questions.why: Squaring is not reversible, so it can enlarge the solution set.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 22.1, Raising Equations to Powers, p. 628

questions.prompt: How do you evaluate an infinite expression such as sqrt(2+sqrt(2+sqrt(2+...)))?
questions.back: Call it x. The expression contains itself, so x = sqrt(2+x). Then x^2 = x+2 and x = 2, the positive root.
questions.why: Self-similarity turns an infinite expression into a finite equation, once you know the value exists.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 22.2, Self-similarity, p. 631

questions.prompt: If x+1/x = t, what is x^2+1/x^2?
questions.why: Squaring gives x^2+2+1/x^2 = t^2.

ref.label: Introduction to Algebra, section 22.3, Symmetry, p. 635

questions.prompt: How many elements are in the union of sets A and B?
questions.why: Elements in both sets are counted twice by |A|+|B|, so subtract them once.

questions.prompt: How many ways can n distinct objects be arranged in a row? How many ways can k of them be arranged in a row?
questions.back: n factorial. For k of them, n(n-1)(n-2)...(n-k+1).
questions.why: There are n choices for the first place, n-1 for the second, and so on.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 1.5, Permutations, p. 19

questions.prompt: What is complementary counting and when does it help?
questions.back: Count what you do not want and subtract from the total. It helps when the condition says "at least one" or the bad cases are fewer.
questions.why: The wanted and unwanted cases split the total with no overlap.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 2.3, Complementary Counting, p. 35

questions.prompt: In a counting problem with restrictions, which choice should you make first?
questions.back: The most restricted one.
questions.why: Choosing it first keeps the later choice counts independent of earlier ones.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 2.5, Counting with Restrictions, p. 41

questions.prompt: How many distinct arrangements does a word have with n letters, where one letter repeats a times and another b times?
questions.back: n factorial divided by (a factorial times b factorial), with one more factorial in the denominator for each repeated letter.
questions.why: Each distinct word is counted a factorial times b factorial times if the copies are treated as different.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 3.2, Permutations with Repeated Elements, p. 49

questions.prompt: How many ways can n distinct people sit around a round table, when rotations count as the same?
questions.back: (n-1) factorial. If reflections also count as the same, half that.
questions.why: Each seating is counted n times among the n factorial row arrangements, once per rotation.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 3.4, Counting with Symmetries, p. 57

questions.prompt: Give the formula for C(n, k), the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set.
questions.back: n factorial divided by (k factorial times (n-k) factorial).
questions.why: Ordered selections number n factorial/(n-k) factorial, and each subset appears k factorial times.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 4.3, How to Compute Combinations, p. 69

questions.prompt: Why does C(n, k) = C(n, n-k)?
questions.back: Choosing the k items to take is the same as choosing the n-k items to leave.
questions.why: The map from a subset to its complement is a one-to-one correspondence.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 4.4, Our First Combinatorial Identity, p. 72

questions.prompt: Give a counting proof that C(n, k) = C(n, n-k).
rubric: Interprets C(n, k) as the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set.
Pairs each k-element subset with its complement, which has n-k elements.
Shows the pairing is one-to-one and covers every (n-k)-element subset.
Concludes the two counts are equal.
questions.why: A one-to-one correspondence between two sets proves they have the same size.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 4.4, Our First Combinatorial Identity, p. 72

questions.prompt: When is probability the number of successful outcomes over the number of outcomes?
questions.back: Only when every outcome is equally likely.
questions.why: With two dice, the sums 2 to 12 are not equally likely, so you count the 36 ordered rolls instead.

questions.prompt: How do counting techniques enter probability problems?
questions.back: Count the successful outcomes and the total outcomes in the same equally likely sample space, then divide.
questions.why: Both counts must treat outcomes the same way, ordered or unordered.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 8.3, Complementary Probabilities, p. 128

questions.prompt: When do you multiply probabilities?
questions.back: For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A)P(B). For dependent events, multiply P(A) by the probability of B given that A happened.
questions.why: The second factor is the fraction of the A outcomes in which B also happens.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 8.4, Probability and Multiplication, p. 130

questions.prompt: When can you add probabilities?
questions.back: When the events cannot happen together. Then P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B).
questions.why: Overlapping events would be counted twice, as in the union rule for sets.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 8.2, Probability and Addition, p. 123

questions.why: Swapping the players shows the two "larger" events have equal probability, and with a tie they cover everything.

questions.prompt: How do you compute a probability when a point is chosen at random on a segment?
questions.back: Divide the length of the successful part by the total length.
questions.why: A uniform choice makes probability proportional to length.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 10.2, Probability Using Lengths, p. 154

questions.prompt: Two numbers are chosen independently and uniformly from intervals. How do you find a probability about them?
questions.back: Plot the pair as a point in a rectangle and divide the area of the successful region by the area of the rectangle.
questions.why: Independent uniform choices give a uniform point in the rectangle.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 10.3, Probability Using Areas, p. 156

questions.prompt: Define the expected value of a random quantity with values x1, ..., xn.
questions.back: The sum of each value times its probability: p1 x1 + ... + pn xn.
questions.why: It is the long run average of the quantity over many trials.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 11.2, Definition of Expected Value, p. 166

questions.prompt: Must the expected value be one of the possible outcomes?
questions.back: No. A fair die has expected value 3.5.
questions.why: Expected value is a weighted average, and an average need not be a data value.

questions.prompt: State Pascal's identity.
questions.why: A k-subset of {1, ..., n} either contains n or does not.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 12.2, Constructing Pascal’s Triangle, p. 176

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the entries in row n of Pascal's triangle?
questions.why: The entries count the subsets of an n-element set by size, and there are 2^n subsets.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, chapter 12, Pascal’s Triangle, pp. 175 to 190

questions.prompt: Give a counting proof that C(n, 0)+C(n, 1)+...+C(n, n) = 2^n.
rubric: Counts the subsets of an n-element set in two ways.
First way: each element is in or out, giving 2^n.
Second way: sorts subsets by size k, giving C(n, k) for each k.
Equates the two counts.
questions.why: Counting one set two ways is the standard combinatorial proof.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, chapter 12, Pascal’s Triangle, pp. 175 to 190

questions.prompt: State the hockey stick identity.
questions.why: The terms lie along a diagonal of Pascal's triangle and the sum lies just below the last one, like a hockey stick.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 13.5, The Identity, p. 199

questions.prompt: Prove the hockey stick identity by induction on n using Pascal's identity.
rubric: Checks the base case n = r: C(r, r) = 1 = C(r+1, r+1).
Assumes the sum up to C(n, r) is C(n+1, r+1).
Adds C(n+1, r) to both sides.
Applies Pascal's identity: C(n+1, r+1)+C(n+1, r) = C(n+2, r+1).
questions.why: Each new term merges with the running total by Pascal's identity.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 13.5, The Identity, p. 199

questions.prompt: State the binomial theorem.
questions.back: (x+y)^n is the sum over k from 0 to n of C(n, k) x^(n-k) y^k.
questions.why: Each term picks y from k of the n factors and x from the rest.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 14.3, The Theorem, p. 211

questions.prompt: How do you find the sum of the coefficients of a polynomial such as (2x-1)^7?
questions.back: Substitute x = 1. Here the sum is 1.
questions.why: At x = 1 every power of x is 1, so only the coefficients remain.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 14.4, Applications of the Binomial Theorem, p. 213

questions.prompt: Explain why the coefficient of x^(n-k) y^k in (x+y)^n is C(n, k).
rubric: Writes (x+y)^n as a product of n factors.
Notes each term of the expansion picks x or y from each factor.
Shows a term equals x^(n-k) y^k exactly when y is picked from k factors.
Counts the ways to choose those k factors as C(n, k).
questions.why: The coefficient counts the choices that produce the term.

ref.label: Introduction to Counting & Probability, section 14.3, The Theorem, p. 211

questions.prompt: What does a | b mean?
questions.back: a divides b: there is an integer k with b = ak.
questions.why: Divisibility is defined by an integer multiple, not by a decimal division.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 1.4, Divisibility of Integers, p. 11

questions.prompt: If a | b and a | c, what else does a divide?
questions.back: Every combination bx+cy with integers x and y.
questions.why: If b = am and c = an then bx+cy = a(mx+ny).

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 1.6, Using Divisors, p. 18

questions.prompt: Prove that if a | b and a | c, then a | (bx+cy) for all integers x and y.
rubric: Writes b = am and c = an for integers m and n.
Substitutes to get bx+cy = amx+any.
Factors to a(mx+ny).
Notes mx+ny is an integer, so a divides bx+cy.
questions.why: The definition of divisibility turns the claim into factoring.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 1.6, Using Divisors, p. 18

questions.prompt: To test whether n is prime, which divisors must you try?
questions.back: The primes up to sqrt(n).
questions.why: If n = ab with 1 < a ≤ b, then a ≤ sqrt(n), and some prime factor of a is also at most sqrt(n).

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 2.3, Identifying Primes I, p. 28

questions.prompt: Is 1 prime, composite, or neither?
questions.back: Neither. A prime has exactly two positive divisors and 1 has one.
questions.why: Excluding 1 keeps prime factorization unique.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 2.2, Primes and Composites, p. 25

questions.prompt: Prove that a composite number n has a prime factor at most sqrt(n).
rubric: Writes n = ab with 1 < a ≤ b.
Shows a^2 ≤ ab = n, so a ≤ sqrt(n).
Takes a prime factor p of a, which divides n.
Concludes p ≤ a ≤ sqrt(n).
questions.why: The smaller factor of any factorization is at most the square root.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 2.3, Identifying Primes I, p. 28

questions.prompt: State the division algorithm for integers a and b > 0.
questions.back: There are unique integers q and r with a = bq+r and 0 ≤ r < b.
questions.why: r is the remainder and q the quotient.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 3.5, Remainders, p. 46

questions.prompt: State the step of the Euclidean algorithm.
questions.back: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, r), where r is the remainder of a on division by b. Repeat until the remainder is 0.
questions.why: Any common divisor of a and b divides r = a-bq, and any common divisor of b and r divides a.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 3.7, The Euclidean Algorithm, p. 53

questions.prompt: Prove that gcd(a, b) = gcd(a-b, b).
rubric: Shows every common divisor d of a and b divides a-b.
Shows every common divisor of a-b and b divides (a-b)+b = a.
Concludes the two pairs have the same common divisors.
Concludes they have the same greatest common divisor.
questions.why: Equal sets of common divisors have equal maxima.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 3.7, The Euclidean Algorithm, p. 53

questions.prompt: State the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.
questions.back: Every integer greater than 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way, up to the order of the factors.
questions.why: Unique factorization is what makes prime exponents useful for divisors, gcd, and lcm.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 4.2, Factor Trees, p. 64

questions.prompt: How are gcd(a, b) and lcm(a, b) related?
questions.back: gcd(a, b) * lcm(a, b) = ab for positive a and b.
questions.why: For each prime the gcd takes the smaller exponent and the lcm the larger, and the two add to the sum of exponents.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 4.7, Relationships Between LCMs and GCDs, p. 80

questions.prompt: How many positive divisors does p1^e1 p2^e2 ... pk^ek have?
questions.why: A divisor picks each prime exponent from 0 to ei independently.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 5.2, Counting Divisors, p. 91

questions.prompt: Which positive integers have an odd number of divisors?
questions.back: The perfect squares.
questions.why: Divisors pair as d and n/d, and only sqrt(n) pairs with itself.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 5.3, Divisor Counting Problems, p. 94

questions.prompt: What is the product of all positive divisors of n?
questions.back: n^(t/2), where t is the number of divisors.
questions.why: Pairing d with n/d gives t/2 pairs, each with product n.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 5.4, Divisor Products, p. 101

questions.prompt: Prove that the product of the positive divisors of n is n^(t/2), where t is the number of divisors.
rubric: Lets P be the product and lists the divisors d.
Notes n/d runs over the same divisors as d does.
Multiplies the two expressions for P to get P^2 = n^t.
Takes the positive square root: P = n^(t/2).
questions.why: Multiplying the product by itself in reversed order pairs every d with n/d, which also handles perfect squares.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 5.4, Divisor Products, p. 101

questions.prompt: How many times does a prime p divide n factorial?
questions.back: floor(n/p)+floor(n/p^2)+floor(n/p^3)+..., which is Legendre's formula.
questions.why: floor(n/p^k) counts the multiples of p^k up to n, and each counts one more factor of p.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 6.3, Factorials, Exponents and Divisibility, p. 111

questions.prompt: Define a perfect number.
questions.back: A positive integer equal to the sum of its divisors other than itself, such as 6 and 28.
questions.why: Abundant numbers exceed that sum and deficient numbers fall short of it.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 6.4, Perfect, Abundant, and Deficient Numbers, p. 115

questions.prompt: Why must p be prime for 2^p-1 to be prime?
questions.back: If p = ab with a, b > 1, then 2^a-1 divides 2^p-1.
questions.why: x-1 divides x^b-1, and setting x = 2^a gives the factor.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 6.2, Some Special Primes, p. 109

questions.prompt: What does the base b numeral (d_k ... d_1 d_0) mean?
questions.back: d_k b^k + ... + d_1 b + d_0, with each digit from 0 to b-1.
questions.why: Each place counts a bundle of the next power of b.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 8.3, Base Numbers, p. 145

questions.prompt: How do you convert a positive integer to base b?
questions.back: Divide by b repeatedly. The remainders, read from last to first, are the digits.
questions.why: Each remainder is the next lowest digit, and the quotient holds the higher digits.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 8.5, Converting Integers Between Bases, p. 150

questions.why: b units in one place make one unit of the next place.

questions.prompt: How can you test divisibility by b-1 for a number written in base b?
questions.back: Add its base b digits. The number is divisible by b-1 exactly when the digit sum is.
questions.why: b leaves remainder 1 on division by b-1, so every power of b does too.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 9.5, Base Number Division and Divisibility, p. 172

questions.prompt: What determines the units digit of a product or a power?
questions.back: Only the units digits of the factors. The units digits of powers of a number repeat in a cycle of length 1, 2, or 4.
questions.why: The units digit is the remainder mod 10, and remainders multiply.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 10.2, Units Digits in Arithmetic, p. 177

questions.prompt: What is the units digit of n written in base b?
questions.back: The remainder of n on division by b.
questions.why: Every other digit stands for a multiple of b.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 10.3, Base Number Units Digits, p. 184

questions.prompt: Which fractions in lowest terms have terminating decimals?
questions.back: Those with denominator 2^a 5^c.
questions.why: Only such a denominator divides a power of 10.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 11.2, Terminating Decimals, p. 195

questions.prompt: Write 0.(abc) repeating as a fraction.
questions.back: abc/999, where abc is the three digit block.
questions.why: Multiplying by 1000 shifts one period, and subtracting leaves 999x = abc.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 11.4, Converting Decimals to Fractions, p. 205

questions.prompt: Define a ≡ b (mod m).
questions.back: m divides a-b. Equivalently, a and b leave the same remainder on division by m.
questions.why: Congruence groups the integers by remainder.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 12.2, Congruence, p. 218

questions.prompt: If a ≡ b and c ≡ d (mod m), what can you say about a+c, ac, and a^k?
questions.back: a+c ≡ b+d, ac ≡ bd, and a^k ≡ b^k (mod m) for positive integers k.
questions.why: Congruences can be added, multiplied, and raised to powers like equations.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 12.5, Multiplication and Exponentiation, p. 232

questions.prompt: Prove that if a ≡ b and c ≡ d (mod m), then ac ≡ bd (mod m).
rubric: Writes a = b+mx and c = d+my.
Expands ac = bd+m(by+dx+mxy).
Concludes m divides ac-bd.
questions.why: The difference ac-bd is a multiple of m once both differences are.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 12.5, Multiplication and Exponentiation, p. 232

questions.prompt: State the divisibility test for 11.
questions.back: Take the alternating sum of the digits from the right. The number is divisible by 11 exactly when that sum is.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 13.2, Divisibility Rules, p. 247

questions.prompt: Prove that a number is congruent to its digit sum mod 9.
rubric: Writes the number as the sum of d_k 10^k.
Notes 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9), so 10^k ≡ 1 (mod 9).
Concludes the sum is congruent to the sum of d_k mod 9.
questions.why: Powers of 10 vanish from the expression mod 9, leaving the digits.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 13.3, Divisibility Rules With Algebra, p. 255

questions.prompt: When does a have an inverse mod m?
questions.back: Exactly when gcd(a, m) = 1.
questions.why: An inverse x needs ax-1 to be a multiple of m, which has a solution only when a and m share no factor.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 14.2, Modular Inverses and Simple Linear Congruences, p. 262

questions.prompt: When does ax ≡ b (mod m) have a solution?
questions.back: Exactly when gcd(a, m) divides b. Then there are gcd(a, m) solutions mod m.
questions.why: ax-my = b has integer solutions exactly when gcd(a, m) divides b.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 14.3, Solving Linear Congruences, p. 267

questions.prompt: What does the Chinese Remainder Theorem say about x ≡ a (mod m), x ≡ b (mod n)?
questions.back: If gcd(m, n) = 1, there is exactly one solution mod mn.
questions.why: Coprime moduli give independent conditions, and the mn residues match the m times n pairs of remainders.

ref.label: Introduction to Number Theory, section 14.4, Systems of Linear Congruences, p. 272

questions.prompt: What do collinear and coplanar mean?
questions.back: Collinear points lie on one line. Coplanar points lie in one plane.
questions.why: Two points are always collinear and three points are always coplanar.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 1.2, Points, Lines, and Planes, p. 2

questions.prompt: What may a geometric proof use?
questions.back: Definitions, given facts, accepted postulates, and theorems already proved. A diagram may suggest but cannot prove.
questions.why: A figure can mislead, so each step must follow from what is known.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 1.5, The Burden of Proof, p. 10

questions.prompt: What is true of vertical angles?
questions.back: They are equal.
questions.why: Each is supplementary to the same adjacent angle.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 2.3, Straight and Vertical Angles, p. 21

questions.prompt: How is an exterior angle of a triangle related to the interior angles?
questions.back: It equals the sum of the two interior angles not adjacent to it.
questions.why: Both the exterior angle and that sum equal 180 degrees minus the adjacent interior angle.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 2.6, Exterior Angles, p. 36

questions.prompt: Prove that an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
rubric: Names the triangle ABC and the exterior angle at C, formed by extending BC past C.
Notes the exterior angle and angle C are supplementary.
Uses angle A + angle B + angle C = 180 degrees.
Subtracts to get the exterior angle equal to angle A + angle B.
questions.why: Both quantities equal 180 degrees minus angle C.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 2.6, Exterior Angles, p. 36

questions.prompt: Which side and angle conditions prove two triangles congruent, and which one does not?
questions.back: SSS, SAS, ASA, and AAS prove congruence. SSA does not, except when the angle is right (HL).
questions.why: Two sides and a non-included acute angle can fit two different triangles.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 3.5, SSA Not-Necessarily Congruence, p. 63

questions.prompt: What is true of the base angles of an isosceles triangle?
questions.back: They are equal. The converse also holds: equal angles face equal sides.
questions.why: The triangle is congruent to its own reflection across the bisector of the apex angle.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 3.6, Isosceles and Equilateral Triangles, p. 65

questions.prompt: Prove that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
rubric: Names triangle ABC with AB = AC.
Lets M be the midpoint of BC and draws AM.
Shows triangles ABM and ACM are congruent by SSS.
Concludes angle B = angle C as corresponding parts.
questions.why: The median to the base splits the triangle into two congruent halves.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 3.6, Isosceles and Equilateral Triangles, p. 65

questions.prompt: Two triangles share a base and have equal altitudes to it. What do you know?
questions.back: They have equal area.
questions.why: Area is half base times height, and both factors match.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 4.3, Same Base/Same Altitude, p. 88

questions.prompt: In triangles with the same altitude, how do areas compare?
questions.back: Their areas are in the ratio of their bases.
questions.why: With the height fixed, area is proportional to base.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 4.3, Same Base/Same Altitude, p. 88

questions.prompt: Prove that a median divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area.
rubric: Names the median AM of triangle ABC, with M the midpoint of BC.
Notes triangles ABM and ACM have the same altitude from A.
Notes their bases BM and MC are equal.
Concludes their areas are equal.
questions.why: Equal bases and a shared altitude give equal areas.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 4.3, Same Base/Same Altitude, p. 88

questions.prompt: State the AA similarity test.
questions.back: Two triangles with two pairs of equal angles are similar.
questions.why: The third angles then match as well, and the angles fix the shape.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 5.2, AA Similarity, p. 101

questions.prompt: Two similar figures have side ratio k. What is the ratio of their areas?
questions.why: Area scales with the product of two lengths, each scaled by k.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, chapter 5, Similar Triangles, pp. 99 to 132

questions.prompt: Prove that the segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half as long.
rubric: Names triangle ABC with midpoints M of AB and N of AC.
Shows triangles AMN and ABC are similar by SAS similarity, with ratio 1/2 and the shared angle A.
Concludes MN = BC/2.
Uses equal corresponding angles AMN and ABC to conclude MN is parallel to BC.
questions.why: SAS similarity gives both the length ratio and the equal angles.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 5.3, SAS Similarity, p. 108

questions.back: For integers m > n > 0, the numbers m^2-n^2, 2mn, and m^2+n^2 form a triple.

questions.prompt: State Heron's formula.
questions.back: Area = sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)), where s = (a+b+c)/2.
questions.why: It gives a triangle's area from its three sides alone.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 6.5, Heron’s Formula, p. 156

questions.prompt: Name the right triangles with integer sides you should recognize at sight.
questions.why: Spotting a triple saves a square root computation.

questions.prompt: State the angle bisector theorem.
questions.back: The bisector of angle A meets BC at D with BD/DC = AB/AC.
questions.why: The triangles ABD and ACD have the same height from A, and their areas are in the ratio AB:AC.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 7.3, Angle Bisectors of a Triangle, p. 177

questions.prompt: How does the centroid divide each median?
questions.back: In the ratio 2:1, with the longer part from the vertex.
questions.why: The three medians meet at the centroid two thirds of the way from each vertex.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 7.4, Medians, p. 183

questions.prompt: Where do the perpendicular bisectors of a triangle meet, and what is special about the point?
questions.back: At the circumcenter, which is the same distance from all three vertices.
questions.why: Each perpendicular bisector is the set of points equidistant from two vertices.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 7.2, Perpendicular Bisectors of a Triangle, p. 173

questions.prompt: Give the area of a triangle in terms of its inradius r and semiperimeter s.
questions.back: Area = rs.
questions.why: The incenter splits the triangle into three triangles with heights r and bases the sides.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 7.3, Angle Bisectors of a Triangle, p. 177

questions.prompt: Prove that every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is the same distance from A and B.
rubric: Names the midpoint M of AB and a point P on the perpendicular bisector.
Notes AM = MB, PM is shared, and angles PMA and PMB are right.
Concludes triangles PMA and PMB are congruent by SAS.
Concludes PA = PB.
questions.why: SAS congruence matches the two distances.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 7.1, Bisectors, p. 170

questions.prompt: What is true of the diagonals of a parallelogram?
questions.back: They bisect each other.
questions.why: The two triangles formed at the crossing point are congruent by ASA.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 8.3, Parallelograms, p. 215

questions.prompt: What is special about the diagonals of a rhombus?
questions.back: They are perpendicular and bisect the angles. They also bisect each other, as in any parallelogram.
questions.why: Each diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other because the sides are equal.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 8.4, Rhombi, p. 219

questions.prompt: How long is the median of a trapezoid, the segment joining the midpoints of the legs?
questions.back: The average of the two bases.
questions.why: Splitting along a diagonal gives two triangle midsegments of half of each base.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 8.2, Trapezoids, p. 208

questions.prompt: Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
rubric: Names parallelogram ABCD with diagonals meeting at E.
Uses AB parallel to CD for equal alternate interior angles EAB = ECD and EBA = EDC.
Uses AB = CD, opposite sides of a parallelogram.
Concludes triangles ABE and CDE are congruent by ASA, so AE = CE and BE = DE.
questions.why: Parallel sides give the angles and opposite sides give the included side.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 8.3, Parallelograms, p. 215

questions.prompt: What is each interior angle of a regular n-gon?
questions.back: (n-2)180/n degrees.
questions.why: The angle sum (n-2)180 is shared equally among n angles.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 9.2, Angles in a Polygon, p. 246

questions.prompt: How many diagonals does a convex n-gon have?
questions.why: Each vertex joins to n-3 others by a diagonal, and each diagonal has two ends.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, chapter 9, Polygons, pp. 244 to 265

questions.prompt: Give the area of a regular polygon in terms of its apothem a and perimeter p.
questions.back: ap/2.
questions.why: Triangles from the center to each side have height a and bases summing to p.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 9.3, Polygon Area, p. 249

questions.prompt: State the triangle inequality.
questions.back: Each side of a triangle is less than the sum of the other two.
questions.why: The straight segment is the shortest path between its endpoints.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 10.3, The Triangle Inequality, p. 274

questions.prompt: How do the sides and angles of a triangle compare?
questions.back: The larger side is opposite the larger angle, and the larger angle is opposite the larger side.
questions.why: The order of the sides matches the order of the opposite angles.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 10.1, Sides and Angles of a Triangle, p. 266

questions.prompt: In a triangle with longest side c, how do you tell whether it is acute, right, or obtuse?
questions.back: Compare c^2 with a^2+b^2. Less means acute, equal means right, greater means obtuse.
questions.why: The angle opposite c grows as c grows with a and b fixed.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 10.2, Pythagoras: Not Just For Right Triangles?, p. 270

questions.prompt: State the inscribed angle theorem.
questions.back: An inscribed angle is half the central angle (the arc) it subtends. Inscribed angles on the same arc are equal.
questions.why: The central angle is the exterior angle of an isosceles triangle formed with the center.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 12.1, Inscribed Angles, p. 304

questions.prompt: Give the angle formed by two chords crossing inside a circle and by two secants meeting outside.
questions.back: Inside: half the sum of the intercepted arcs. Outside: half the difference of the intercepted arcs.
questions.why: Draw a chord to make an inscribed triangle and use the exterior angle theorem.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 12.2, Angles Inside and Outside Circles, p. 310

questions.prompt: State two facts about tangents to a circle.
questions.back: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency. The two tangent segments from an outside point are equal.
questions.why: The second follows from congruent right triangles sharing the segment to the center.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 12.3, Tangents, p. 316

questions.prompt: Prove the inscribed angle theorem when one side of the inscribed angle passes through the center.
rubric: Names inscribed angle ABC with BC a diameter through center O.
Notes OA = OB, so triangle OAB is isosceles with angle OAB = angle OBA.
Uses the exterior angle theorem: angle AOC = angle OAB + angle OBA = 2 angle ABC.
Concludes angle ABC is half the central angle AOC.
questions.why: The radius makes an isosceles triangle, and the central angle is its exterior angle.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 12.1, Inscribed Angles, p. 304

questions.prompt: State the power of a point theorem for two chords, two secants, and a tangent.
questions.back: Chords AB and CD through P: PA * PB = PC * PD. Secants from outside: the same product for each. Tangent PT: PT^2 = PA * PB.
questions.why: Each case comes from similar triangles made by inscribed angles.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 13.1, What is Power of a Point?, p. 340

questions.prompt: Prove that if chords AB and CD meet at P inside a circle, then PA * PB = PC * PD.
rubric: Draws AC and BD.
Notes angle CAB = angle CDB, inscribed on the same arc CB.
Notes angle APC = angle DPB as vertical angles.
Concludes triangles PAC and PDB are similar by AA, so PA/PD = PC/PB, and cross-multiplies.
questions.why: Inscribed angles and vertical angles give similar triangles.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 13.1, What is Power of a Point?, p. 340

questions.prompt: Give the volume of a prism and of a pyramid with base area B and height h.
questions.back: Prism: Bh. Pyramid: Bh/3.
questions.why: A cube splits into three congruent pyramids, which shows the factor 1/3 in one case.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 14.2, Prisms, p. 360

questions.prompt: How many regular polyhedra are there? Name them.
questions.back: Five: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.
questions.why: The face angles at a vertex must sum to less than 360 degrees, which leaves only five combinations.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 14.4, Regular Polyhedra, p. 370

questions.prompt: What is Euler's formula for a convex polyhedron?
questions.why: A cube has 8-12+6 = 2.

questions.prompt: Give the volume and lateral area of a cone with radius r, height h, and slant height l.
questions.back: Volume pi r^2 h/3. Lateral area pi r l.
questions.why: A cone is a pyramid with a circular base, and its unrolled side is a sector of radius l.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 15.2, Cones, p. 385

questions.prompt: Give the volume and surface area of a sphere of radius r.
questions.back: Volume 4 pi r^3/3. Surface area 4 pi r^2.
questions.why: These are Archimedes' results.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 15.3, Spheres, p. 390

questions.prompt: Give the volume and lateral area of a cylinder with radius r and height h.
questions.back: Volume pi r^2 h. Lateral area 2 pi r h.
questions.why: The side unrolls into a rectangle of width 2 pi r and height h.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 15.1, Cylinders, p. 380

questions.prompt: A dilation has scale factor k. How does it change lengths, areas, and volumes?
questions.back: Lengths by k, areas by k^2, volumes by k^3. Angles do not change.
questions.why: Each dimension scales by k.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 16.4, Dilation, p. 418

questions.prompt: How do you find the shortest path from A to a line and then to B, with A and B on the same side?
questions.back: Reflect B over the line to B'. The shortest path follows the straight segment from A to B'.
questions.why: Reflection keeps distance to the line, so every path equals a path from A to B', and the straight one is shortest.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 16.3, Reflections, p. 413

questions.prompt: Give the distance from (x0, y0) to the line ax+by+c = 0.
questions.back: |ax0+by0+c|/sqrt(a^2+b^2).
questions.why: The vector (a, b) is normal to the line, and the formula projects onto it.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 17.5, Distance Between a Point and a Line, p. 461

questions.prompt: Give the midpoint and the distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2).
questions.back: Midpoint ((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2). Distance sqrt((x2-x1)^2+(y2-y1)^2).
questions.why: The distance is the Pythagorean theorem on the horizontal and vertical legs.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 17.1, Lines, p. 437

questions.prompt: Using coordinates, prove that the midpoints of the sides of any quadrilateral form a parallelogram.
rubric: Assigns general coordinates A, B, C, D.
Computes the four midpoints.
Shows the vector from the AB midpoint to the BC midpoint is (C-A)/2.
Shows the vector from the DA midpoint to the CD midpoint is also (C-A)/2, so one pair of opposite sides is parallel and equal.
Concludes the figure is a parallelogram.
questions.why: A quadrilateral with one pair of opposite sides parallel and equal is a parallelogram.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 17.4, Proofs with Analytic Geometry, p. 452

questions.prompt: Define sine, cosine, and tangent of an acute angle in a right triangle.
questions.back: sin = opposite/hypotenuse. cos = adjacent/hypotenuse. tan = opposite/adjacent.
questions.why: Similar right triangles give the same ratios, so they depend only on the angle.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 18.1, Trigonometry and Right Triangles, p. 478

questions.prompt: State the law of sines and the law of cosines.
questions.back: Law of sines: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Law of cosines: c^2 = a^2+b^2-2ab cos C.
questions.why: The law of cosines extends the Pythagorean theorem, and both follow from dropping an altitude.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 18.3, Law of Sines and Law of Cosines, p. 494

questions.prompt: Give the area of a triangle from two sides and the included angle.
questions.back: ab sin(C)/2.
questions.why: The height to side a is b sin C.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 18.2, Not Just For Right Triangles, p. 488

questions.prompt: Name common extra lines to draw in a geometry problem.
questions.back: Radii to points of tangency or intersection, altitudes to make right triangles, a line parallel to a side to make similar triangles, and diagonals.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 19.1, The Extra Line, p. 505

questions.prompt: When does assigning a variable to a length or angle help?
questions.back: When several lengths depend on one unknown. Name it, express the others in terms of it, and find an equation.
questions.why: One unknown with one equation is often easier than chasing many values.

ref.label: Introduction to Geometry, section 19.2, Assigning Variables, p. 510

questions.prompt: What is a fast first move for a symmetric system such as x+y = a, y+z = b, z+x = c?
questions.back: Add all the equations: 2(x+y+z) = a+b+c. Then subtract each original equation from x+y+z.
questions.why: Symmetric systems often give a total in one step.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 1.4, Larger Systems of Linear Equations, p. 14

questions.prompt: When is substitution better than elimination?
questions.back: When one equation already gives a variable alone, or is easy to solve for one.
questions.why: Substitution then reduces the system without scaling equations.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 1.2, Substitution, p. 6

questions.prompt: When does a function have an inverse, and how do you test it on a graph?
questions.back: When it is one-to-one. The graph meets each horizontal line at most once.
questions.why: Two inputs with the same output would leave the inverse with two values.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 2.4, Inverse Functions, p. 43

questions.prompt: Define the domain and range of a function.
questions.back: The domain is the set of allowed inputs. The range is the set of outputs the function takes.
questions.why: Domain restrictions come from division by zero, even roots of negatives, and logs of nonpositive numbers.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 2.1, Function Basics, p. 24

questions.prompt: Give |z|^2 and the real part of z in terms of z and its conjugate.
questions.back: |z|^2 = z times conj(z). Re(z) = (z+conj(z))/2.
questions.why: With z = a+bi, z conj(z) = a^2+b^2 and z+conj(z) = 2a.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 3.3, Real and Imaginary Parts, p. 65

questions.prompt: What does |z-w| mean in the complex plane?
questions.back: The distance between the points z and w.
questions.why: It is the length of the vector from w to z.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 3.2, The Complex Plane, p. 61

questions.prompt: Prove that |zw| = |z||w| for complex z and w.
rubric: Uses |u|^2 = u conj(u).
Uses conj(zw) = conj(z) conj(w).
Computes |zw|^2 = zw conj(z) conj(w) = |z|^2 |w|^2.
Takes nonnegative square roots.
questions.why: Conjugation respects products, which turns the claim into algebra.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 3.3, Real and Imaginary Parts, p. 65

questions.prompt: What does the discriminant of ax^2+bx+c with real coefficients tell you?
questions.back: b^2-4ac > 0: two real roots. = 0: one double root. < 0: two nonreal conjugate roots.
questions.why: It is the quantity under the square root in the quadratic formula.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 4.4, The Discriminant, p. 96

questions.prompt: How do you find a quadratic with roots r and s?
questions.back: x^2-(r+s)x+rs, or any nonzero multiple of it.
questions.why: Expanding (x-r)(x-s) gives it, which is Vieta's formulas in reverse.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 4.2, Relating Roots and Coefficients, p. 84

questions.prompt: Give the focus and directrix of the parabola x^2 = 4py.
questions.back: Focus (0, p). Directrix y = -p.
questions.why: Points equidistant from (0, p) and the line y = -p satisfy x^2 = 4py.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 5.1, Parabolas, p. 107

questions.prompt: For the ellipse x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2 = 1 with a > b, give the foci and the defining property.
questions.back: Foci (±c, 0) with c^2 = a^2-b^2. The distances from any point to the two foci sum to 2a.
questions.why: At the end of the minor axis the two distances are equal, each a, which gives c^2 = a^2-b^2.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 5.5, Ellipses, p. 129

questions.prompt: For the hyperbola x^2/a^2-y^2/b^2 = 1, give the foci and the asymptotes.
questions.back: Foci (±c, 0) with c^2 = a^2+b^2. Asymptotes y = ±(b/a)x.
questions.why: For large |x|, the 1 becomes negligible and the curve approaches x^2/a^2 = y^2/b^2.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 5.6, Hyperbolas, p. 142

items.title: Alcumus, Intermediate Algebra: Polynomial Division Algorithms, Remainder and Factor Theorem, and Basic Polynomial Forms
items.minutesBasis: 15 minutes a topic, proposed

questions.prompt: State the division algorithm for polynomials.
questions.back: For polynomials f and g with g not 0, there are unique q and r with f = gq+r and deg r < deg g (or r = 0).
questions.why: Long division stops when the remainder's degree drops below the divisor's.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 6.2, Introduction to Polynomial Division, p. 166

questions.prompt: State the remainder theorem.
questions.back: The remainder when f(x) is divided by x-a is f(a).
questions.why: f(x) = (x-a)q(x)+r with r a constant, and x = a kills the first term.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 6.4, The Remainder Theorem, p. 185

questions.prompt: Prove the remainder theorem.
rubric: Divides f(x) by x-a to get f(x) = (x-a)q(x)+r.
Notes r has degree less than 1, so r is a constant.
Substitutes x = a to get f(a) = r.
questions.why: The divisor vanishes at a, so only the remainder survives.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 6.4, The Remainder Theorem, p. 185

items.minutesBasis: 15 minutes a topic, proposed
items.what: In the Intermediate Algebra course, work Integer / Rational Roots and Basic Polynomial Roots until each shows mastered on your progress report. A topic you mastered earlier counts. Tick this when all 2 are mastered.

questions.prompt: State the factor theorem.
questions.back: x-a divides f(x) exactly when f(a) = 0.
questions.why: It is the remainder theorem with remainder 0.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 7.1, The Factor Theorem, p. 193

questions.prompt: State the rational root theorem.
questions.back: If p/q in lowest terms is a root of a polynomial with integer coefficients, then p divides the constant term and q divides the leading coefficient.
questions.why: Clearing denominators and reducing mod p and mod q forces the divisibility.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 7.3, Rational Roots, p. 206

questions.prompt: State the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra.
questions.back: Every nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root. So a degree n polynomial has exactly n roots counted with multiplicity.
questions.why: Applying the factor theorem repeatedly splits it into n linear factors.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 7.5, Graphing and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, p. 215

questions.prompt: Prove the rational root theorem.
rubric: Substitutes x = p/q into a_n x^n+...+a_0 = 0 and multiplies by q^n.
Gets a_n p^n + a_(n-1) p^(n-1) q + ... + a_0 q^n = 0.
Notes every term except a_0 q^n is divisible by p, so p divides a_0 q^n, and gcd(p, q) = 1 gives p divides a_0.
Argues the same way with q: q divides a_n p^n, so q divides a_n.
questions.why: Clearing denominators makes all but one term divisible by p, and likewise by q.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 7.3, Rational Roots, p. 206

items.minutesBasis: 15 minutes a topic, proposed

questions.prompt: A polynomial with real coefficients has root 2+3i. What other root must it have?
questions.back: 2-3i. Nonreal roots of real polynomials come in conjugate pairs.
questions.why: Conjugating f(z) = 0 gives f(conj(z)) = 0 because the coefficients are real.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 8.2, Nonreal Roots, p. 239

questions.prompt: Give Vieta's formulas for the roots r, s, t of x^3+ax^2+bx+c.
questions.back: r+s+t = -a. rs+st+tr = b. rst = -c.
questions.why: Expand (x-r)(x-s)(x-t) and match coefficients.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 8.3, Vieta’s Formulas, p. 244

questions.prompt: A polynomial with rational coefficients has root 1+sqrt(2). What other root must it have?
questions.back: 1-sqrt(2).
questions.why: The minimal polynomial x^2-2x-1 of 1+sqrt(2) divides it, and that polynomial has both roots.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 8.1, Irrational Roots, p. 230

questions.why: Multiplying out telescopes to a^n-b^n.

questions.prompt: Factor a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc.
questions.back: (a+b+c)(a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca).
questions.why: The second factor is half the sum of (a-b)^2, (b-c)^2, and (c-a)^2, which gives AM-GM for three cubes.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 9.2, Sums and Differences of Powers, p. 268

questions.prompt: A polynomial in a, b, c vanishes whenever a = b. What factor must it have?
questions.back: a-b.
questions.why: Treat it as a polynomial in a with coefficients in b and c, and apply the factor theorem at a = b.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 9.3, The Factor Theorem for Multivariable Polynomials, p. 277

questions.prompt: When does an infinite geometric series converge, and to what?
questions.back: When |r| < 1. It converges to a/(1-r).
questions.why: The partial sums a(1-r^n)/(1-r) have r^n tending to 0.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 10.4, Geometric Series, p. 302

questions.prompt: How do you swap the order of summation in a nested sum over 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n?
questions.back: Sum over j from 1 to n of the sum over i from 1 to j equals the sum over i from 1 to n of the sum over j from i to n.
questions.why: Both run over the same set of pairs (i, j).

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 10.6, Nested Sums and Products, p. 325

questions.prompt: Give the sum 1+2+...+n.
questions.why: Pair the list with itself in reverse to get n sums of n+1.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 10.2, Arithmetic Series, p. 292

questions.prompt: State the principle of mathematical induction.
questions.back: If a statement holds for n = 1, and its truth for n implies its truth for n+1, then it holds for every positive integer n.
questions.why: The base case starts a chain, and the inductive step passes it along.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 11.3, Induction, p. 348

questions.prompt: If a/b = c/d = k with b+d not 0, what is (a+c)/(b+d)?
questions.back: k.
questions.why: a = kb and c = kd, so a+c = k(b+d).

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 11.2, Ratios, p. 343

questions.prompt: Prove by induction that 1^2+2^2+...+n^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.
rubric: Checks n = 1: both sides equal 1.
Assumes the formula for n.
Adds (n+1)^2 and factors (n+1)(n(2n+1)+6(n+1))/6.
Shows n(2n+1)+6(n+1) = (n+2)(2n+3), giving the formula for n+1.
questions.why: The inductive step reduces to a polynomial identity.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 11.3, Induction, p. 348

items.title: Alcumus, Intermediate Algebra: General Inequality Skills, AM-GM Inequality, and Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
items.minutesBasis: 15 minutes a topic, proposed
items.what: In the Intermediate Algebra course, work General Inequality Skills, AM-GM Inequality, and Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality until each shows mastered on your progress report. A topic you mastered earlier counts. Tick this when all 3 are mastered.

questions.prompt: State the AM-GM inequality for two nonnegative numbers and its equality case.
questions.back: (a+b)/2 ≥ sqrt(ab), with equality exactly when a = b.
questions.why: It is equivalent to (sqrt(a)-sqrt(b))^2 ≥ 0.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 12.3, AM-GM Inequality with Two Variables, p. 384

questions.prompt: State the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
questions.back: (a1^2+...+an^2)(b1^2+...+bn^2) ≥ (a1 b1+...+an bn)^2, with equality when the vectors are proportional.
questions.why: The quadratic sum of (ai x+bi)^2 is nonnegative, so its discriminant is at most 0.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 12.5, The Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality, p. 392

questions.prompt: Prove the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for real numbers.
rubric: Considers the quadratic f(x) = sum of (ai x+bi)^2, which is at least 0 for all x.
Expands it as (sum ai^2)x^2+2(sum ai bi)x+(sum bi^2).
Notes a quadratic that is never negative has discriminant at most 0, after handling all ai = 0 separately.
Writes the discriminant condition and rearranges to the inequality.
questions.why: The discriminant argument is the standard short proof.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 12.5, The Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality, p. 392

questions.prompt: State the change of base formula and the product, quotient, and power rules for logs.
questions.back: log_b(x) = log_c(x)/log_c(b). log(xy) = log x + log y. log(x/y) = log x-log y. log(x^k) = k log x.
questions.why: Each follows from the matching exponent law.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 13.3, Logarithmic Identities, p. 424

questions.prompt: What is log_a(b) times log_b(a)?
questions.why: By change of base, it equals (ln b/ln a)(ln a/ln b).

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 13.4, Using Logarithm Identities, p. 433

questions.prompt: Prove the change of base formula log_b(x) = log_c(x)/log_c(b).
rubric: Lets y = log_b(x), so b^y = x.
Takes log_c of both sides: y log_c(b) = log_c(x).
Divides by log_c(b), which is not 0 because b is not 1.
questions.why: Taking a log in any base turns the exponent into a factor.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 13.3, Logarithmic Identities, p. 424

questions.prompt: How do you denest sqrt(a+2sqrt(b))?
questions.back: Find x and y with x+y = a and xy = b. Then sqrt(a+2sqrt(b)) = sqrt(x)+sqrt(y).
questions.why: (sqrt(x)+sqrt(y))^2 = x+y+2sqrt(xy).

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 14.2, Evaluating Expressions With Radicals, p. 465

questions.prompt: What is the radical conjugate of a+sqrt(b) and why is it useful?
questions.back: a-sqrt(b). Their product a^2-b is rational, which clears radicals from denominators.
questions.why: The difference of squares removes the root.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 14.3, Radical Conjugates, p. 470

questions.prompt: Define even and odd functions and describe their graphs.
questions.back: Even: f(-x) = f(x), symmetric about the y-axis. Odd: f(-x) = -f(x), symmetric about the origin.
questions.why: x^2 is even and x^3 is odd.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 15.3, Even and Odd Functions, p. 492

questions.prompt: How do you find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function p/q?
questions.back: deg p < deg q: y = 0. Equal degrees: y = ratio of leading coefficients. deg p > deg q: no horizontal asymptote.
questions.why: For large |x| the leading terms dominate.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 15.1, Rational Functions and Their Graphs, p. 476

questions.prompt: Prove that every function f defined on all reals is the sum of an even function and an odd function.
rubric: Defines g(x) = (f(x)+f(-x))/2 and h(x) = (f(x)-f(-x))/2.
Checks g(-x) = g(x).
Checks h(-x) = -h(x).
Checks g+h = f.
questions.why: Averaging f with its reflection gives the even part, and the difference gives the odd part.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 15.3, Even and Odd Functions, p. 492

questions.prompt: For an integer n, what is floor(x+n)?
questions.back: floor(x)+n.
questions.why: Shifting by an integer shifts the greatest integer below x by the same amount.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 16.4, Floor and Ceiling, p. 529

questions.prompt: State the triangle inequality for absolute values.
questions.back: |a+b| ≤ |a|+|b|, with equality when a and b have the same sign or one is 0.
questions.why: On the number line, distance from 0 to a+b is at most the two step lengths.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 16.2, Absolute Value, p. 517

questions.prompt: How is the graph of y = |f(x)| related to the graph of y = f(x)?
questions.back: The parts below the x-axis are reflected above it, and the rest stays.
questions.why: |f(x)| = f(x) where f is nonnegative and -f(x) where it is negative.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 16.3, Graphing Absolute Value, p. 523

questions.prompt: What do finite differences tell you about a polynomial sequence?
questions.back: A degree d polynomial has constant dth differences, and they equal d factorial times the leading coefficient.
questions.why: Each difference lowers the degree by one.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 17.5, Finite Differences, p. 571

questions.prompt: Prove that the sum over k ≥ 1 of k/2^k equals 2.
rubric: Names the sum S and notes it converges.
Writes S/2 as the sum of k/2^(k+1), shifted one place.

Concludes S = 2.
questions.why: Subtracting a shifted copy turns an arithmetico-geometric series into a geometric one.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 17.4, Arithmetico-Geometric Series, p. 567

questions.prompt: State the mean inequality chain for positive numbers.
questions.back: Quadratic mean ≥ arithmetic mean ≥ geometric mean ≥ harmonic mean, with equality exactly when all the numbers are equal.
questions.why: Each step is a classical inequality, such as AM-GM in the middle.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 18.1, Mean Inequality Chain, p. 581

questions.prompt: State the rearrangement inequality.
questions.back: For sorted a1 ≤ ... ≤ an and b1 ≤ ... ≤ bn, the sum of ai times a permutation of the bi is largest when both are sorted the same way and smallest when sorted oppositely.
questions.why: Swapping two out-of-order terms never decreases the sum.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 18.2, The Rearrangement Inequality, p. 593

questions.prompt: What is the first move in most functional equations?
questions.back: Substitute special values such as 0, 1, or y = x, and record what each gives.
questions.why: Special values often pin down f(0) or relate f(x) to f(-x).

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 19.1, Finding Values, p. 611

questions.prompt: How do you solve f(x)+2f(1/x) = g(x)?
questions.back: Replace x with 1/x to get a second equation, then solve the two linear equations for f(x).
questions.why: The map x to 1/x is its own inverse, so the substitution closes the system.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 19.4, Cyclic Functions, p. 621

questions.prompt: Let f: R to R satisfy f(x+y) = f(x)+f(y) for all reals. Prove f(0) = 0, f(-x) = -f(x), and f(n) = n f(1) for every integer n.
rubric: Sets x = y = 0 to get f(0) = 2f(0), so f(0) = 0.
Sets y = -x to get f(0) = f(x)+f(-x), so f(-x) = -f(x).
Proves f(n) = n f(1) for positive n by induction using f(n+1) = f(n)+f(1).
Extends to negative n with f(-n) = -f(n).
questions.why: Each claim comes from one substitution, then induction.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 19.2, Finding Functions with Substitution, p. 615

questions.prompt: Express x^2+y^2 and x^3+y^3 in terms of s = x+y and p = xy.
questions.why: Symmetric expressions are polynomials in the elementary symmetric sums.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 20.6, Symmetric Sums Revisited, p. 658

questions.prompt: Describe the method of undetermined coefficients.
questions.back: Write the unknown polynomial or expression with letter coefficients, expand, and match coefficients to solve for them.
questions.why: Two polynomials are equal exactly when their coefficients are equal.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 20.3, Method of Undetermined Coefficients, p. 644

questions.prompt: How do you find the greatest common divisor of two polynomials?
questions.back: Use the Euclidean algorithm with polynomial division until the remainder is 0. The last nonzero remainder is the gcd.
questions.why: Each step keeps the same common divisors, as with integers.

ref.label: Intermediate Algebra, section 20.5, Common Divisors of Polynomials, p. 655

items.title: Chapter 1 Review and Challenge Problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 26. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: How many four-digit positive integers have at least one digit equal to 7?
questions.why: Count the complement. There are 9000 four-digit numbers and 8 * 9 * 9 * 9 = 5832 with no 7, which leaves 3168.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 1.2, Basic Counting Techniques, p. 2

questions.prompt: A fair die is rolled 4 times. What is the probability that at least one roll is a 6?
questions.why: The chance of no 6 is (5/6)^4 = 625/1296, so the answer is 1 minus that, 671/1296.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 1.3, Basic Probability Techniques, p. 11

questions.prompt: What is the coefficient of x^3 in the expansion of (2x+1)^5?
questions.why: The term is C(5, 3)(2x)^3 = 10 * 8 x^3, so the coefficient is 80.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 1.5, Pascal’s Triangle and the Binomial Theorem, p. 20

questions.prompt: How do constants and sums move through summation notation?
questions.back: The sum of c a_k equals c times the sum of a_k, and the sum of (a_k+b_k) equals the sum of a_k plus the sum of b_k.
questions.why: Summation is repeated addition, so it distributes over sums and pulls out constant factors.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 1.6, Summation Notation, p. 25

items.title: Intermediate Counting & Probability, chapter 2, sections 2.1 to 2.6, pp. 27 to 46
items.minutesBasis: 20 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
items.what: Work each problem in the text before you read its solution.

items.title: Chapter 2 Review and Challenge Problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 46. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: State De Morgan's laws for sets.
questions.back: The complement of A ∪ B is (complement of A) ∩ (complement of B). The complement of A ∩ B is (complement of A) ∪ (complement of B).
questions.why: An element is outside A ∪ B exactly when it is outside both.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 2.3, Operations on Sets, p. 33

questions.prompt: Which statements are equivalent to "if P then Q": its converse, its inverse, or its contrapositive?
questions.back: Only the contrapositive, "if not Q then not P". The converse and the inverse are equivalent to each other but not to the original.
questions.why: The truth tables of the statement and its contrapositive match row by row.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 2.4, Truth and Logic, p. 37

questions.prompt: What is the negation of "for every x there is a y with P(x, y)"?
choices: There is an x such that for every y, P(x, y) is false.
For every x there is a y with P(x, y) false.
There is an x and a y with P(x, y) false.
For every x and every y, P(x, y) is false.
questions.why: Negation swaps each quantifier and negates the statement inside. "For every" becomes "there is", and "there is" becomes "for every".

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 2.5, Quantifiers, p. 43

questions.prompt: Sets A and B have 12 and 9 elements, and 4 elements are in both. How many elements are in A ∪ B?
questions.why: |A ∪ B| = 12+9-4 = 17, since the 4 shared elements are counted twice in 12+9.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 2.3, Operations on Sets, p. 33

items.minutesBasis: 31 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
