items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 79. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: How many integers from 1 to 1000 are divisible by none of 2, 3, and 5?

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 3.4, Counting Problems With PIE, p. 58

questions.prompt: State the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion for n sets.
questions.back: |A1 ∪ ... ∪ An| = sum of |Ai|-sum of |Ai ∩ Aj| + sum of triple intersections-... + (-1)^(n+1) |A1 ∩ ... ∩ An|.
questions.why: An element in exactly m of the sets is counted C(m,1)-C(m,2)+...±C(m,m) = 1 time.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 3.5, PIE With Many Properties, p. 65

questions.prompt: How many ways can 5 letters go into 5 addressed envelopes, one each, so that no letter is in its own envelope?
questions.why: PIE over the letters in their own envelopes gives 5 factorial times (1-1+1/2-1/6+1/24-1/120) = 44.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 3.5, PIE With Many Properties, p. 65

questions.prompt: How many integers from 1 to 60 are divisible by at least two of 2, 3, and 5?
questions.why: Multiples of 6, 10, and 15 number 10, 6, and 4. Each multiple of 30 (there are 2) is counted 3 times but should count once, so subtract 2 * 2 to get 16.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 3.6, Counting Items With More Than 1 of Something, p. 68

questions.prompt: Prove that the number of permutations of n objects with no fixed point is n factorial times the sum over k from 0 to n of (-1)^k/k factorial.
rubric: Lets Ai be the set of permutations fixing object i.
Notes any k given objects are all fixed by (n-k) factorial permutations.
Applies PIE: the count is the sum over k of (-1)^k C(n, k)(n-k) factorial.
Simplifies C(n, k)(n-k) factorial to n factorial/k factorial.
questions.why: The derangement count is the complement of the union of the fixed-point sets.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 3.5, PIE With Many Properties, p. 65

items.minutesBasis: 32 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate

items.title: Chapter 4 Review and Challenge Problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 114. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: How many ordered quadruples (a, b, c, d) of nonnegative integers satisfy a+b+c+d = 10?
questions.why: Stars and bars: arrange 10 stars and 3 bars, C(13, 3) = 286.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 4.4, 1-1 Correspondence Basics, p. 94

questions.prompt: State stars and bars for nonnegative and for positive solutions of x1+...+xk = n.
questions.back: Nonnegative: C(n+k-1, k-1). Positive: C(n-1, k-1).
questions.why: A solution matches a row of n stars split by k-1 bars. For positive parts, choose k-1 of the n-1 gaps between stars.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 4.4, 1-1 Correspondence Basics, p. 94

questions.prompt: How many ordered triples of positive integers satisfy a+b+c = 12?
questions.why: Choose 2 of the 11 gaps between 12 stars: C(11, 2) = 55.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 4.4, 1-1 Correspondence Basics, p. 94

questions.prompt: How many 5-element subsets of {1, 2, ..., 12} contain no two consecutive integers?
questions.why: Subtract 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 from the sorted elements. This maps such subsets one-to-one onto 5-element subsets of {1, ..., 8}, so the count is C(8, 5) = 56.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 4.6, Clever 1-1 Correspondences, p. 105

questions.prompt: Prove that the number of k-element subsets of {1, ..., n} with no two consecutive elements is C(n-k+1, k).
rubric: Sorts a subset as a1 < a2 < ... < ak.
Maps it to b_i = a_i-(i-1), which gives b1 < b2 < ... < bk in {1, ..., n-k+1}.
Shows the map is reversible: a_i = b_i+(i-1) has gaps of at least 2.
Concludes the count is C(n-k+1, k).
questions.why: A bijection to ordinary subsets of a smaller set removes the gap condition.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 4.6, Clever 1-1 Correspondences, p. 105

items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 127. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: State the pigeonhole principle and its general form.
questions.back: If more than n objects go into n boxes, some box holds at least 2. If more than kn objects go into n boxes, some box holds at least k+1.
questions.why: If every box held at most k, there would be at most kn objects.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 5.3, Basic Pigeonhole Problems, p. 119

questions.prompt: Socks come in 4 colors. How many socks must you draw, in the dark, to be sure of 3 of one color?
questions.why: With 8 socks you could have 2 of each color. The 9th sock forces a third of some color, so the answer is 9.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 5.3, Basic Pigeonhole Problems, p. 119

questions.prompt: Prove that among any 5 points in a unit square, some two are at distance at most sqrt(2)/2.
rubric: Divides the square into 4 squares of side 1/2.
Applies the pigeonhole principle: two of the 5 points lie in the same small square (boundary included).
Notes the diameter of a square of side 1/2 is sqrt(2)/2.
Concludes those two points are at distance at most sqrt(2)/2.
questions.why: The boxes are the 4 small squares, and their diameter bounds the distance.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 5.3, Basic Pigeonhole Problems, p. 119

questions.prompt: Prove that any n+1 integers chosen from {1, 2, ..., 2n} include two that are relatively prime.
rubric: Applies the pigeonhole principle: two chosen numbers lie in the same pair.
Notes they are consecutive integers.
Shows consecutive integers are relatively prime, since a common divisor divides their difference 1.
questions.why: The pairs of consecutive integers are the pigeonholes.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 5.4, More Advanced Pigeonhole Problems, p. 122

items.title: Intermediate Counting & Probability, chapter 6, sections 6.1 to 6.5, pp. 130 to 142
items.minutesBasis: 13 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate

items.title: Chapter 6 Review and Challenge Problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 142. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: State linearity of expectation and say when it applies.
questions.back: E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] for any random variables, independent or not. Write a count as a sum of indicator variables and add their probabilities.
questions.why: Expectation is a weighted sum, and sums can be rearranged without any independence.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 6.3, Summing Expectations Constructively, p. 135

questions.prompt: A random permutation of 10 objects is chosen. What is the expected number of objects in their original positions?
questions.why: Each object is fixed with probability 1/10, and there are 10 objects, so linearity gives 1.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 6.2, Basic Examples, p. 131

questions.prompt: A standard 52-card deck with 26 red cards is shuffled. What is the expected number of adjacent pairs of positions holding two red cards?
questions.why: There are 51 adjacent pairs. Each is red-red with probability (26/52)(25/51), so the expectation is 25/2.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 6.3, Summing Expectations Constructively, p. 135

questions.prompt: Six fair dice are rolled. What is the expected number of different faces that appear?
questions.why: Each face appears with probability 1-(5/6)^6. Summing over 6 faces gives 6(1-(5/6)^6) = 31031/7776.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 6.3, Summing Expectations Constructively, p. 135

items.title: Intermediate Counting & Probability, chapter 7, sections 7.1 to 7.5, pp. 145 to 158
items.minutesBasis: 14 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
items.what: Work each problem in the text before you read its solution.

items.title: Chapter 7 Review and Challenge Problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 158. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: Count the ways to put n objects into k boxes when the objects are distinct and the boxes are distinct, with no other condition.
questions.back: k^n.
questions.why: Each of the n objects chooses one of k boxes independently.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 7.2, Basic Distributions, p. 146

questions.prompt: In how many ways can 8 identical candies be given to 3 children so that each child gets at least one?
questions.why: Positive solutions of a+b+c = 8 number C(7, 2) = 21.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 7.3, Distributions With Extra Conditions, p. 149

questions.prompt: In how many ways can 5 distinct balls go into 3 distinct boxes with no box empty?
questions.why: PIE over empty boxes: 3^5-3 * 2^5+3 * 1^5 = 150.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 7.3, Distributions With Extra Conditions, p. 149

questions.prompt: In how many ways can 10 identical balls go into 4 distinct boxes if each box holds at most 4?
questions.why: Stars and bars gives C(13, 3) = 286. Subtract cases with a box of at least 5: 4 * C(8, 3) = 224, then add back cases with two such boxes: C(4, 2) * C(3, 3) = 6. The count is 68.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 7.4, More Complicated Distribution Problems, p. 154

items.title: Intermediate Counting & Probability, chapter 8, pp. 161 to 171
items.minutesBasis: 11 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
items.what: Work each problem in the text before you read its solution.

items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems at the end of the chapter. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: What does strong induction assume in the inductive step?
questions.back: That the statement holds for every value from the base case up to n, not only for n. Then it proves the statement for n+1.
questions.why: Strong induction suits claims where case n+1 depends on smaller cases other than n, such as factoring into primes.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, chapter 8, Mathematical Induction, pp. 161 to 171

questions.prompt: Prove by induction that 1+3+5+...+(2n-1) = n^2 for every positive integer n.
rubric: Checks n = 1: 1 = 1^2.
Assumes the sum of the first n odd numbers is n^2.
Adds the next odd number 2n+1.
Shows n^2+2n+1 = (n+1)^2, which is the statement for n+1.
questions.why: The inductive step adds one term and factors.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, chapter 8, Mathematical Induction, pp. 161 to 171

questions.prompt: A false "proof" by induction claims all horses in any group have the same color. It assumes groups of n horses are one color and overlaps two groups of n among n+1 horses. Where does it fail?
choices: The step from n = 1 to n = 2 fails because the two groups of 1 horse do not overlap.
The base case n = 1 is false.
Induction cannot be used for statements about sets.
The step fails for every n because groups of n horses never overlap.
questions.why: The overlap argument needs a horse common to both groups. With n+1 = 2 the two groups share no horse, so the chain breaks at the first step.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, chapter 8, Mathematical Induction, pp. 161 to 171

items.title: Intermediate Counting & Probability, chapter 9, sections 9.1 to 9.5, pp. 172 to 189
items.minutesBasis: 18 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
items.what: Work each problem in the text before you read its solution.

items.title: Chapter 9 Review and Challenge Problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 189. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: State Binet's formula for the Fibonacci numbers with F1 = F2 = 1.
questions.back: F_n = (φ^n-ψ^n)/sqrt(5), where φ = (1+sqrt(5))/2 and ψ = (1-sqrt(5))/2.
questions.why: φ and ψ are the roots of x^2 = x+1, the characteristic equation of the recurrence.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 9.4, A Formula for the Fibonacci Numbers, p. 183

questions.prompt: In how many ways can a 1 by 10 strip be tiled with 1 by 1 squares and 1 by 2 dominoes?
questions.why: The count t_n satisfies t_n = t_(n-1)+t_(n-2) by the last tile, with t_1 = 1 and t_2 = 2. So t_10 = F_11 = 89.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 9.2, A Motivating Problem, p. 172

questions.prompt: How many strings of 10 binary digits contain no two consecutive 1s?
questions.why: Such strings of length n satisfy the Fibonacci recursion by their last digit, starting 2, 3, so length 10 gives 144.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 9.3, Some Fibonacci Problems, p. 175

questions.prompt: Prove that F1+F2+...+Fn = F_(n+2)-1 for every positive integer n.
rubric: Checks n = 1: F1 = 1 = F3-1.
Assumes the sum up to Fn is F_(n+2)-1.
Adds F_(n+1) to get F_(n+2)+F_(n+1)-1.
Uses the recurrence to write this as F_(n+3)-1.
questions.why: Induction with the defining recurrence closes the step.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 9.3, Some Fibonacci Problems, p. 175

items.title: Intermediate Counting & Probability, chapter 10, sections 10.1 to 10.7, pp. 192 to 222
items.minutesBasis: 31 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
items.what: Work each problem in the text before you read its solution.

items.title: Chapter 10 Review and Challenge Problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 222. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: How do you solve a linear recurrence a_n = p a_(n-1) + q a_(n-2)?
questions.back: Find the roots r and s of x^2 = px+q. If r and s differ, a_n = A r^n + B s^n, with A and B fixed by the first two terms.
questions.why: Each r^n with r a root satisfies the recurrence, and the solutions form a two-dimensional space.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 10.3, Linear Recurrences, p. 200

questions.prompt: Give a formula and the recursion for the Catalan numbers.
questions.back: C_n = C(2n, n)/(n+1). C_(n+1) = sum over k from 0 to n of C_k C_(n-k).
questions.why: They count balanced parentheses, triangulations, and many other structures that split into two smaller pieces.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 10.6, Formulas for the Catalan Numbers, p. 216

questions.prompt: In how many ways can a convex octagon be divided into triangles by nonintersecting diagonals?
questions.why: Triangulations of a convex (n+2)-gon number the Catalan number C_n, so an octagon gives C_6 = 132.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 10.5, Problems Involving Catalan Numbers, p. 206

questions.prompt: A sequence has a_0 = 1, a_1 = 4, and a_n = 5a_(n-1)-6a_(n-2). Find a_6.
questions.why: The roots of x^2 = 5x-6 are 2 and 3, and the start values give a_n = 2 * 3^n-2^n. So a_6 = 1458-64 = 1394.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 10.3, Linear Recurrences, p. 200

questions.prompt: How many strings of 5 left and 5 right parentheses are balanced?
questions.why: Balanced strings of n pairs number C_n, and C_5 = 42.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 10.5, Problems Involving Catalan Numbers, p. 206

items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 241. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: Define conditional probability and state Bayes' rule.
questions.back: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B). Bayes: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B).
questions.why: Conditioning restricts the sample space to B, and both sides of Bayes equal P(A and B)/P(B).

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 11.3, Some Definitions and Notation, p. 230

questions.prompt: A family has two children, and at least one is a boy. Each child is a boy or a girl with probability 1/2, independently. What is the probability that both are boys?
questions.why: Of the equally likely outcomes BB, BG, GB, GG, the condition keeps three, and one of them is BB, so the answer is 1/3.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 11.2, Basic Examples of Conditional Probability, p. 227

questions.prompt: One percent of people have a condition. A test is positive for 90 percent of people with it and 5 percent of people without it. A person tests positive. What is the probability they have the condition?
questions.why: P(sick and positive) = 0.009 and P(positive) = 0.009+0.0495 = 0.0585. Their ratio is 2/13.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 11.4, Harder Examples, p. 232

questions.prompt: In the Monty Hall game, the host knows where the car is and always opens a goat door you did not pick, then offers a switch. What is your chance of winning if you switch?
questions.why: Switching wins exactly when your first pick was a goat, which has probability 2/3.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 11.5, Let’s Make a Deal, p. 238

items.title: Intermediate Counting & Probability, chapter 12, sections 12.1 to 12.4, pp. 243 to 261
items.minutesBasis: 19 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate

items.title: Chapter 12 Review and Challenge Problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 261. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: State Vandermonde's identity.
questions.back: The sum over k of C(m, k) C(n, r-k) equals C(m+n, r).
questions.why: Choose r people from m men and n women by first deciding how many men, k.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 12.3, More Identities, p. 254

questions.prompt: Give the committee-chair identity relating k C(n, k) and C(n-1, k-1).
questions.back: k C(n, k) = n C(n-1, k-1).
questions.why: Both count committees of k from n with a chair: pick the committee then the chair, or the chair then the rest.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 12.2, Basic Identities, p. 243

questions.prompt: Compute the sum over k from 0 to 10 of k C(10, k).
questions.why: k C(10, k) = 10 C(9, k-1), and the C(9, j) sum to 2^9, so the total is 10 * 512 = 5120.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 12.2, Basic Identities, p. 243

questions.prompt: Compute the sum over k from 0 to 8 of C(8, k)^2.
questions.why: Write C(8, k)^2 = C(8, k)C(8, 8-k) and apply Vandermonde: C(16, 8) = 12870.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 12.3, More Identities, p. 254

questions.prompt: Give a counting proof that k C(n, k) = n C(n-1, k-1).
rubric: Counts committees of k people from n with one member named chair.
First way: choose the committee in C(n, k) ways, then the chair in k ways.
Second way: choose the chair in n ways, then the other k-1 members from n-1 in C(n-1, k-1) ways.
Equates the two counts.
questions.why: Counting the same set two ways gives the identity.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 12.2, Basic Identities, p. 243

items.minutesBasis: 30 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate

items.title: Chapter 13 Review and Challenge Problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 294. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: How do you compute a probability or expected time with a state diagram?
questions.back: Name each state, write one unknown per state, and write an equation for each by conditioning on the next step. Solve the linear system.
questions.why: From each state the process moves to known states with known probabilities.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 13.2, State Diagrams and Random Walks, p. 266

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped until two heads appear in a row. What is the expected number of flips?
questions.why: With E the expectation from the start and F after one head, E = 1+(F+E)/2 and F = 1+E/2. Solving gives E = 6.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 13.3, Events With Infinite States, p. 277

questions.prompt: You start with 3 dollars and bet 1 dollar on fair coin flips until you have 0 or 10 dollars. What is the probability you reach 10?
questions.why: p_k = (p_(k-1)+p_(k+1))/2 with p_0 = 0 and p_10 = 1 forces p_k = k/10, so the answer is 3/10.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 13.2, State Diagrams and Random Walks, p. 266

questions.prompt: How do you classify positions in a two-player game where the player who cannot move loses?
questions.back: A position is losing if every move leads to a winning position, and winning if some move leads to a losing position. Work up from the terminal positions.
questions.why: The player to move wins exactly when there is a move that leaves the opponent in a losing position.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 13.4, Two-player Strategy Games, p. 284

questions.prompt: Two players alternately remove 1, 2, or 3 stones from a pile, and whoever cannot move loses. For how many starting sizes from 1 to 100 does the first player lose with best play?
questions.why: The losing sizes are the multiples of 4, because any move from a multiple of 4 leaves a non-multiple and the opponent can return to a multiple. There are 25 of them.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 13.4, Two-player Strategy Games, p. 284

items.title: Intermediate Counting & Probability, chapter 14, sections 14.1 to 14.7, pp. 298 to 327
items.minutesBasis: 30 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate

items.title: Chapter 14 Review and Challenge Problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 327. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: Give the generating function of 1, 1, 1, ... and the coefficient of x^n in 1/(1-x)^k.
questions.back: 1/(1-x). The coefficient of x^n in 1/(1-x)^k is C(n+k-1, k-1).
questions.why: Multiplying k copies of 1+x+x^2+... counts the solutions of e1+...+ek = n, which is stars and bars.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 14.2, Basic examples of Generating Functions, p. 299

questions.prompt: What is the coefficient of x^10 in (1+x+x^2+x^3)^4?
questions.why: It counts the ways four numbers from 0 to 3 sum to 10, which is the number of ways they sum to 2 by symmetry: 10.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 14.4, Distributions (as Generating Functions), p. 307

questions.prompt: State Euler's partition identity.
questions.back: The number of partitions of n into distinct parts equals the number of partitions of n into odd parts.
questions.why: The product of (1+x^k) equals the product of 1/(1-x^(2k-1)) because (1+x^k) = (1-x^(2k))/(1-x^k).

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 14.5, The Generating Function for Partitions, p. 314

questions.prompt: How many partitions of 10 into distinct parts are there?

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 14.5, The Generating Function for Partitions, p. 314

questions.prompt: Prove with generating functions that partitions of n into distinct parts and into odd parts are equally many.
rubric: Writes the distinct-parts generating function as the product over k of (1+x^k).
Writes the odd-parts generating function as the product over odd m of 1/(1-x^m).
Rewrites 1+x^k = (1-x^(2k))/(1-x^k).
Cancels every even-index factor (1-x^(2k)) against a denominator, leaving the odd-parts product.
questions.why: Equal generating functions have equal coefficients.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 14.5, The Generating Function for Partitions, p. 314

items.title: Chapter 15 Review and Challenge Problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: The problems after the summary on p. 360. Write each solution out. Mark this item missed if you miss any, and note which.

questions.prompt: State the handshake lemma.
questions.back: The sum of the degrees of the vertices of a graph equals twice the number of edges.
questions.why: Each edge adds 1 to the degree of each of its two ends.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 15.3, Basic Properties of Graphs, p. 334

questions.prompt: When does a connected graph have an Eulerian circuit, and when an Eulerian path?
questions.back: A circuit exactly when every vertex has even degree. A path that is not a circuit exactly when exactly two vertices have odd degree.
questions.why: Each pass through a vertex uses two of its edges, so only the ends of a path can have odd degree.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 15.6, Eulerian and Hamiltonian Paths, p. 354

questions.prompt: What is the largest number of edges a simple planar graph with 10 vertices can have?
questions.why: A simple planar graph with v ≥ 3 vertices has at most 3v-6 edges, here 24, and a triangulation reaches it.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 15.5, Planar Graphs, p. 349

questions.prompt: A tree has 12 vertices. How many edges does it have?
questions.why: Every tree on n vertices has n-1 edges, so 11.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 15.4, Cycles and Paths, p. 342

questions.prompt: Prove that every graph has an even number of vertices of odd degree.
rubric: States the handshake lemma: the degree sum is 2E, an even number.
Splits the degree sum into the even-degree part and the odd-degree part.
Notes the even-degree part is even, so the odd-degree part is even.
Concludes a sum of odd numbers is even only when there is an even number of terms.
questions.why: Parity of the degree sum forces the count.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 15.3, Basic Properties of Graphs, p. 334

questions.prompt: How many subsets of {1, 2, ..., 15}, including the empty set, have a sum divisible by 5?
questions.why: A roots of unity filter on the product of (1+x^k) gives (2^15+4 * 2^3)/5 = 6560. A direct count by computer agrees.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 14.2, Basic examples of Generating Functions, p. 299

questions.prompt: Ten labeled seats stand around a round table. In how many ways can 3 of the seats be chosen so that no two chosen seats are adjacent?
questions.why: On a circle of n seats the count is n/(n-k) C(n-k, k), here 10/7 * 35 = 50. A case split on whether seat 1 is chosen gives the same.

ref.label: Intermediate Counting & Probability, section 4.6, Clever 1-1 Correspondences, p. 105

questions.prompt: How do you find the inverse of y = f(x) algebraically?
questions.back: Swap x and y, then solve for y.
questions.why: Swapping reflects the graph over y = x, which is what the inverse does.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 1.4, Inverse Functions, p. 19

questions.prompt: What is the domain of f(g(x))?
questions.back: The x in the domain of g with g(x) in the domain of f.
questions.why: Both functions must accept their inputs.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 1.3, Composition, p. 16

questions.prompt: How do radians and degrees relate, and what is the arc length on a circle of radius r?
questions.back: pi radians = 180 degrees. Arc length s = r θ with θ in radians.
questions.why: A radian is the angle whose arc equals the radius.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 2.2, Radians, p. 40

questions.prompt: What are the amplitude and period of y = A sin(Bx+C)+D?
questions.back: Amplitude |A|. Period 2 pi/|B|.
questions.why: B compresses the input, so one full cycle takes 2 pi/|B|.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 2.4, Transformations of Trig Functions, p. 55

questions.prompt: Give the ranges of arcsin, arccos, and arctan.
questions.back: arcsin: [-pi/2, pi/2]. arccos: [0, pi]. arctan: (-pi/2, pi/2).
questions.why: Each range is an interval on which the function is one-to-one and takes every value.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 2.5, Inverse Trig Functions, p. 64

A topic you mastered earlier counts. Tick this when all 5 are mastered.

questions.prompt: State the angle addition formulas for sine and cosine.
questions.back: sin(a+b) = sin a cos b + cos a sin b. cos(a+b) = cos a cos b-sin a sin b.
questions.why: They can be proved with rotation or with the distance formula on the unit circle.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 3.2, Sums and Differences of Angles, p. 91

questions.prompt: Give three forms of cos 2θ and the formula for sin 2θ.
questions.back: cos 2θ = cos^2 θ-sin^2 θ = 2cos^2 θ-1 = 1-2sin^2 θ. sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ.
questions.why: Set a = b = θ in the addition formulas and use sin^2+cos^2 = 1.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 3.3, Double and Half Angles, p. 100

questions.prompt: Write sin a + sin b as a product.
questions.why: Apply the addition formulas to (a+b)/2 ± (a-b)/2 and add.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 3.4, Sum-to-product and Product-to-sum, p. 106

questions.prompt: Derive tan(a+b) = (tan a + tan b)/(1-tan a tan b) from the sine and cosine addition formulas.
rubric: Writes tan(a+b) = sin(a+b)/cos(a+b).
Substitutes both addition formulas.
Divides numerator and denominator by cos a cos b.
Simplifies to the stated formula.
questions.why: Dividing by cos a cos b converts every term into tangents.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 3.2, Sums and Differences of Angles, p. 91

questions.prompt: State the law of cosines.
questions.back: c^2 = a^2+b^2-2ab cos C.
questions.why: Drop an altitude and apply the Pythagorean theorem to both pieces.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 4.2, Law of Cosines, p. 136

questions.prompt: State the extended law of sines.
questions.back: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = 2R, where R is the circumradius.
questions.why: The diameter through B makes an inscribed right triangle with an angle equal to A.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 4.3, Law of Sines, p. 141

questions.prompt: Give the area of a triangle in terms of its sides and circumradius.
questions.back: abc/(4R).
questions.why: Area = ab sin(C)/2 and sin C = c/(2R).

ref.label: Precalculus, section 4.4, More Triangle Relationships, p. 148

questions.prompt: Prove that a/sin A = 2R for a triangle with an acute angle A and circumradius R.
rubric: Draws the diameter BD of the circumcircle through B.
Notes angle BDC = angle A, inscribed angles on arc BC.
Notes angle BCD is a right angle, inscribed in a semicircle.
Concludes sin A = BC/BD = a/(2R).
questions.why: The diameter makes a right triangle with hypotenuse 2R and an angle equal to A.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 4.3, Law of Sines, p. 141

questions.prompt: Convert between polar and rectangular coordinates.
questions.back: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ. r^2 = x^2+y^2 and tan θ = y/x, with the quadrant chosen by the signs of x and y.
questions.why: The point lies at distance r from the origin in direction θ.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 5.2, Polar Coordinates, p. 167

questions.prompt: Parameterize the line through point P in direction v.
questions.back: P + t v for real t.
questions.why: Each value of t moves t copies of v from P.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 5.1, Parameterization, p. 158

questions.prompt: What is true of the nonreal roots of a polynomial with real coefficients?
questions.back: They come in conjugate pairs.
questions.why: Conjugating the equation f(z) = 0 leaves the real coefficients unchanged.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 6.4, Nonreal Roots of Polynomials, p. 208

questions.prompt: How do addition and the modulus look in the complex plane?
questions.back: Addition is vector addition. The modulus |z| is the distance from 0 to z.
questions.why: The plane identifies a+bi with the point (a, b).

ref.label: Precalculus, section 6.2, The Complex Plane, p. 198

questions.prompt: What happens to moduli and arguments when you multiply complex numbers in polar form?
questions.back: Moduli multiply and arguments add.
questions.why: This is the angle addition formulas in complex form.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 7.1, Polar Form of Complex Numbers, p. 218

questions.prompt: State Euler's formula and De Moivre's theorem.
questions.back: e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ. (cos θ + i sin θ)^n = cos nθ + i sin nθ.
questions.why: Raising to a power multiplies the argument by n.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 7.2, Exponential Form of Complex Numbers, p. 224

questions.prompt: What are the nth roots of unity and what is their sum for n ≥ 2?
questions.back: e^(2 pi i k/n) for k = 0, ..., n-1. Their sum is 0.
questions.why: They are the roots of z^n-1, whose z^(n-1) coefficient is 0.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 7.3, Roots of Unity, p. 232

questions.prompt: Prove that the nth roots of unity sum to 0 for n ≥ 2.
rubric: Writes the roots as 1, w, w^2, ..., w^(n-1) with w = e^(2 pi i/n).
Notes w is not 1 because n ≥ 2.
Sums the geometric series: (w^n-1)/(w-1).
Uses w^n = 1 to get 0.
questions.why: The roots form a geometric series whose ratio is a root of unity other than 1.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 7.3, Roots of Unity, p. 232

questions.why: The modulus is unchanged and θ is added to every argument.

questions.prompt: How can you tell that points a, b, c in the complex plane are collinear?
questions.back: (c-a)/(b-a) is real.
questions.why: The quotient's argument is the angle between the vectors from a, which is 0 or pi exactly when they are collinear.

questions.prompt: Give the distance between complex numbers z and w.
questions.why: z-w is the vector from w to z.

questions.prompt: Give two formulas for the dot product and the test for perpendicular vectors.
questions.back: u·v = u1 v1 + u2 v2 = |u||v| cos θ. Nonzero vectors are perpendicular exactly when u·v = 0.
questions.why: The law of cosines on the triangle formed by u, v, and u-v links the two formulas.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 9.2, The Dot Product, p. 304

questions.prompt: Give the projection of u onto a nonzero vector v.
questions.why: The scalar factor makes u minus the projection perpendicular to v.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 9.4, Projections, p. 322

questions.prompt: When are two vectors in the plane linearly dependent?
questions.back: When one is a scalar multiple of the other.
questions.why: Then they lie on one line through the origin.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 9.3, Lines and Linear Dependence, p. 312

items.minutesBasis: 15 minutes a topic, proposed

questions.prompt: Give the determinant of the matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] and its geometric meaning.
questions.back: ad-bc. Its absolute value is the area scale factor of the transformation.
questions.why: The unit square maps to the parallelogram spanned by the columns, whose area is |ad-bc|.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 10.4, The Determinant, p. 354

questions.prompt: Give the inverse of [[a, b], [c, d]].
questions.back: (1/(ad-bc)) [[d, -b], [-c, a]], when ad-bc is not 0.
questions.why: Multiplying gives (ad-bc) times the identity, divided by ad-bc.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 10.6, Inverting a Matrix, p. 369

questions.prompt: Is matrix multiplication commutative?
questions.back: No. AB and BA usually differ, though it is associative.
questions.why: Matrices act as transformations, and doing two in the other order can differ.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 10.2, Multiplying Matrices, p. 339

questions.prompt: Give the matrix that rotates the plane by θ counterclockwise.
questions.back: [[cos θ, -sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]].
questions.why: Its columns are the images of (1, 0) and (0, 1).

ref.label: Precalculus, section 10.3, Matrices as Transformations, p. 347

questions.prompt: How do you compute the determinant of a 3 by 3 matrix?
questions.back: Expand along a row: each entry times its 2 by 2 minor, with signs +, -, + in the first row.
questions.why: Cofactor expansion reduces the size by one.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 11.3, Determinants of 3 × 3 Matrices, p. 395

questions.prompt: How is det(AB) related to det A and det B?
questions.back: det(AB) = det(A) det(B).
questions.why: Volume scale factors multiply when transformations are composed.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 11.3, Determinants of 3 × 3 Matrices, p. 395

questions.prompt: What are the direction and length of the cross product u × v?
questions.back: Perpendicular to u and v by the right-hand rule. Length |u||v| sin θ, the area of the parallelogram they span.
questions.why: u × v is zero exactly when u and v are parallel.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 12.3, The Cross Product, p. 442

questions.prompt: Write the equation of the plane through point P with normal vector n.
questions.back: n·(X-P) = 0, or ax+by+cz = d with n = (a, b, c).
questions.why: Every vector in the plane is perpendicular to the normal.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 12.1, Lines and Planes in Three Dimensions, p. 421

questions.prompt: What does |u·(v × w)| measure?
questions.back: The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by u, v, and w. It equals |det| of the matrix with rows u, v, w.
questions.why: Base area |v × w| times height along the normal.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 12.4, Geometric Interpretation of the Determinant, p. 450

questions.prompt: Give the centroid of triangle ABC in vectors.
questions.why: The point two thirds along the median from A is A+(2/3)((B+C)/2-A).

ref.label: Precalculus, section 13.2, Vectors in the Triangle, p. 469

questions.prompt: When do vectors and complex numbers suit a geometry problem?
questions.back: When the problem is about midpoints, ratios along segments, parallel lines, or rotations, which become linear combinations or multiplication.
questions.why: Those relations turn into short algebra with one origin.

ref.label: Precalculus, section 13.3, Vectors, Complex Numbers, and Challenging Problems, p. 476

questions.prompt: Describe proof by contradiction.
questions.back: Assume the statement is false and derive something impossible. Then the statement must be true.
questions.why: A true statement cannot imply a false one, so the assumption fails.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, chapter 0, Prove It, pp. 1 to 2

questions.prompt: Prove that sqrt(3) is irrational.
rubric: Assumes sqrt(3) = p/q in lowest terms.
Derives p^2 = 3q^2, so 3 divides p^2 and therefore p, since 3 is prime.
Writes p = 3r to get q^2 = 3r^2, so 3 divides q.
Notes p and q share the factor 3, a contradiction.
questions.why: The contradiction uses that a prime dividing a square divides the base.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, chapter 0, Prove It, pp. 1 to 2

questions.prompt: Describe proof by contrapositive.
questions.back: To prove "if P then Q", prove "if not Q then not P" instead.
questions.why: A statement and its contrapositive are true or false together.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, chapter 0, Prove It, pp. 1 to 2

questions.prompt: State the change of base formula for logarithms.
questions.back: log_b(x) = log_a(x)/log_a(b) for positive a and b other than 1.
questions.why: Take log_a of both sides of b^(log_b x) = x.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, chapter 1, Logarithms, pp. 3 to 9

questions.why: By change of base the product telescopes to log_2(64) = 6.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, chapter 1, Logarithms, pp. 3 to 9

questions.prompt: Solve log_2(x)+log_4(x) = 6.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, chapter 1, Logarithms, pp. 3 to 9

questions.prompt: How many digits does 2^100 have?
questions.why: The digit count is floor(100 log_10 2)+1 = floor(30.10)+1 = 31.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, chapter 1, Logarithms, pp. 3 to 9

questions.prompt: What is the largest value of a sin x + b cos x?
questions.back: sqrt(a^2+b^2).
questions.why: Write a sin x + b cos x = sqrt(a^2+b^2) sin(x+φ) for a suitable angle φ.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 2.4, Tying It All Together, p. 15

questions.prompt: Compute sin 15° cos 15°.
questions.why: It equals sin(30°)/2 by the double angle formula, which is 1/4.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 2.5, Solving Problems Using Trigonometric Identities, p. 20

questions.prompt: What is the maximum value of 3 sin x + 4 cos x?
questions.why: The maximum of a sin x + b cos x is sqrt(a^2+b^2) = sqrt(9+16) = 5.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 2.4, Tying It All Together, p. 15

questions.prompt: What is the period of y = tan(2x)?
questions.why: tan has period pi, and doubling the input halves the period.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 2.2, Graphing Trigonometric Functions, p. 12

questions.prompt: State Stewart's theorem for a cevian AD of length d, with BD = m, DC = n, and BC = a = m+n.
questions.back: b^2 m + c^2 n = a(d^2+mn), where b = CA and c = AB.
questions.why: Apply the law of cosines at D in triangles ABD and ACD and eliminate the cosine.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 3.3, More Important Lines, p. 29

questions.prompt: Find the area of a triangle with sides 13, 14, and 15.
questions.why: Heron's formula with s = 21 gives sqrt(21 * 8 * 7 * 6) = 84.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 3.2, Areas, Areas, Areas, p. 27

questions.prompt: Find the circumradius of a triangle with sides 13, 14, and 15.
questions.why: R = abc/(4K) = 2730/336 = 65/8, using the area K = 84.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 3.2, Areas, Areas, Areas, p. 27

questions.prompt: In a triangle with sides 13, 14, and 15, find the length of the median to the side of length 14.
questions.why: The median formula m^2 = (2 * 13^2+2 * 15^2-14^2)/4 = 148 gives m = 2*sqrt(37).

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 3.3, More Important Lines, p. 29

questions.prompt: What is true of the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, and what is the converse?
questions.back: They are supplementary. A convex quadrilateral with a pair of supplementary opposite angles is cyclic.
questions.why: Opposite inscribed angles together subtend the whole circle, 360 degrees of arc.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 4.1, Properties of Cyclic Quadrilaterals, p. 33

questions.prompt: State Ptolemy's theorem.
questions.back: For a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, AC * BD = AB * CD + AD * BC.
questions.why: The product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of opposite sides.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 4.3, Ptolemy’s Theorem, p. 35

questions.prompt: A regular pentagon has side 1. Use Ptolemy's theorem on four of its vertices to find the length of a diagonal.
questions.why: Four vertices form a cyclic quadrilateral with sides 1, 1, 1, d and both diagonals d. Ptolemy gives d^2 = d+1, so d = (1+sqrt(5))/2.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 4.3, Ptolemy’s Theorem, p. 35

questions.prompt: Show that Ptolemy's theorem applied to a rectangle gives the Pythagorean theorem.
rubric: Notes a rectangle is cyclic, since its opposite angles are right and sum to 180 degrees.
Names the sides a and b and the diagonals, both of length c.
Applies Ptolemy: c * c = a * a + b * b.
Notes the diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs a and b.
questions.why: A rectangle's diagonal is the hypotenuse, and Ptolemy's products become squares.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 4.3, Ptolemy’s Theorem, p. 35

questions.prompt: For the ellipse x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2 = 1 with a > b, where are the foci and what is the eccentricity?
questions.back: At (±c, 0) with c^2 = a^2-b^2. Eccentricity e = c/a, which is less than 1.
questions.why: At the end of the minor axis, the distances to both foci are a, so c^2+b^2 = a^2.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 5.2, Ellipses, p. 40

questions.prompt: How do you remove the xy term from Ax^2+Bxy+Cy^2+... = 0?
questions.back: Rotate the axes by θ with cot 2θ = (A-C)/B.
questions.why: The rotation choice makes the new cross term coefficient (C-A)sin 2θ + B cos 2θ vanish.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 5.5, That Pesky xy Term, p. 49

questions.prompt: What is the distance between the foci of x^2/25+y^2/9 = 1?
questions.why: c = sqrt(25-9) = 4, so the distance is 2c = 8.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 5.2, Ellipses, p. 40

questions.prompt: The hyperbola x^2/16-y^2/9 = 1 has asymptotes y = ±mx. Find m.
questions.why: The asymptotes of x^2/a^2-y^2/b^2 = 1 are y = ±(b/a)x, so m = 3/4.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 5.3, Hyperbolas, p. 44

questions.prompt: State Newton's sums for a cubic with roots r, s, t and elementary symmetric sums e1, e2, e3.
questions.back: With p_k = r^k+s^k+t^k: p1 = e1, p2 = e1 p1-2e2, p3 = e1 p2-e2 p1+3e3, and p_k = e1 p_(k-1)-e2 p_(k-2)+e3 p_(k-3) for k > 3.
questions.why: Each root satisfies x^3 = e1 x^2-e2 x+e3. Multiply by x^(k-3) and sum over the roots.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 6.6, Newton’s Sums, p. 65

questions.prompt: Find the sum of the squares of the roots of x^3-6x^2+11x-6.
questions.why: The sum of squares is e1^2-2e2 = 36-22 = 14.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 6.4, Coefficients and Roots, p. 60

questions.prompt: Let r, s, t be the roots of x^3-x-1. Find r^3+s^3+t^3.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 6.6, Newton’s Sums, p. 65

questions.prompt: Given a polynomial with roots r_i, how do you get one whose roots are the reciprocals 1/r_i?
questions.back: Reverse the order of the coefficients, provided 0 is not a root.
questions.why: x^n P(1/x) has the reversed coefficients and vanishes exactly at the reciprocals.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 6.5, Transforming Polynomials, p. 62

questions.prompt: When does a function have an inverse function, and how is the inverse found?
questions.back: When it is one-to-one on its domain. Solve y = f(x) for x in terms of y.
questions.why: Each output must come from exactly one input for the inverse to be a function.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 7.1, The Inverse of a Function, p. 69

questions.prompt: What substitution solves f(x)+a f(1/x) = g(x)?
questions.back: Replace x with 1/x, which gives f(1/x)+a f(x) = g(1/x). Solve the two linear equations for f(x).
questions.why: x to 1/x undoes itself, so the two equations involve the same two unknowns.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 7.3, Solving Functional Identities, p. 71

questions.prompt: A function satisfies f(x)+2f(1/x) = 3x for every nonzero x. Find f(2).

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 7.3, Solving Functional Identities, p. 71

questions.prompt: Let f satisfy f(x+y) = f(x)+f(y) for all reals. Prove f(q) = q f(1) for every rational q.
rubric: Shows f(0) = 0 and f(nx) = n f(x) for positive integers n by induction, then for all integers with f(-x) = -f(x).
Writes q = m/n and notes n f(m/n) = f(m) = m f(1).
Divides by n to get f(m/n) = (m/n) f(1).
questions.why: Integer scaling gives f(m) = m f(1), and then f(m/n) = f(m)/n.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 7.3, Solving Functional Identities, p. 71

questions.prompt: What is the limit of sin(x)/x as x approaches 0, with x in radians?
questions.why: Comparing areas gives cos x ≤ sin(x)/x ≤ 1 near 0, and cos x approaches 1.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 8.6, Trig Limits, p. 83

questions.prompt: Define e as a limit.
questions.back: e = lim (1+1/n)^n as n grows without bound.
questions.why: This is the limit of compounding interest at rate 100 percent more and more often.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 8.7, e, p. 84

questions.prompt: Find the limit of (x^2-4)/(x-2) as x approaches 2.
questions.why: For x not 2 the expression equals x+2, which approaches 4.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 8.3, Working with Limits, p. 78

questions.prompt: Find the limit of (1+3/n)^n as n grows without bound.
questions.why: Writing it as ((1+3/n)^(n/3))^3 gives e^3, written exp(3).

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 8.7, e, p. 84

questions.prompt: State De Moivre's theorem.
questions.back: (r(cos θ+i sin θ))^n = r^n(cos nθ+i sin nθ).
questions.why: Multiplying complex numbers multiplies moduli and adds arguments.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 9.5, DeMoivre’s Theorem, p. 92

questions.why: |1+i| = sqrt(2), so the modulus is sqrt(2)^10 = 32.

questions.prompt: How do row operations change a determinant?
questions.back: Swapping two rows negates it. Multiplying a row by k multiplies it by k. Adding a multiple of one row to another leaves it unchanged.
questions.why: These rules let you reduce a matrix to triangular form, whose determinant is the product of the diagonal.

questions.prompt: Find the area of the triangle with vertices (0, 0, 0), (1, 2, 3), and (4, 5, 6).
questions.why: The cross product (1, 2, 3) × (4, 5, 6) = (-3, 6, -3) has length sqrt(54), and the area is half that, 3*sqrt(6)/2.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 11.2, The Cross Product in Coordinates, p. 113

questions.prompt: How is the inverse of a square matrix A built from minors?
questions.back: A^(-1) = (1/det A) times the adjugate, the transpose of the matrix of cofactors. It exists only when det A is not 0.
questions.why: Expanding by cofactors gives A times its adjugate equal to det A times the identity.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 11.7, The Inverse of a Matrix, p. 120

questions.prompt: State the AM-GM inequality for n nonnegative numbers.
questions.back: (a1+...+an)/n ≥ (a1 a2 ... an)^(1/n), with equality exactly when all ai are equal.
questions.why: It follows from the two-variable case by induction or from convexity of the logarithm.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 14.2, Arithmetic Mean-Geometric Mean Inequality, p. 160

questions.prompt: Find the minimum of x+4/x for x > 0.
questions.why: AM-GM gives x+4/x ≥ 2sqrt(4) = 4, with equality at x = 2, so the minimum is 4.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 14.2, Arithmetic Mean-Geometric Mean Inequality, p. 160

questions.prompt: Positive x and y satisfy 2x+3y = 12. Find the largest possible value of xy.
questions.why: AM-GM on 2x and 3y: 6 ≥ sqrt(6xy), so xy ≤ 6, with equality at x = 3, y = 2. The answer is 6.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 14.4, Maximization and Minimization, p. 164

questions.prompt: Find the minimum of x^2+y^2 over real x, y with 3x+4y = 10.
questions.why: Cauchy gives (9+16)(x^2+y^2) ≥ (3x+4y)^2 = 100, so the minimum is 4.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 14.3, Cauchy’s Inequality, p. 162

questions.prompt: Prove that (a+b)(1/a+1/b) ≥ 4 for positive a and b.
rubric: Expands the product to 2+a/b+b/a.
Applies AM-GM to a/b and b/a: their sum is at least 2.
Concludes the product is at least 4.
Notes equality holds exactly when a = b.
questions.why: The product reduces to a sum of a positive number and its reciprocal.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 14.2, Arithmetic Mean-Geometric Mean Inequality, p. 160

questions.prompt: State Pascal's identity and its counting reason.
questions.back: C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1)+C(n-1, k). A k-subset of n items either contains a fixed item or does not.
questions.why: The two cases split the subsets with no overlap.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 15.2, Pascal’s Identity, p. 170

questions.prompt: What is block walking, and how does it explain Pascal's identity?
questions.back: Counting shortest grid paths. The paths to a point arrive from the left or from below, so their count is the sum of the two neighbors, as in Pascal's triangle.
questions.why: The number of paths to (a, b) is C(a+b, a).

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 15.4, Block Walking, p. 173

questions.prompt: How many shortest grid paths go from (0, 0) to (5, 5) without passing through (2, 2)?
questions.why: All paths: C(10, 5) = 252. Through (2, 2): C(4, 2) * C(6, 3) = 120. The answer is 132.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 15.4, Block Walking, p. 173

questions.prompt: Which of the integers, the rationals, and the reals are countable?
questions.back: The integers and the rationals are countable. The reals are not.
questions.why: The rationals can be listed along diagonals of a grid, while Cantor's diagonal argument defeats any list of reals.

questions.prompt: Prove that the real numbers in (0, 1) cannot be listed as a sequence.

Notes y is in (0, 1) and differs from every xn.
Concludes the list is incomplete, a contradiction.
questions.why: Cantor's diagonal number differs from each listed number in one place.

questions.prompt: What is the locus of points P with PA/PB = k for a constant k, not 1?

questions.prompt: State Menelaus' theorem.

questions.prompt: Define inversion in a circle of center O and radius r, and state what it does to lines and circles.
questions.back: P maps to P' on ray OP with OP * OP' = r^2. Lines through O stay lines through O. Lines not through O become circles through O and the reverse. Circles not through O become circles not through O.
questions.why: Inversion trades tangency and circles through the center for lines, which can simplify a figure.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 22.2, Inversion, p. 243

questions.prompt: What is a homothety, and what does it preserve?
questions.back: A dilation about a center with ratio k. It maps lines to parallel lines, multiplies lengths by |k|, and preserves angles.
questions.why: Two circles are related by a homothety centered at a center of similitude.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 22.3, Homothecy, p. 245

questions.prompt: How long is the projection of a segment of length L onto a line at angle θ to it?
questions.back: L |cos θ|.
questions.why: The projection is the adjacent side of a right triangle with hypotenuse L.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 22.1, Projections, p. 241

questions.prompt: State Fermat's little theorem.
questions.back: If p is prime and p does not divide a, then a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p).
questions.why: Multiplying 1, 2, ..., p-1 by a permutes the nonzero residues mod p.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 23.6, Fermat’s Theorem, p. 258

questions.prompt: State Wilson's theorem.
questions.back: (p-1) factorial ≡ -1 (mod p) for every prime p.
questions.why: Each residue from 2 to p-2 pairs with a different inverse, leaving 1 times (p-1).

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 23.8, Wilson’s Theorem, p. 262

questions.prompt: Give the formula for Euler's φ function and Euler's theorem.
questions.back: φ(n) = n times the product over primes p dividing n of (1-1/p). If gcd(a, n) = 1 then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n).
questions.why: φ(n) counts the residues mod n that are prime to n.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 23.7, The φ Function, p. 260

questions.prompt: Prove Fermat's little theorem: if p is prime and p does not divide a, then a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p).
rubric: Considers the residues a, 2a, ..., (p-1)a mod p.
Shows they are distinct and nonzero, since ia ≡ ja forces p | (i-j)a and p does not divide a.
Concludes they are 1, 2, ..., p-1 in some order, so their product is (p-1) factorial.
Gets a^(p-1) (p-1) factorial ≡ (p-1) factorial and cancels (p-1) factorial, which is prime to p.
questions.why: Multiplication by a permutes the nonzero residues.

questions.prompt: When does ax+by = c have integer solutions, and what are they all?
questions.back: Exactly when gcd(a, b) divides c. With one solution (x0, y0) and g = gcd(a, b), all are x = x0+(b/g)t, y = y0-(a/g)t for integers t.
questions.why: Differences of solutions satisfy a(x-x0) = -b(y-y0), and dividing by g leaves coprime coefficients.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 24.1, ax + by = c, p. 266

questions.prompt: How many pairs of nonnegative integers (x, y) satisfy 3x+5y = 100?
questions.why: Need 5y ≡ 100 (mod 3), so y ≡ 2 (mod 3), giving y = 2, 5, ..., 20. That is 7 pairs.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 24.1, ax + by = c, p. 266

questions.prompt: Give the form of all primitive Pythagorean triples.
questions.back: m^2-n^2, 2mn, m^2+n^2 with m > n > 0, gcd(m, n) = 1, and m, n of opposite parity, up to swapping the legs.
questions.why: The conditions make the three numbers coprime, and every primitive triple arises this way.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 24.2, x^2 + y^2 = z^2, p. 269

questions.prompt: The smallest solution in positive integers of x^2-2y^2 = 1 is (3, 2). What is x in the next solution?
questions.why: (3+2sqrt(2))^2 = 17+12sqrt(2), so the next solution is (17, 12) and x = 17.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 24.4, The Pell Equation, p. 271

questions.prompt: What is the method of infinite descent?
questions.back: Show that any positive integer solution produces a smaller positive integer solution. Since positive integers cannot decrease forever, there is no solution.
questions.why: Fermat used it to show x^4+y^4 = z^2 has no solution in positive integers.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 24.3, x^4 + y^4 = z^2, p. 270

items.title: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, chapter 25, sections 25.1 to 25.6, pp. 275 to 283
items.minutesBasis: 9 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate

questions.prompt: State Euler's formula for a connected planar graph.
questions.back: V-E+F = 2, counting the outer face.
questions.why: Removing an edge from a cycle lowers E and F by 1 together, and a tree has V-(V-1)+1 = 2.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 25.2, Planar Graphs, p. 276

questions.prompt: How many edges does a regular icosahedron have?
questions.why: It has 20 triangular faces, and each edge is on two faces, so E = 20 * 3/2 = 30.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 25.3, Example: The Platonic Solids, p. 277

questions.prompt: When does a connected graph have an Euler trail that is not a circuit?
questions.back: When exactly two vertices have odd degree. The trail starts at one and ends at the other.
questions.why: A trail enters and leaves each middle vertex, using its edges in pairs.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 25.5, Euler Trails, p. 279

questions.prompt: How many colors suffice to color any planar map so adjacent regions differ?
questions.back: Four, by the four color theorem.
questions.why: A five color proof is short, and the four color proof needed a computer.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 25.6, Colorings, p. 280

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, section 23.6, Fermat’s Theorem, p. 258

questions.prompt: Find the sum of all real x with |x-3| = 2x+1.
questions.why: For x ≥ 3, x-3 = 2x+1 gives x = -4, which fails. For x < 3, 3-x = 2x+1 gives x = 2/3, which works. The sum is 2/3.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, chapter 26, Parting Shots, from p. 284

questions.prompt: A problem asks for the number of integer solutions of a Diophantine equation. You find a factorization that turns it into (x-a)(y-b) = N. What is the next step?
choices: List the factor pairs of N, including negative pairs.
Take square roots of both sides.
Set each factor equal to sqrt(N).
List only the positive factor pairs of N.
questions.why: Each integer solution corresponds to one ordered factor pair of N, and negative pairs give solutions too.

ref.label: The Art of Problem Solving, Volume 2, chapter 26, Parting Shots, from p. 284

lessons.title: Chapter 1: What This Book Is About and How to Read It

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 1, sections 1.1 to 1.4, pp. 1 to 11
items.minutesBasis: 11 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
items.what: Third edition. Work the examples before reading their solutions.

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 1 problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: An hour on a problem before any hint, as Chen says. Write every proof out. Mark this item missed if you give up on one, and note which.

questions.prompt: What separates a problem from an exercise in Zeitz's sense?
questions.back: An exercise is answered by a known procedure. A problem needs you to find the approach before you can start.
questions.why: Zeitz builds the book around problems, which need investigation.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 1.1, “Exercises” vs. “Problems”, p. 1

questions.prompt: Name Zeitz's three levels of problem solving.
questions.back: Strategy, tactics, and tools.
questions.why: Strategy is the overall plan, tactics are methods that work on many problems, and tools are narrow techniques.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 1.2, The Three Levels of Problem Solving, p. 3

questions.prompt: In Zeitz's terms, which of these is a tactic?
choices: Getting your hands dirty with small cases
Taking a break and returning later
questions.why: Pigeonhole is a method that applies across many problems. Small cases and taking a break are strategies, and a factorization is a tool.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 1.2, The Three Levels of Problem Solving, p. 3

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 2, sections 2.1 to 2.4, pp. 12 to 57
items.minutesBasis: 46 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
items.what: Third edition. Work the examples before reading their solutions.

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 2 problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: An hour on a problem before any hint, as Chen says. Write every proof out. Mark this item missed if you give up on one, and note which.

questions.prompt: Name three strategies for getting started on a problem once you are oriented.
questions.back: Get your hands dirty with small cases, find the penultimate step, and solve an easier related problem.
questions.why: Each turns a stuck problem into one you can make progress on.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 2.2, Strategies for Getting Started, subsection I’m Oriented. Now What?, p. 24

questions.prompt: What are the parts of a proof by induction?
questions.back: A base case and an inductive step showing that the statement for n implies it for n+1. Strong induction may assume all cases up to n.
questions.why: Together they reach every integer from the base case on.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 2.3, Methods of Argument, subsection Mathematical Induction, p. 42

questions.prompt: Prove that 2^n > n^2 for every integer n ≥ 5.
rubric: Checks n = 5: 32 > 25.
Assumes 2^n > n^2 for some n ≥ 5.
Shows 2n^2 ≥ (n+1)^2 for n ≥ 5, since n^2-2n-1 > 0 there, and concludes.
questions.why: The step needs 2n^2 ≥ (n+1)^2, which holds from n = 3 on.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 2.3, Methods of Argument, subsection Mathematical Induction, p. 42

questions.prompt: What does Zeitz mean by recasting a problem?
questions.back: Restating it in another form, such as a picture, a graph, a counting model, or an equivalent algebra problem, where a known method applies.
questions.why: A change of representation can make a hard problem routine.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 2.4, Other Important Strategies, subsection Pictures Don’t Help? Recast the Problem in Other Ways, p. 51

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 3, sections 3.1 to 3.4, pp. 58 to 104
items.minutesBasis: 47 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
items.what: Third edition. Work the examples before reading their solutions.

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 3 problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: An hour on a problem before any hint, as Chen says. Write every proof out. Mark this item missed if you give up on one, and note which.

questions.prompt: State the extreme principle.
questions.back: Look at the largest, smallest, or otherwise extreme element. Its extremeness often gives the key inequality or contradiction.
questions.why: An extreme object exists in any finite set, and it often cannot be improved, which constrains the configuration.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 3.2, The Extreme Principle, p. 70

questions.prompt: What are an invariant and a monovariant?
questions.back: An invariant is a quantity a process never changes. A monovariant changes in one direction only, such as always decreasing.
questions.why: An invariant rules out reaching states with a different value. A monovariant on positive integers proves a process stops.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 3.4, Invariants, p. 88

questions.prompt: An 8 by 8 board has two opposite corner squares removed. Prove it cannot be tiled by 1 by 2 dominoes.
rubric: Colors the board like a chessboard.
Notes the two removed corners have the same color, so 32 squares of one color and 30 of the other remain.
Notes every domino covers one square of each color.
Concludes 31 dominoes would cover 31 of each color, a contradiction.
questions.why: Coloring gives an invariant that every tiling would have to respect.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 3.4, Invariants, subsection Modular Arithmetic and Coloring, p. 95

questions.prompt: What is the smallest number of people that guarantees three of them share a birth month?
questions.why: With 24 people there can be 2 per month. The 25th forces a third in some month, so the answer is 25.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 3.3, The Pigeonhole Principle, subsection Basic Pigeonhole, p. 80

questions.prompt: There are n red and n blue points in the plane, no three collinear. Prove they can be paired into n red-blue segments, no two of which cross.
rubric: Considers all pairings of red with blue and picks one with the least total segment length, which exists since there are finitely many.
Supposes two of its segments R1B1 and R2B2 cross at a point X.
Replaces them with R1B2 and R2B1 and uses the triangle inequality at X to show the total strictly decreases, with no three points collinear.
Concludes the minimal pairing has no crossing.
questions.why: The extreme principle picks the shortest pairing, which cannot contain a crossing.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 3.2, The Extreme Principle, p. 70

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 4, sections 4.1 to 4.4, pp. 105 to 142
items.minutesBasis: 38 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
items.what: Third edition. Work the examples before reading their solutions.

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 4 problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: An hour on a problem before any hint, as Chen says. Write every proof out. Mark this item missed if you give up on one, and note which.

questions.prompt: When does a connected graph have an Eulerian walk that returns to its start?
questions.back: Exactly when every vertex has even degree.
questions.why: Each visit to a vertex uses one edge in and one edge out.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 4.1, Graph Theory, subsection Eulerian and Hamiltonian Walks, p. 108

questions.prompt: What is a roots of unity filter?
questions.back: To sum the coefficients of f(x) at exponents divisible by n, average f(w^k) over the nth roots of unity w^k.
questions.why: The sum of w^(jk) over k is n when n divides j and 0 otherwise.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 4.2, Complex Numbers, subsection Roots of Unity, p. 122

questions.why: With w a primitive cube root of unity, the sum is (2^12+(1+w)^12+(1+w^2)^12)/3. Since 1+w and 1+w^2 are sixth roots of unity, both 12th powers are 1, giving (4096+2)/3 = 1366.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 4.2, Complex Numbers, subsection Roots of Unity, p. 122

questions.prompt: How do generating functions solve a linear recurrence?
questions.back: Multiply the recurrence by x^n and sum, solve for the generating function as a rational function, and expand by partial fractions.
questions.why: The recurrence becomes an algebraic equation for the generating function.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 4.3, Generating Functions, subsection Recurrence Relations, p. 130

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 5, sections 5.1 to 5.5, pp. 143 to 188
items.minutesBasis: 46 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
items.what: Third edition. Work the examples before reading their solutions.

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 5 problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: An hour on a problem before any hint, as Chen says. Write every proof out. Mark this item missed if you give up on one, and note which.

questions.prompt: What is the telescope tool?
questions.back: Write each term as a difference f(k+1)-f(k), so the sum collapses to f(n+1)-f(1).
questions.why: Every middle term appears once with each sign.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 5.3, Sums and Products, subsection Geometric Series and the Telescope Tool, p. 158

questions.prompt: Compute the sum over k from 1 to 99 of 1/(sqrt(k)+sqrt(k+1)).
questions.why: Rationalizing gives sqrt(k+1)-sqrt(k), which telescopes to sqrt(100)-1 = 9.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 5.3, Sums and Products, subsection Geometric Series and the Telescope Tool, p. 158

questions.prompt: Prove that 1+1/4+1/9+...+1/n^2 < 2 for every positive integer n.
rubric: Notes 1/k^2 < 1/(k(k-1)) for k ≥ 2.
Telescopes the sum from k = 2 to n to 1-1/n.
Concludes the total is less than 1+1 = 2.
questions.why: Replacing each term with a larger telescoping term bounds the sum.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 5.3, Sums and Products, subsection Geometric Series and the Telescope Tool, p. 158

questions.prompt: What is "massaging" an inequality in Zeitz's sense?
questions.back: Replacing an expression with a slightly larger or smaller one that is easier to handle, while keeping the inequality true.
questions.why: A little loss in sharpness can make the expression telescope or factor.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 5.5, Inequalities, subsection Massage, Cauchy-Schwarz, and Chebyshev, p. 181

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 6, sections 6.1 to 6.4, pp. 189 to 223
items.minutesBasis: 35 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
items.what: Third edition. Work the examples before reading their solutions.

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 6 problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: An hour on a problem before any hint, as Chen says. Write every proof out. Mark this item missed if you give up on one, and note which.

questions.prompt: What is the balls in urns encoding?
questions.back: Represent a distribution of k identical balls into n urns as a string of k balls and n-1 dividers, which gives C(k+n-1, n-1).
questions.why: Strings of stars and dividers correspond one-to-one with distributions.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 6.2, Partitions and Bijections, subsection Balls in Urns and Other Classic Encodings, p. 203

questions.prompt: In how many ways can a 2 by 8 rectangle be tiled with 1 by 2 dominoes?
questions.why: The last column holds a vertical domino or two stacked horizontal ones, so t_n = t_(n-1)+t_(n-2) with t_1 = 1 and t_2 = 2, and t_8 = 34.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 6.4, Recurrence, subsection Tiling and the Fibonacci Recurrence, p. 215

questions.prompt: Give a combinatorial proof that the sum over k of C(n, k)^2 equals C(2n, n).
rubric: Counts n-element subsets of a set of n red and n blue items.
Sorts them by the number k of red items chosen.
Notes C(n, k)C(n, n-k) = C(n, k)^2 subsets have k red items.
Sums over k and equates with C(2n, n).
questions.why: Counting one collection two ways gives the identity.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 6.1, Introduction to Counting, subsection Combinatorial Arguments, p. 192

questions.prompt: When should you count the complement first?
questions.back: When the condition is "at least one" or the forbidden cases are simpler than the allowed ones.
questions.why: Total minus forbidden equals allowed.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 6.3, The Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion, subsection Count the Complement, p. 207

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 7, sections 7.1 to 7.5, pp. 224 to 257
items.minutesBasis: 34 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
items.what: Third edition. Work the examples before reading their solutions.

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 7 problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: An hour on a problem before any hint, as Chen says. Write every proof out. Mark this item missed if you give up on one, and note which.

questions.prompt: State Fermat's little theorem in the form that holds for every integer a.
questions.back: a^p ≡ a (mod p) for every prime p and every integer a.
questions.why: If p divides a both sides are 0, and otherwise divide by a to get a^(p-1) ≡ 1.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 7.2, Congruence, subsection Fermat’s Little Theorem, p. 234

questions.prompt: What are the last two digits of 7^2026?

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 7.2, Congruence, p. 232

questions.prompt: How many integers from 1 to 100 are relatively prime to 100?

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 7.3, Number Theoretic Functions, subsection Phi and Mu, p. 238

questions.prompt: Give a counting proof of Fermat's little theorem: for a prime p and positive integer a, p divides a^p-a.
rubric: Counts strings of length p over an alphabet of a letters: a^p.
Removes the a constant strings, leaving a^p-a.
Notes rotating a nonconstant string gives p distinct strings, because p is prime.
Concludes the nonconstant strings split into classes of size p, so p divides a^p-a.
questions.why: Rotation classes of nonconstant strings all have size p.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 7.5, Miscellaneous Instructive Examples, subsection A Combinatorial Proof of Fermat’s Little Theorem, p. 250

questions.prompt: Which primes are sums of two squares?
questions.back: 2 and the primes congruent to 1 mod 4. Primes congruent to 3 mod 4 are not.
questions.why: Squares are 0 or 1 mod 4, so a sum of two squares is never 3 mod 4. Fermat's two squares theorem gives the rest.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 7.5, Miscellaneous Instructive Examples, subsection Sums of Two Squares, p. 251

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 8, sections 8.1 to 8.5, pp. 258 to 315
items.minutesBasis: 58 pages at 3 minutes a page, an estimate
items.what: Third edition. Work the examples before reading their solutions.

items.title: Zeitz, chapter 8 problems
items.minutesBasis: Proposed
items.what: An hour on a problem before any hint, as Chen says. Write every proof out. Mark this item missed if you give up on one, and note which.

questions.prompt: State the inscribed angle theorem and one corollary.
questions.back: An inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc. So an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.
questions.why: The central angle is twice the inscribed angle on the same arc.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 8.2, Survival Geometry I, subsection Circles and Angles, p. 265

questions.prompt: Give a test that four points are concyclic.
questions.back: ABCD is cyclic exactly when angle ABD = angle ACD (B and C on the same side of AD), or when a pair of opposite angles is supplementary.
questions.why: These are the converse forms of the inscribed angle theorem.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 8.4, The Power of Elementary Geometry, subsection Concyclic Points, p. 284

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. Find its inradius.
questions.why: Area = rs gives r = 24/12 = 2. The formula (a+b-c)/2 agrees.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 8.3, Survival Geometry II, subsection Area, p. 271

questions.prompt: Prove the angle bisector theorem with areas: if AD bisects angle A of triangle ABC with D on BC, then BD/DC = AB/AC.
rubric: Notes triangles ABD and ACD share the altitude from A, so their areas are in the ratio BD/DC.
Notes D is equidistant from lines AB and AC because it lies on the bisector.
So their areas are also in the ratio AB/AC, with that common distance as height.
Equates the two ratios.
questions.why: Computing one area ratio two ways gives the theorem.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 8.4, The Power of Elementary Geometry, subsection Area, Cevians, and Concurrent Lines, p. 287

questions.prompt: What does a homothety with center O and ratio k do?
questions.back: It sends each point P to the point P' with OP' = k OP as vectors. Lines go to parallel lines and lengths scale by |k|.
questions.why: Homothety relates similar figures with parallel corresponding sides, such as the medial triangle and the original.

ref.label: Zeitz, The Art and Craft of Problem Solving, section 8.5, Transformations, subsection Homothety, p. 306
