questions.prompt: How many positive divisors does 360 have?
questions.why: 360 = 2^3*3^2*5. The divisor count is the product of (exponent+1), so 4*3*2 = 24.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Divisibility, section Prime Factorization

questions.prompt: Compute Euler's totient phi(36).

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Euler's totient function

questions.prompt: Compute lcm(12, 18, 30).
questions.why: 12 = 2^2*3, 18 = 2*3^2, 30 = 2*3*5. Take each prime at its highest power: 2^2*3^2*5 = 180.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Divisibility, section GCD & LCM

questions.prompt: You factor one integer n up to 10^12 by trial division. How many candidate divisors must you try in the worst case?
questions.why: If n has no prime factor up to sqrt(n), the n left over is prime. So trial division stops after about sqrt(n) candidates.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Divisibility, section Prime Factorization

questions.prompt: How does the Euclidean algorithm compute gcd(a, b), and how fast is it?
questions.back: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), with gcd(a, 0) = a. It takes O(log min(a, b)) steps.
questions.why: Each pair of steps at least halves the smaller argument, which bounds the step count by a logarithm.

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Euclidean algorithm for computing the greatest common divisor

items.title: USACO Guide: Modular Arithmetic
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Modular Arithmetic, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Compute the modular inverse of 3 modulo 10^9+7.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Modular Arithmetic, section Modular Inverse

questions.prompt: Compute 2^100 mod (10^9+7).
questions.why: Binary exponentiation squares the base and multiplies on the set bits of 100, using O(log 100) multiplications.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Modular Arithmetic, section Modular Exponentiation

questions.prompt: Find x with 0 < x < 13 and 5x = 1 (mod 13).
questions.why: 5*8 = 40 = 3*13+1. Fermat gives the same value: 5^11 mod 13 = 8.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Modular Arithmetic, section Modular Inverse

questions.prompt: Read n, then n lines with integers a and b (0 <= a, b <= 10^9). Print a^b modulo 10^9+7 for each line. Treat 0^0 as 1.
questions.why: Square the base and halve the exponent each step. Multiply into the result when the low bit of b is set. Each query takes O(log b).

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Binary Exponentiation

questions.prompt: When p is prime and a is not divisible by p, what is the modular inverse of a, and why?
questions.back: a^(p-2) mod p. Fermat's little theorem gives a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p), so a*a^(p-2) = 1.
questions.why: The inverse comes from one binary exponentiation in O(log p).

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Modular Arithmetic, section Modular Inverse

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Combinatorics, section Stars and Bars

questions.prompt: You must answer 10^5 queries of C(n, k) mod 10^9+7 with n up to 10^6. Which method fits?
choices: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to 10^6, then answer each query in O(1)
Fill Pascal's triangle up to row 10^6
Multiply the k factors of each numerator from scratch per query
Compute each binomial with doubles and round
questions.why: The factorial method costs O(n+log MOD) once and O(1) per query. Pascal's triangle needs O(n^2) time and memory, which is far too much at n = 10^6.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Combinatorics, section Method 2: Factorial Definition (Modular Inverses)

questions.prompt: Give the expected value identity that the Combinatorics module calls linearity of expectation.
questions.back: E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] for any random variables X and Y, independent or not.
questions.why: It lets you sum the expectation of each indicator variable instead of handling the joint distribution.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Combinatorics, section Linearity of Expectation

questions.prompt: CSES Josephus Queries: with n = 10 children, who is the 6th child removed?
questions.why: Removal order for n = 10 is 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, then 3. After 10 the circle wraps, child 1 is skipped, and child 3 goes.

ref.label: CSES 2164: Josephus Queries

questions.prompt: CSES Sum of Divisors: compute sigma(1)+sigma(2)+...+sigma(10).
questions.why: Each d contributes d*floor(10 / d): 10+10+9+8+10+6+7+8+9+10 = 87.

ref.label: CSES 1082: Sum of Divisors

questions.prompt: CSES Common Divisors: for the array 12 18 7 30 25 45, what is the largest gcd of any pair?
questions.why: gcd(30, 45) = 15 and no pair shares a larger divisor. The CSES method counts, for each d from high to low, how many elements d divides, and stops at the first d with count 2.

ref.label: CSES 1081: Common Divisors

questions.prompt: CSES Divisor Analysis: what is the product of the divisors of 72, modulo 10^9+7?
questions.why: 72 has 12 divisors, so the product is 72^(12/2) = 72^6 = 139314069504, which is 314068531 mod 10^9+7.

ref.label: CSES 2182: Divisor Analysis

questions.prompt: CSES Prime Multiples: how many integers in 1..100 are divisible by at least one of 2, 3, or 7?
questions.why: Inclusion-exclusion: 50+33+14-16-7-4+2 = 72.

ref.label: CSES 2185: Prime Multiples

questions.prompt: CSES Exponentiation II asks for a^(b^c) mod p with p = 10^9+7 prime. How do you shrink the exponent?
choices: Compute b^c mod (p-1), then raise a to that power mod p
Compute b^c mod p, then raise a to that power mod p
Compute b^c exactly with big integers
questions.why: Fermat's little theorem makes a^(p-1) = 1 mod p, so exponents repeat with period p-1. The case a divisible by p gives 0 either way when the exponent is positive.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Modular Arithmetic, section Modular Inverse

items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to DP, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Frog 1: heights are 1 5 3 7 4 8. From stone i the frog jumps to i+1 or i+2 at cost |h_i-h_j|. What is the minimum total cost from the first stone to the last?

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Introduction to DP, section Example, Frog 1

questions.prompt: What is the difference between push DP and pull DP?
questions.back: Push DP updates future states from the current state. Pull DP computes the current state from past states.
questions.why: Both visit the same transitions. The choice decides which loop owns the update.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Introduction to DP, section With Dynamic Programming

questions.prompt: Which two properties make a problem a fit for dynamic programming?
choices: A greedy choice property and a matroid structure
Sorted input and a monotone answer
questions.why: Optimal substructure lets a solution be built from subproblem solutions. Overlapping subproblems are what caching saves.

ref.label: CLRS 4th ed., Section 14.3, Elements of dynamic programming, p. 382

items.title: USACO Guide: Knapsack DP
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Knapsack DP, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Dice Combinations: how many ordered sequences of die rolls (1 to 6) sum to 10?
questions.why: dp[x] = dp[x-1]+...+dp[x-6] with dp[0] = 1 gives dp[10] = 492.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Knapsack DP, section Solution, Dice Combinations

questions.prompt: Book Shop: prices 4 8 5 3, pages 5 12 8 1, budget 10. Each book at most once. What is the most pages you can buy?
questions.why: Books with prices 4 and 5 cost 9 and give 5+8 = 13 pages. The 8-price book leaves 2, which buys nothing, so it gives only 12.

ref.label: CSES 1158: Book Shop

questions.prompt: In 0/1 knapsack with a 1D array dp[c], why does the inner capacity loop run from high to low?
questions.back: Going downward reads dp[c-w] before this item updates it, so each item is used at most once.
questions.why: An upward loop would let the same item be added again, which solves the unbounded knapsack instead.

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Knapsack Problem, section 0-1 Knapsack

questions.prompt: Coin Combinations II counts each multiset of coins once, whatever the order. How do the loops go in the 1D DP?
choices: Coins in the outer loop, sums in the inner loop
Sums in the outer loop, coins in the inner loop
Either order gives the same count
Sums from high to low with coins inside
questions.why: With coins outside, each combination is built in one fixed coin order, so it is counted once. Sums outside count every ordering, which is Coin Combinations I.

ref.label: CSES 1636: Coin Combinations II

items.title: USACO Guide: Paths on Grids
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Paths on Grids, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: What is the length of the longest common subsequence of AGGTAB and GXTXAYB?
questions.why: GTAB is common to both, and no common subsequence of length 5 exists.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Paths on Grids, section Solution, Longest Common Subsequence

questions.prompt: A 4 by 4 grid has traps at row 2 column 2 and row 3 column 4 (1-based). Moving only right or down, how many paths go from the top left to the bottom right?
questions.why: dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c]+dp[r][c-1], with 0 on traps. Filling the grid gives 4.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Paths on Grids, section Solution, Grid Paths

questions.prompt: What is the edit distance between kitten and sitting (insert, delete, or replace one character per move)?
questions.why: Replace k with s, replace e with i, and insert g. No two moves suffice.

ref.label: CSES 1639: Edit Distance

questions.prompt: State the LCS recurrence for prefixes a[1..i] and b[1..j].
questions.back: If a_i = b_j then dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]+1. Otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
questions.why: The table has (n+1)(m+1) cells and each takes O(1), so LCS runs in O(nm).

ref.label: CLRS 4th ed., Section 14.4, Longest common subsequence, p. 393

items.title: USACO Guide: Longest Increasing Subsequence
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Longest Increasing Subsequence, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: What is the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 5 3 5?
questions.why: 1 4 5 9 has length 4, and no strictly increasing subsequence of length 5 exists.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Longest Increasing Subsequence, section Fast Solution

questions.prompt: Same sequence 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 5 3 5. What is the length of the longest non-decreasing subsequence?
questions.why: 1 1 2 3 5 has length 5. Equal values may now repeat.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Longest Increasing Subsequence, section Fast Solution

questions.prompt: In the O(N log N) LIS method, what does d[len] hold, and which search updates it for a strictly increasing LIS?
questions.back: d[len] is the smallest possible last element of an increasing subsequence of length len. Each x replaces the first d entry that is >= x (lower_bound), or extends d if none is.
questions.why: d stays sorted, so each step is one binary search. The answer is the size of d.

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Longest increasing subsequence, section Solution in O(n log n) with dynamic programming and binary search

questions.prompt: Read n and a sequence of n integers. Print the length of its longest strictly increasing subsequence. Aim for O(n log n).
questions.why: Keep the sorted array of smallest tails. lower_bound finds the first tail >= x, which keeps the subsequence strict.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Longest Increasing Subsequence, section Fast Solution

questions.prompt: You switch the LIS code to longest non-decreasing subsequence. What changes?
choices: Use lower_bound on the reversed array
questions.why: upper_bound finds the first tail strictly greater than x, so an equal value can extend a run instead of replacing it.

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Longest increasing subsequence, section Longest non-decreasing subsequence

items.title: USACO Guide: Bitmask DP, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: With n = 5, how many pairs (S, T) are there where S is a bitmask of n bits and T is a submask of S?
questions.why: Each element is in both, in S only, or in neither, which gives 3^5 = 243 pairs. Iterating all submasks of all masks costs O(3^n).

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Bitmask DP, section Merging Subsets

questions.prompt: A directed graph on 4 vertices has edges 1->2, 1->3, 2->3, 3->2, 2->4, 3->4. How many paths start at 1, end at 4, and visit every vertex once?
questions.why: 1-2-3-4 and 1-3-2-4. dp[mask][v] counts such paths and gives the same 2.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Bitmask DP, section Bitmask DP

questions.prompt: What is the state and running time of the bitmask DP for Hamiltonian paths on N vertices?
questions.back: dp[mask][v] = ways (or cost) to visit exactly the set mask and end at v. It has 2^N*N states with N transitions each, so O(2^N N^2).
questions.why: N up to about 20 fits this bound.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Bitmask DP, section Bitmask DP

questions.prompt: A problem has N <= 20 people and asks for the fewest rides that carry everyone, given a weight limit. Which technique fits?
choices: Range DP over a sorted list
questions.why: 2^20 subsets is about 10^6 states. CSES Elevator Rides stores, per subset, the fewest rides and the lightest last ride.

ref.label: CSES 1653: Elevator Rides

items.title: USACO Guide: Range DP
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Range DP, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Removal Game on 2 9 4 7 1: players alternately take the first or last number. What is the first player's best total when both play optimally?
questions.why: dp[l][r] = best score difference for the player to move on a[l..r]. It gives -9 on the whole list. The sum is 23, so the first player scores (23-9) / 2 = 7.

ref.label: CSES 1097: Removal Game

questions.prompt: In range DP over subarrays, in which order are states filled, and what is the usual running time?
questions.back: By increasing length, so every shorter subarray is ready. O(N^2) subarrays with O(N) work each gives O(N^3).
questions.why: The module states this order and bound.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Range DP, section Tutorial

items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Digit DP, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: How many integers from 1 to 1000 have no two equal adjacent digits?
questions.why: 1 to 9: 9. Two digits: 81. Three digits: 729. 1000 fails. Total 819.

ref.label: CSES 2220: Counting Numbers

questions.prompt: How many integers from 1 to 10000 have digit sum exactly 10?
questions.why: A digit DP over (position, sum, tight) counts them. The count is 282.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Digit DP, section Tutorial

questions.prompt: What state does a digit DP usually carry while building a number digit by digit up to a bound?
questions.back: The position, a flag for whether the prefix is already below the bound, a flag for whether nonzero digits have started, and the problem's own value such as a digit sum.
questions.why: The below-the-bound flag decides whether the next digit may go up to 9 or only up to the bound's digit.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Digit DP, section Tutorial

questions.prompt: Coin Combinations II: coins 2 3 5, target 9. How many ways are there if the order of the coins does not matter?

questions.prompt: Counting Towers allows n up to 10^6 and t up to 100 tests. What is the plan?

Run the DP from scratch per test
Use bitmask DP over the 2 columns
Use matrix exponentiation per test with a 10 by 10 matrix
questions.why: The DP over height has two states per level. One pass to 10^6 serves every test.

questions.prompt: Vacation: days give (A, B, C) happiness (10, 40, 70), (20, 50, 80), (30, 60, 90). The same activity may not repeat on consecutive days. What is the best total?
questions.why: C, B, C gives 70+50+90 = 210. dp[i][k] = best through day i ending with activity k.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC C: Vacation

questions.why: The same three-state DP gives 46.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC C: Vacation

questions.prompt: Frog 2 with K = 3 and heights 10 30 40 50 20. What is the minimum cost?
questions.why: Jump 1 to 2 for 20, then 2 to 5 for 10. dp[i] takes the min over the K stones before i.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC B: Frog 2

questions.prompt: Coins: three coins each show heads with probability 1/2. What is the probability of more heads than tails?
questions.why: By symmetry with an odd count, it is 1/2. The DP over (coins tossed, heads) gives the same.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC I: Coins

questions.prompt: Longest Path: a DAG on 5 vertices has edges 5->3, 2->3, 2->4, 5->2, 5->1, 1->4, 4->3, 1->3. How many edges are on the longest path?
questions.why: 5->2->4->3 and 5->1->4->3 both have 3 edges. Memoize f(v) = 1+max f(w) over edges v->w.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC G: Longest Path

questions.prompt: Knapsack 1: read N and W, then N lines w_i v_i. Print the largest total value with total weight at most W. W is at most 10^5.
questions.why: dp over capacity, with the capacity loop running downward so each item is used once. That takes O(NW).

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC D: Knapsack 1

questions.prompt: Knapsack 2 has W up to 10^9 but each value v_i is at most 10^3 and N at most 100. What is the DP?
choices: dp[v] = least weight that reaches value exactly v, then take the largest v with dp[v] <= W
dp[w] = best value at weight w, as in Knapsack 1
Meet in the middle over all items
questions.why: Total value is at most 10^5, so indexing by value gives a small table. Indexing by weight would need 10^9 entries.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC E: Knapsack 2

questions.prompt: Stones: A = {2, 3}. For how many pile sizes K from 1 to 10 does the first player win?
questions.why: win[k] is true when some move reaches a losing pile. The losing piles are 0, 1, 5, 6, 10, so the winning ones in 1..10 are 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC K: Stones

questions.prompt: Deque: a = 10 100 10. Taro maximizes X-Y and Jiro minimizes it. What is X-Y?
questions.why: Either end Taro takes, Jiro then takes 100 and Taro gets the last 10, so X-Y = 20-100 = -80.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC L: Deque

questions.prompt: Candies: three children may each get 0 to 2 candies. In how many ways can exactly 3 candies be shared?
questions.why: Triples with entries in 0..2 summing to 3: 6 permutations of (0,1,2) plus (1,1,1) makes 7. The DP uses prefix sums to run in O(NK).

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC M: Candies

questions.prompt: Slimes: sizes 3 1 2 4. Merging two adjacent slimes costs their total. What is the least total cost?
questions.why: Merge 1+2 (3), then 3+3 (6), then 6+4 (10), for 19. Range DP over dp[l][r] plus the range sum.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC N: Slimes

questions.prompt: Independent Set: a path 1-2-3-4. How many ways color vertices black or white with no two adjacent blacks?
questions.why: Tree DP keeps (ways if white, ways if black) per vertex. A path of 4 vertices gives 8.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC P: Independent Set

questions.prompt: Walk: in the complete directed graph on 3 vertices with no self loops, how many directed paths of length 3 are there?
questions.why: Each path picks a start (3 ways) and then 2 choices per step, so 3*2^3 = 24. This is the sum of entries of A^3.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC R: Walk

questions.prompt: Flowers: N up to 2*10^5, keep flowers with increasing heights and maximize the total beauty. What makes the DP fast?
choices: A segment tree or Fenwick tree indexed by height that stores the best dp value, queried as a prefix max
An O(N^2) loop over earlier flowers
questions.why: dp[h] = a_i+max dp over smaller heights. A prefix max structure answers that in O(log N), for O(N log N) total.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC Q: Flowers

questions.prompt: Matching: N up to 21 men and women. Which DP counts perfect matchings?
choices: dp[mask] over sets of women already used, with man popcount(mask) placed next
dp[i][j] over man i and woman j
questions.why: Process men in order. The number of women used tells which man is next, so one bitmask over women suffices, about 2^21*21 steps.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC O: Matching

questions.prompt: Digit Sum: how many integers from 1 to 100 have a digit sum that is a multiple of 5?
questions.why: Digit DP over (position, sum mod D, tight) counts them. The count is 19.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC S: Digit Sum

questions.prompt: Permutation: how many permutations of 1..5 match the pattern > < > < ?
questions.why: dp[i][j] = ways where the last element is the j-th smallest of the first i, with prefix sums for each step. The count is 16.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC T: Permutation

questions.prompt: Frog 3: heights 1 3 4 8 and C = 5. A jump from i to j costs (h_j-h_i)^2+C. What is the least total cost?
questions.why: 1 to 3 (4+5), 3 to 4 (1+5), 4 to 8 (16+5) gives 36. 1 to 4 (9+5) then 4 to 8 (16+5) gives 35, the minimum.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC Z: Frog 3

questions.prompt: Grid 2: a 3 by 4 grid has walls at (2, 2) and (1, 4). Moving right or down, how many paths go from (1, 1) to (3, 4)?
questions.why: Count all paths, then subtract paths through walls by inclusion over sorted walls. A small grid DP confirms 3.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC Y: Grid 2

questions.prompt: Grouping: iterating all submasks of all masks of N = 16 rabbits takes how many (mask, submask) pairs?
questions.why: 3^16 = 43046721, which fits the time limit.

ref.label: AtCoder EDPC U: Grouping

questions.prompt: Frog 3 has N up to 2*10^5. Which technique turns its O(N^2) DP into O(N log N) or O(N)?
questions.back: The convex hull trick. dp[i] = h_i^2+C+min over j of (-2 h_j*h_i+dp[j]+h_j^2), which is a minimum over lines evaluated at h_i.
questions.why: Slopes -2 h_j decrease as j grows, so lines arrive in sorted slope order.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Convex Hull Trick, section Tutorial

items.title: USACO Guide: Shortest Paths with Unweighted Edges
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Shortest Paths with Unweighted Edges, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: An undirected graph on 7 vertices has edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 3-4, 4-5, 5-6, 3-7, 7-6. How many edges are on a shortest path from 1 to 6?
questions.why: BFS from 1 reaches 2 and 3 at distance 1, then 4 and 7 at distance 2, then 5 and 6 at distance 3.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Shortest Paths with Unweighted Edges, section Unweighted Shortest Path

questions.prompt: A directed graph has edges with weights 0 or 1: 1->2 (1), 1->3 (0), 3->4 (1), 2->4 (0), 4->5 (1), 3->5 (1), 2->5 (0). What is the shortest distance from 1 to 5?
questions.why: 1->3 costs 0 and 3->5 costs 1, for 1. 0/1 BFS pushes 0-edges to the front of the deque and 1-edges to the back.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Shortest Paths with Unweighted Edges, section Extension, 0/1 BFS

questions.prompt: Edge weights are only 0 or 1, with 10^6 vertices and edges. Which method gives shortest paths in O(V+E)?
questions.why: Plain BFS treats 0-edges as 1-edges and gives wrong distances. A deque keeps the frontier sorted by distance without a heap.

ref.label: cp-algorithms, 0-1 BFS

items.title: USACO Guide: Disjoint Set Union
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Disjoint Set Union, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Start with 8 singleton sets. Apply unions (1,2), (3,4), (2,3), (5,6), (1,4). How many sets remain?
questions.why: The first four unions each merge two sets, leaving 4. The union (1,4) joins two vertices already in one set.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Disjoint Set Union, section Implementation

questions.prompt: With both path compression and union by size or rank, what is the amortized cost of a DSU operation?
questions.back: O(alpha(n)), where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function. It is at most 4 for any practical n.
questions.why: Either optimization alone gives O(log n). Together they give the inverse Ackermann bound.

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Disjoint Set Union

questions.prompt: Q queries add an edge or ask whether two vertices are connected, with no deletions. Which fits?
choices: A DSU, at O(alpha(N)) amortized per query
A fresh DFS per connectivity query
questions.why: Edges are only added, which is what a DSU supports. A DFS per query costs O(NQ), the slow bound the module rejects.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Disjoint Set Union, section Solution, Focus Problem

questions.prompt: Read n and m. Then m lines each name an edge a b (1 <= a, b <= n). After each edge, print the number of connected components.
questions.why: Each successful union lowers the count by one. A union of two vertices already in one set changes nothing.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Disjoint Set Union, section Implementation

items.title: USACO Guide: Topological Sort
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Topological Sort, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: A DAG on 4 vertices has edges 1->2, 1->3, 2->4, 3->4. How many topological orders does it have?
questions.why: 1 must come first and 4 last. 2 and 3 can go in either order, so there are 2.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Topological Sort, section Topological Sort

questions.prompt: How does Kahn's algorithm detect a cycle?
questions.back: It repeatedly removes vertices of in-degree 0. If fewer than all vertices are output, the remaining vertices lie on or behind a cycle.
questions.why: A vertex on a cycle never reaches in-degree 0, so it never enters the queue.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Topological Sort, section BFS

questions.prompt: You need the lexicographically smallest topological order. What change to Kahn's algorithm gives it?
choices: Replace the queue with a min priority queue
Run DFS and reverse the finish order
questions.why: Always taking the smallest available vertex gives the smallest order. The module names this change.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Topological Sort, section BFS

questions.prompt: What is the time cost of a topological sort by DFS or by Kahn's algorithm?
questions.back: O(V+E). Each vertex and each edge is handled once.
questions.why: CLRS sorts by decreasing DFS finish time, which costs the same as one DFS.

ref.label: CLRS 4th ed., Section 20.4, Topological sort, p. 573

lessons.title: Shortest Paths with Non-Negative Edge Weights

items.title: USACO Guide: Shortest Paths with Non-Negative Edge Weights
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Shortest Paths with Non-Negative Edge Weights, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Directed edges: 1->2 (4), 1->3 (1), 3->2 (2), 2->4 (1), 3->4 (5), 4->5 (3). What is the shortest distance from 1 to 5?
questions.why: 1->3->2->4->5 costs 1+2+1+3 = 7. Dijkstra settles 3 at 1, 2 at 3, 4 at 4, and 5 at 7.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Shortest Paths with Non-Negative Edge Weights, section Dijkstra

questions.prompt: A graph has negative edge weights and you must report whether a negative cycle is reachable from the source. Which algorithm fits?
choices: Bellman-Ford, checking for a relaxation in round n
questions.why: Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges n-1 times. Any relaxation in an extra round proves a negative cycle. Dijkstra assumes non-negative weights.

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Bellman-Ford

questions.prompt: Give the running times of Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, and heap-based Dijkstra on N vertices and M edges.
questions.back: Bellman-Ford O(NM). Floyd-Warshall O(N^3). Dijkstra with a binary heap O(M log N).
questions.why: The module also gives an O(N^2) Dijkstra for dense graphs.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Shortest Paths with Non-Negative Edge Weights, section Dijkstra

questions.prompt: N = 500, many queries ask shortest paths between arbitrary pairs, and weights may be negative but there is no negative cycle. Which fits?
questions.why: 500^3 is about 1.25*10^8 simple steps, and then each query is a table lookup. The module picks Floyd-Warshall for this reason.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Shortest Paths with Non-Negative Edge Weights, section Floyd-Warshall

items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Minimum Spanning Trees, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Undirected edges: 1-2 (3), 1-3 (1), 2-3 (7), 2-4 (5), 3-4 (2), 4-5 (7), 3-5 (8). What is the weight of a minimum spanning tree?
questions.why: Kruskal takes 1-3 (1), 3-4 (2), 1-2 (3), skips 2-4 and 2-3, then takes 4-5 (7). Total 13.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Minimum Spanning Trees, section Kruskal's

questions.prompt: A dense graph has V = 5000 and about V^2 edges. Which MST method fits best?
choices: Prim's with a linear scan, O(V^2)
Prim's with a heap, O(E log E)
questions.why: With E near V^2 the linear scan version avoids the log factor and the heap. The module recommends it for dense graphs.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Minimum Spanning Trees, section Prim's

questions.prompt: State the cut property behind Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms.
questions.back: For any cut of the graph, a minimum-weight edge crossing the cut belongs to some minimum spanning tree.
questions.why: Both algorithms add such a light edge at each step, which keeps the chosen edges inside some MST.

ref.label: CLRS 4th ed., Section 21.1, Growing a minimum spanning tree, p. 586

questions.prompt: Game Routes: a DAG has edges 1->2, 1->3, 2->4, 3->4, 2->5, 4->5. How many paths go from 1 to 5?
questions.why: ways(v) = sum over edges v->w of ways(w), with ways(5) = 1. That gives ways(4) = 1, ways(2) = 2, ways(3) = 1, ways(1) = 3.

ref.label: CSES 1681: Game Routes

questions.prompt: Flight Discount: directed flights 1->2 (3), 2->4 (10), 1->3 (8), 3->4 (5). One flight may be halved, rounded down. What is the cheapest price from 1 to 4?
questions.why: 1->2 (3) then 2->4 halved (5) costs 8. Run Dijkstra on states (city, coupon used) or combine distances from 1 and to 4 around each edge.

questions.prompt: High Score asks for the maximum score from room 1 to room n, or -1 if it can be made arbitrarily large. What decides -1?

Any positive cycle in the graph

ref.label: CSES 1673: High Score

questions.prompt: Course Schedule asks for an order of n courses with m prerequisites, or IMPOSSIBLE. What does it reduce to?
choices: Topological sort, IMPOSSIBLE when the graph has a cycle
questions.why: A valid order exists exactly when the prerequisite graph is acyclic.

items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: More Operations on Sorted Sets, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: A sorted set holds 1 4 9 16 25. What does a query for the first element >= 10 return?
questions.why: 16 is the smallest element not below 10. A sorted set answers it in O(log N).

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, More Operations on Sorted Sets, section Sorted Sets

questions.prompt: A sorted set holds 1 4 9 16 25. What does a query for the largest element < 10 return?
questions.why: 9 is the largest element below 10. In C++ take the iterator from lower_bound(10) and step back once.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, More Operations on Sorted Sets, section Sorted Sets

questions.prompt: You need a sorted set that also returns the k-th smallest element and counts elements below x, both in O(log N). What does the module name?
questions.why: A plain sorted set cannot index by rank. The order statistic tree from the policy-based data structures adds find_by_order and order_of_key.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, More Operations on Sorted Sets, section Sorted Sets

questions.prompt: Bit Inversions: after each flip, report the longest run of equal bits. Which two sorted structures does the module keep?
questions.back: A set dif of the indices where the bit differs from the one before, including 0 and n, and a multiset of the gaps between consecutive elements of dif. The answer is the largest gap.
questions.why: A flip at x toggles x and x+1 in dif. Each toggle removes one gap from the multiset and adds two, or the reverse, in O(log N).

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, More Operations on Sorted Sets, section Example, Bit Inversions

items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: (Optional) Sorted Sets with Custom Comparators, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: A set of Edge uses a functor comparing only the weight w. Two edges with the same weight but different endpoints are inserted. What happens?
choices: Only the first is kept, because the comparator treats them as equal
Both are kept in insertion order
Both are kept, sorted by endpoint
questions.why: A set treats a and b as equal when neither compares less than the other. Break ties on the other fields to keep both.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) Sorted Sets with Custom Comparators, section Functors

questions.prompt: Overloading which operator on a struct gives you std::less for it, and which gives std::greater?
questions.back: Overloading operator< gives less<T>. Overloading operator> gives greater<T>, which can store a set in reverse order.
questions.why: Both functors call the operator you defined.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) Sorted Sets with Custom Comparators, section Built-In Functors

questions.prompt: cmp is a lambda that compares two Edge objects. Which line declares a set of Edge ordered by it?
questions.why: The second template argument is the comparator type, which decltype(cmp) names. The lambda object itself is passed to the constructor.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) Sorted Sets with Custom Comparators, section With Lambda Expressions

items.title: USACO Guide: Stacks, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Nearest Smaller Values on 2 5 1 4 8 3 2 5: for each position print the 1-based index of the nearest earlier smaller value, or 0. What is the sum of the printed numbers?
questions.why: The answers are 0 1 0 3 4 3 3 7, which sum to 21. A monotonic stack finds them in O(N).

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Stacks, section Application, Nearest Smaller Element

questions.prompt: Why does the nearest smaller element stack run in O(N) total?
questions.back: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so all pops together cost O(N).
questions.why: The stack holds increasing values, and a popped value can never be the answer for a later index.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Stacks, section Application, Nearest Smaller Element

questions.prompt: For each bar of a histogram you need the nearest lower bar on each side to find the largest rectangle. Which tool fits?
choices: A monotonic stack, one pass per side
A sliding window of fixed size
questions.why: Nearest smaller on the left and on the right are two monotonic stack passes. The rectangle at bar i spans between them.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Stacks, section Application, Nearest Smaller Element

questions.prompt: Read n and an array. For each position print the 1-based position of the nearest earlier element with a strictly smaller value, or 0 if none. Print the answers on one line.
questions.why: Pop while the stack top is >= the current value. The top that remains is the answer.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Stacks, section Application, Nearest Smaller Element

items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Sliding Window, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Array 1 3 -1 -3 5 3 6 7 with window size 3. What is the sum of the window maxima?
questions.why: The maxima are 3 3 5 5 6 7, which sum to 29.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Sliding Window, section Sliding Window Maximum in O(N)

questions.prompt: How does a monotonic deque give every sliding window maximum in O(N)?
questions.back: Keep indices with decreasing values. Pop from the back while the new value is larger, push the new index, and pop the front once it leaves the window. The front is the maximum.
questions.why: Each index enters and leaves the deque once.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Sliding Window, section Method 1, Deque

questions.prompt: Besides a deque, which structure does the module show for a queue that reports its maximum in amortized O(1)?
choices: Two stacks that each store running maxima
A max heap with lazy deletion only
questions.why: Push onto the first stack and pop from the second, refilling it from the first when empty. Each stack entry stores the max below it.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Sliding Window, section Method 2, Two Stacks

items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Point Update Range Sum, problems

questions.prompt: In a Fenwick tree, what is lowbit(12), the value of i & -i for i = 12?
questions.why: 12 is 1100 in binary, so its lowest set bit is 4. Node 12 covers the range 9..12.

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Fenwick Tree, section One-based indexing approach

questions.prompt: A Fenwick tree computes the prefix sum up to index 13 by repeatedly removing the lowest set bit. How many tree nodes does it read?
questions.why: 13 -> 12 -> 8 -> 0 reads nodes 13, 12, and 8. The count equals the number of set bits of 13.

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Fenwick Tree

questions.prompt: In a Fenwick tree indexed from 1, which range of the array does node i store?
questions.back: The sum of positions i-lowbit(i)+1 through i, where lowbit(i) = i & -i.
questions.why: A prefix query walks i -= lowbit(i) and an update walks i += lowbit(i), each O(log N) steps.

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Fenwick Tree

questions.prompt: Read n and q, then an array of n values. Each query is 1 k u (set position k to u) or 2 a b (print the sum of positions a..b). Use a Fenwick tree.
questions.why: Store the current values so a set becomes an add of u-a[k]. A range sum is prefix(b)-prefix(a-1).

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Point Update Range Sum, section Binary Indexed Tree

choices: A sparse table with two overlapping power-of-two blocks
questions.why: Minimum is idempotent, so two overlapping blocks of length 2^k cover the range exactly once each. Build costs O(N log N).

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Sparse Table

questions.prompt: Range Update Queries adds x to a range and asks for one value. How can a Fenwick tree do it?
choices: Store a difference array: add x at a and -x at b+1, then the value is a prefix sum
Update every element in the range
Keep a sorted set of updates

questions.prompt: Hotel Queries: each group takes the first hotel with at least r free rooms. Which method finds it in O(log n)?
choices: Walk down a max segment tree, going left whenever the left child's max is at least r
Binary search on a prefix sum array
A Fenwick tree of room counts
questions.why: The descent visits one node per level. After the walk, a point update lowers that hotel's rooms.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, More Applications of Segment Tree, section Walking on a Segment Tree

questions.prompt: Give the time per operation for a segment tree and a Fenwick tree on point update and range sum.
questions.back: O(log N) per update and per query for both. Both build in O(N) or O(N log N).
questions.why: The Fenwick tree has shorter code. The segment tree also handles operations without an inverse, such as minimum.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Point Update Range Sum, section Segment Tree

questions.prompt: The tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 3-4, 3-5, 5-6, 5-7, rooted at 1. What is the size of a maximum matching (edges with no shared vertex)?
questions.why: 1-2, 3-4, and 5-6 form a matching of size 3. With 7 vertices a matching has at most 3 edges.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, DP on Trees, Introduction, section Solution, Tree Matching

questions.prompt: In the module's Tree Matching DP, what do dp_1[v] and dp_2[v] hold?
questions.back: dp_2[v] is the largest matching in v's subtree that uses no edge from v to a child. dp_1[v] is the largest that uses exactly one such edge.
questions.why: dp_2[v] sums max(dp_1[u], dp_2[u]) over children u. dp_1[v] picks the child u for the edge and swaps that child's term for dp_2[u]+1.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, DP on Trees, Introduction, section Solution 1

questions.prompt: What greedy also solves Tree Matching?
choices: Repeatedly match a leaf with its only neighbor
Match the two highest-degree vertices first
questions.why: Some maximum matching uses the leaf's edge, so taking it loses nothing.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, DP on Trees, Introduction, section Solution 2, Greedy

questions.prompt: The tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 3-4, 3-5, 5-6, 5-7, rooted at 1. What is the sum of distances from vertex 3 to all other vertices?
questions.why: Distances from 3 are 1 to vertices 1, 4, 5, and 2 to vertices 2, 6, 7. That is 3+6 = 9.

ref.label: CSES 1133: Tree Distances II

questions.prompt: The tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 3-4, 3-5, 5-6, 5-7, rooted at 1. What is the largest distance from vertex 5 to another vertex?
questions.why: Vertex 2 is at distance 3 from 5 (5-3-1-2).

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, DP on Trees, Solving For All Roots, section Solution, Tree Distances I

questions.prompt: In the all-roots solution to Tree Distances I, what do f[x] and g[x] hold, and what is the answer for x?
questions.back: f[x] is the largest distance from x to a node in its subtree. g[x] is the largest distance from x to a node outside its subtree. The answer is max(f[x], g[x]).
questions.why: One DFS computes f bottom up. A second DFS computes g top down, using the best and second best child branches.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, DP on Trees, Solving For All Roots, section Solution, Tree Distances I

questions.prompt: The tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 3-4, 3-5, 5-6, 5-7, rooted at 1. What is the sum of distances from vertex 6 to all other vertices?
questions.why: Distances from 6 are 1 to vertex 5, 2 to vertices 3 and 7, 3 to vertices 1 and 4, and 4 to vertex 2. The sum is 1+4+6+4 = 15.

ref.label: CSES 1133: Tree Distances II

questions.why: The visit order is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, so tin[5] = 4.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) Euler Tour Technique, section Tour Walkthrough

questions.prompt: The tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 3-4, 3-5, 5-6, 5-7, rooted at 1. With the same tour, how many consecutive tour positions does the subtree of 3 occupy?
questions.why: Vertex 3's subtree is 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, so the range spans 5 positions.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) Euler Tour Technique, section Introduction

questions.prompt: Why does an Euler tour turn subtree queries into range queries?
questions.back: A DFS visits a subtree's vertices consecutively. So the subtree of v is the index range [tin[v], tout[v]], and a Fenwick or segment tree over tour order handles it.
questions.why: Subtree Queries in CSES uses this with point updates and range sums.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) Euler Tour Technique, section Solution, Subtree Queries

questions.prompt: The tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 3-4, 3-5, 5-6, 5-7, rooted at 1. What is LCA(4, 7)?
questions.why: 4's ancestors are 4, 3, 1. 7's are 7, 5, 3, 1. The deepest common one is 3.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) LCA with Euler Tour, section LCA

questions.prompt: How do an Euler tour and a sparse table answer LCA queries?
questions.back: Record each vertex every time the DFS enters or returns to it. LCA(u, v) is the minimum-depth vertex between the first occurrences of u and v. A sparse table gives O(N log N) build and O(1) per query.
questions.why: With a segment tree instead, build is O(N) and queries are O(log N).

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) LCA with Euler Tour, section Sparse Tables

questions.prompt: The tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 3-4, 3-5, 5-6, 5-7, rooted at 1. The Euler tour records a vertex when the DFS enters it and again after each child returns. How long is the tour?
questions.why: Each of the 7 vertices is recorded once on entry, and each of the 6 edges adds one record on return, so the length is 2N-1 = 13.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) LCA with Euler Tour, section LCA

items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: When does ternary search find the minimum of f over integers?
questions.back: When f is unimodal: strictly decreasing, then strictly increasing. Compare f(m1) and f(m2) at two inner points and drop the third that cannot hold the minimum.
questions.why: Flat stretches break it, because equal values do not say which side holds the minimum.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Optimizing Unimodal Functions, section Definitions

questions.prompt: f is convex on integers. Which binary search finds its minimum?
choices: Find the first x with f(x+1)-f(x) >= 0
Find the first x with f(x) >= 0
Find the last x with f(x) < f(0)
questions.why: Consecutive differences of a convex function are non-decreasing, so the sign of f(x+1)-f(x) is monotone.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Optimizing Unimodal Functions, section Binary Search

questions.prompt: Each ternary search step on a range of length L keeps about how much of it?
questions.why: Two points split the range into thirds and one third is dropped. So the range shrinks by 2/3 per step, about log base 1.5 of L steps.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Optimizing Unimodal Functions, section Ternary Search

items.title: USACO Guide: Hashing
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Hashing, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Map a to 1, b to 2, and so on. With base 31 and modulus 10^9+9, what is the polynomial hash of abc computed as h = h*31+value?

ref.label: cp-algorithms, String Hashing

questions.prompt: How does a prefix hash array give the hash of s[a..b] in O(1)?
questions.back: Store h[i] = hash of the first i characters and powers of B. Then hash(a..b) = h[b+1]-h[a]*B^(b-a+1) mod M.
questions.why: All substring hashes then share one scale, so two can be compared directly.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Hashing, section String Hashing

questions.prompt: Why use two moduli (or one near 2^61) when comparing many substring hashes?
choices: With one modulus near 10^9 the birthday bound makes some collision likely among about 10^5 or more hashes
One modulus cannot hash lowercase letters
Two moduli are needed for strings longer than 64
questions.why: Among k hashes the chance of some pair colliding grows like k^2 / M. Two independent moduli make M about 10^18.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Hashing, section Explanation, Two Hashes

questions.prompt: How does XOR hashing compare two multisets or sets?
questions.back: Give each element a random 64-bit value and hash a set as the XOR of its values. Adding or removing an element XORs its value, since x XOR x = 0.
questions.why: The module puts the collision probability for N sets near N^2 / M.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, Hashing, section XOR Hashing/Zobrist Hashing

questions.prompt: Why can unordered_map<long long, int> time out on Codeforces hacks?
choices: Its default integer hash is predictable, so a test can send keys that all land in one bucket
It sorts keys on every insert
It limits the number of keys to 2^16
questions.why: Colliding keys make each operation linear in the bucket size. A random-seeded hash such as splitmix64 fixes it.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) Hashmaps, section Anti-Hash Tests

questions.prompt: What makes a hash function for unordered_map safe against hacked tests?
questions.back: Randomness that changes from run to run. The module's chash XORs the key with a random value read from chrono::steady_clock at startup, multiplies by a large odd constant, and byte-swaps the result.
questions.why: Any deterministic hash can be broken by a test built for it. A per-run random value stops that.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) Hashmaps, section A Faster HashMap in C++

questions.prompt: Does the Hashmaps module expect anti-hash tests in USACO?
choices: No, historically no USACO problem has had one
Yes, every Gold problem has one
questions.why: The module says anti-hash tests appear on Codeforces, where hacking is allowed, and not historically in USACO.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) Hashmaps, section Anti-Hash Tests

items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: How many subsets of 2 4 1 2 5 3 (positions count separately) have sum 7?
questions.why: Meet in the middle splits into halves 2 4 1 and 2 5 3 and pairs left sums with right sums that complete 7. The count is 6.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) Meet In The Middle, section Meet in the Middle Solution

questions.prompt: With n = 40, meet in the middle lists all subset sums of each half of 20. How many sums is that in total?
questions.why: 2*2^20 = 2^21 = 2097152, compared with 2^40 for all subsets.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) Meet In The Middle, section Meet in the Middle Solution

questions.prompt: What is the running time of meet in the middle for counting subsets of n numbers with sum x?
questions.back: O(n*2^(n/2)): list both halves' subset sums, sort one, and binary search for x-s for each sum s of the other.
questions.why: A hash map of counts can replace the binary search.

ref.label: USACO Guide Gold, (Optional) Meet In The Middle, section Meet in the Middle Solution

questions.prompt: n = 40 numbers up to 10^9 and a target x up to 10^9. Count the subsets with sum x. Which method fits?

items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: More Applications of Segment Tree, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum subarray sum of -1 2 -3 5 -2 4 -6 1 (the empty subarray counts as 0)?
questions.why: 5-2+4 = 7. A segment tree node storing (sum, best prefix, best suffix, best) combines children to keep this under point updates.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, More Applications of Segment Tree, section Solution, Subarray Sum Queries

questions.prompt: Which four values does a segment tree node store to answer maximum subarray sum, and how does the best value combine?
questions.back: sum, best prefix, best suffix, and best. best = max(left.best, right.best, left.suffix+right.prefix).
questions.why: prefix = max(left.prefix, left.sum+right.prefix), and suffix is symmetric.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, More Applications of Segment Tree, section Non-Commutative Combiner Functions

questions.prompt: Point Set Range Composite stores linear functions f(x) = ax+b and queries their composition over a range. What must the segment tree respect?
choices: The order of children when combining, because composition is associative but not commutative
A sparse table instead of a segment tree
questions.why: A segment tree works for any associative operation. For non-commutative ones, combine left then right in array order.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, More Applications of Segment Tree, section Non-Commutative Combiner Functions

questions.prompt: How do you find the first index whose value is at least x in O(log N) with a max segment tree?
questions.back: Walk down from the root. Go left if the left child's max is at least x, else go right. Stop at a leaf.
questions.why: This descent is how the module solves Hotel Queries, and it avoids an O(log^2 N) binary search over queries.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, More Applications of Segment Tree, section Walking on a Segment Tree

items.title: USACO Guide: Range Queries with Sweep Line
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Range Queries with Sweep Line, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: How does the module count intersections between horizontal and vertical segments?
questions.back: Sweep by y. A vertical segment adds 1 at its x in a BIT when it starts and removes it when it ends. A horizontal segment queries the BIT over [x1, x2]. Total O(N log N).
questions.why: Each event is one BIT operation after sorting the events.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Range Queries with Sweep Line, section Solution, Intersection Points

questions.prompt: Distinct Values Queries asks for the number of distinct values in [a, b], offline, n and q up to 2*10^5. Which sweep works?
choices: Sort queries by right end. Sweep r, keep a 1 only at the last occurrence of each value in a BIT, and answer with a range sum
Sort queries by left end and use a stack
questions.why: When r reaches a value, move its 1 from the old last occurrence to r. Then [a, r] counts each value once. Each step is O(log n).

ref.label: CSES 1734: Distinct Values Queries

questions.prompt: Springboards: a DP over points needs, for each new point, the best value among earlier points with x and y both smaller. What makes it fast?
choices: Sweep the points sorted by one coordinate and keep a BIT over the other coordinate
questions.why: Sorting handles one dimension. The BIT answers a prefix minimum over the other, giving O(P log P).

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Range Queries with Sweep Line, section Solution, Springboards

items.title: USACO Guide: Range Update Range Query
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Range Update Range Query, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: An array of 8 zeros (1-based) gets +3 on [2, 5], +2 on [4, 8], and +1 on [1, 3]. What is the sum of positions 3 through 6?
questions.why: Position 3 gets 3+1 = 4, positions 4 and 5 get 5 each, and position 6 gets 2. 4+5+5+2 = 16.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Range Update Range Query, section Explanation

questions.prompt: How do two BITs support range add and range sum?
questions.back: Turn a range add into suffix adds. One BIT holds the added values x, and the prefix sum to p counts them as p*x. A second BIT holds the correction x*(start-1) to subtract.
questions.why: prefix(p) = p*sum1(p)-sum2(p). Each operation touches O(log N) nodes.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Range Update Range Query, section Explanation

questions.prompt: What does a lazy segment tree store, and what must every descent do?
questions.back: Each node stores its range value plus a pending update for its children. Every descent pushes the pending update down before visiting children.
questions.why: Without the push, an update to an ancestor can be lost or applied after a newer one.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Range Update Range Query, section Lazy Segment Tree

questions.prompt: Read n and q. Each query is 1 l r x (add x to positions l..r) or 2 l r (print the sum of l..r). The array starts at 0. Use two Fenwick trees.
questions.why: range_add adds x at l and -x at r+1 in the first tree, and x(l-1) at l and -xr at r+1 in the second. prefix(i) = sum1(i)*i-sum2(i).

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Range Update Range Query, section Explanation

items.title: USACO Guide: Sparse Segment Trees
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Sparse Segment Trees, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Range updates and queries arrive online over positions 1..10^9 with Q = 10^5 operations. Which structure fits?
choices: A sparse (dynamic) segment tree that creates nodes on demand
A plain segment tree of size 4*10^9
Coordinate compression of all positions first
questions.why: Nodes are made only on visited paths, so memory is O(Q log C). Compression needs all queries up front, which an online problem does not give.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Sparse Segment Trees, section Resources

questions.prompt: How many nodes does a sparse segment tree create for Q updates over a range of size N?
questions.back: O(Q log N). Each update touches O(log N) nodes, and only those are created.
questions.why: The module notes that the structure is also called a dynamic segment tree.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Sparse Segment Trees, section Resources

questions.prompt: Monkey and Apple-trees needs range paint and range sum over positions up to 10^9. Which structure does the module use?
questions.back: A sparse segment tree with lazy propagation. Nodes are created on demand and lazy tags still work on them.
questions.why: Each operation creates O(log N) nodes, so time and memory are O(Q log N).

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Sparse Segment Trees, section Monkey and Apple-trees

items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: 2D Range Queries, problems

questions.prompt: A 3 by 3 grid holds 1 2 3 in row 1, 4 5 6 in row 2, and 7 8 9 in row 3. What is the sum of rows 2..3 and columns 1..2?
questions.why: 4+5+7+8 = 24. With 2D prefix sums S it is S(3,2)-S(1,2)-S(3,0)+S(1,0).

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, 2D Range Queries, section 2D BIT

questions.prompt: What are the time and memory costs of a 2D BIT on an N by N grid?
questions.back: O(log^2 N) per update or rectangle query, and O(N^2) memory.
questions.why: The module notes the O(N^2) memory is too much when N is large, which motivates the offline 2D BIT.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, 2D Range Queries, section Offline 2D BIT

questions.prompt: N points with coordinates up to N = 10^5, all updates and queries known in advance. How do you cut the 2D BIT's memory?
choices: Compress, per BIT row, only the coordinates that row will ever touch, for O(N log N) memory
Use an unordered_map for the whole grid
Use a 2D array of size 10^5 by 10^5
questions.why: Knowing the updates beforehand lets each row store only its needed columns. The module calls the hash map version slow in time and memory.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, 2D Range Queries, section Offline 2D BIT

items.title: USACO Guide: Divide & Conquer, SRQ
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Divide & Conquer, SRQ, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: How does divide and conquer answer static range queries for any associative operation?
questions.back: Split at mid M. Precompute lef[l] = A[l] op ... op A[M] and rig[r] = A[M+1] op ... op A[r]. A query with l <= M < r is lef[l] op rig[r]. Recurse on the halves for queries inside one half.
questions.why: Offline this costs O((N+Q) log N). Storing every level gives online O(N log N+Q).

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Divide & Conquer, SRQ, section Offline Queries

questions.prompt: Why does a plain sparse table not work for range sums the way it does for range minimum?
choices: Its two overlapping blocks would count the overlap twice
questions.why: Minimum is idempotent, so overlap is harmless. Divide and conquer avoids overlap and works for any associative operation.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Divide & Conquer, SRQ, section Static Array Queries

questions.prompt: What are the offline and online costs of divide and conquer static range queries?
questions.back: Offline O((N+Q) log N). Online O(N log N) preprocessing and O(1) per query, so O(N log N+Q).
questions.why: The online version keeps lef and rig for every level in an N log N table, like a sparse table.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Divide & Conquer, SRQ, section Static Array Queries

questions.prompt: What is the running time of Mo's algorithm, and how are queries ordered?
questions.back: O((N+Q) sqrt N) moves of the window ends. Sort queries by block of l (block size about sqrt N), then by r.
questions.why: Within a block r moves forward at most N times, and l moves at most sqrt N per query.

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Sqrt Decomposition, section Mo's algorithm

questions.prompt: Which signal does the module give that square root decomposition is intended?
choices: Low constraints such as n = 5*10^4 or a time limit above 2 seconds
questions.why: Square root methods cost more than log methods, so problems that intend them keep n small or allow more time.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Square Root Decomposition, section Additional Notes

questions.prompt: In sqrt decomposition of an array into blocks of size about sqrt N, what does a range query cost?
questions.back: O(sqrt N): whole blocks inside the range use stored block totals, and at most two partial blocks are scanned element by element.
questions.why: A point update changes one element and one block total in O(1).

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Sqrt Decomposition

questions.prompt: The tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 2-5, 3-6, 6-7, 6-8, 8-9, rooted at 1. What is the 3rd ancestor of vertex 9?

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Binary Jumping, section Binary Jumping

questions.prompt: The tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 2-5, 3-6, 6-7, 6-8, 8-9, rooted at 1. Company Queries prints -1 when no k-th ancestor exists. What does it print for vertex 5 and k = 3?
questions.why: 5 -> 2 -> 1, and 1 has no parent. So the answer is -1.

ref.label: CSES 1687: Company Queries I

questions.prompt: Binary lifting climbs k = 13 levels using jumps of powers of two. How many jumps does it make?
questions.why: 13 = 8+4+1, so it makes one jump per set bit, 3 jumps.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Binary Jumping, section Binary Jumping

questions.prompt: Company Queries I: read n and q, then the parents of vertices 2..n (vertex 1 is the root). Each query x k asks for the k-th ancestor of x. Print it, or -1 if none.
questions.why: up[v][j] = up[up[v][j-1]][j-1] builds the table in O(n log n). A query takes one jump per set bit of k, with 0 standing for none.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Binary Jumping, section Binary Jumping

questions.prompt: How does binary lifting find LCA(a, b)?
questions.back: Lift the deeper vertex to the same depth. If they are equal, that is the LCA. Otherwise, for j from high to low, jump both by 2^j when their 2^j ancestors differ. The parent of either is the LCA.
questions.why: Preprocessing is O(N log N) and each query is O(log N).

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Lowest Common Ancestor, Binary Lifting

items.title: USACO Guide: Small-To-Large Merging
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Small-To-Large Merging, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: Why does small-to-large merging of sets run in O(N log^2 N)?
questions.back: Always insert the smaller set into the larger. An element that moves lands in a set at least twice as large, so it moves O(log N) times, each move costing O(log N).
questions.why: swap of two std::set objects is O(1), so taking the larger set costs nothing extra.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Small-To-Large Merging, section Better Solution

questions.prompt: Merging the smaller set into the larger is safe with std::swap for sets. Which container does the module warn about?
choices: std::array, whose swap is not O(1)
questions.why: std::swap of std::array exchanges every element, so it costs time linear in the size.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Small-To-Large Merging, section Generalizing

questions.prompt: The tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 2-5, 3-6, 6-7, 6-8, 8-9, rooted at 1. Colors are 1:1, 2:2, 3:3, 4:2, 5:1, 6:3, 7:4, 8:3, 9:5. Distinct Colors asks for each vertex the number of distinct colors in its subtree. What is it for vertex 3?
questions.why: Vertex 3's subtree is 3, 6, 7, 8, 9 with colors 3, 3, 4, 3, 5, so 3 distinct colors.

ref.label: CSES 1139: Distinct Colors

items.title: USACO Guide: Heavy-Light Decomposition, problems

questions.prompt: The tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 2-5, 3-6, 6-7, 6-8, 8-9, rooted at 1. Which child of vertex 1 is its heavy child?
questions.why: Subtree sizes are 3 for vertex 2 (2, 4, 5) and 5 for vertex 3 (3, 6, 7, 8, 9). The heavy child has the larger subtree.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Heavy-Light Decomposition, section Definitions

questions.prompt: Why does any root-to-vertex path cross only O(log N) light edges in heavy-light decomposition?
questions.back: Going down a light edge from v leads to a subtree of size at most half of v's. Sizes halve each time, so there are at most log2 N light edges.
questions.why: Heavy paths are contiguous in the base array, so each path query becomes O(log N) segment tree queries, O(log^2 N) in all.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Heavy-Light Decomposition, section Properties

questions.prompt: Path Queries II asks for the maximum on the path between a and b under point updates. Which method fits?
choices: Heavy-light decomposition with a max segment tree, O(log^2 N) per query
Euler tour with a Fenwick tree
questions.why: Maximum has no inverse, so the subtraction trick of the Euler tour fails. HLD splits the path into O(log N) contiguous ranges.

ref.label: CSES 2134: Path Queries II

questions.prompt: What does one path query or update cost with heavy-light decomposition and a segment tree?
questions.back: O(log^2 N): the path splits into O(log N) heavy path segments and each is one O(log N) segment tree operation.
questions.why: Q queries cost O(Q log^2 N).

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Heavy-Light Decomposition, section Properties

items.title: USACO Guide: Centroid Decomposition
items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Centroid Decomposition, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: The tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 2-5, 3-6, 6-7, 6-8, 8-9, rooted at 1. Which vertex is the centroid (each remaining part has at most 4 vertices after removing it)?
questions.why: Removing 3 leaves {1, 2, 4, 5} and {6, 7, 8, 9}, 4 vertices each. Every other vertex leaves a part of 5 or more.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Centroid Decomposition, section Centroids

questions.prompt: How many layers does centroid decomposition produce, and why?
questions.back: O(log N). Each part after removing a centroid has at most half the vertices, so sizes halve at each layer.
questions.why: Each vertex belongs to O(log N) centroid components, which bounds the total work of most solutions by O(N log N) times the per-vertex cost.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Centroid Decomposition, section Centroid decomposition

questions.prompt: The tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 2-5, 3-6, 6-7, 6-8, 8-9, rooted at 1. Fixed-Length Paths I: how many paths have exactly 3 edges?
questions.why: Centroid decomposition counts them in O(N log N). On this tree a direct count gives 7.

ref.label: CSES 2080: Fixed-Length Paths I

questions.prompt: How do you find a centroid in O(N)?
questions.back: Compute subtree sizes from any root. Start at the root and move to a child whose subtree has more than N/2 vertices until none does.
questions.why: The vertex where you stop has every part at most N/2, including the part above it.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Centroid Decomposition, section Centroids

items.what: Read the module and work its examples in C++.

items.title: USACO Guide: Virtual Tree, problems
items.what: Solve two of the module's problems, easiest first. The guide keeps its own tracker. Read the editorial after 30 minutes stuck, then code it yourself.

questions.prompt: A virtual tree is built for k = 5 key vertices. At most how many vertices can it have?
questions.why: |S| <= 2k-1 = 9. Sorting keys by DFS order and adding LCAs of adjacent keys adds at most k-1 vertices.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Virtual Tree, section Virtual Tree Construction

questions.prompt: How is a virtual tree built for a key set S0?
questions.back: Sort S0 by DFS entry time. Add the LCA of each pair of adjacent keys. Then link each vertex to its nearest kept ancestor, for example with a stack in DFS order.
questions.why: A vertex outside S0 is needed only if two of its child subtrees hold keys, and such a vertex is the LCA of two adjacent keys.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Virtual Tree, section Virtual Tree Construction

questions.prompt: When does a virtual tree help?
choices: When many queries each name a small set of key vertices, so work can scale with the set size instead of N
When the tree has only one query
When the tree is a path
questions.why: The total work becomes O(sum of k log k) instead of O(N) per query.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Virtual Tree, section Virtual Tree Optimization

questions.prompt: A connected graph on 6 vertices is processed into a Kruskal reconstruction tree. How many nodes does the tree have?
questions.why: It keeps 6 leaves and adds one node per merging edge, 5 in all, for 2N-1 = 11.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Kruskal Reconstruction Tree, section Tutorial

questions.prompt: Undirected edges: 1-2 (3), 1-3 (1), 2-3 (7), 2-4 (5), 3-4 (2), 4-5 (7), 3-5 (8). What is the least possible maximum edge weight on a path from 2 to 5?
questions.why: Adding edges in sorted order joins 2 and 5 when the weight-7 edge 4-5 is added. In the Kruskal tree this is the weight at LCA(2, 5).

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Kruskal Reconstruction Tree, section Tutorial

questions.prompt: What query does a Kruskal reconstruction tree answer, and how fast?
questions.back: The minimum possible maximum edge weight on a path between u and v. It is the weight of LCA(u, v) in the tree, O(1) per query after O(N log N) construction with an O(1) LCA.
questions.why: Each internal node is created by one edge in sorted order and is the parent of the two merged components' tops.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Kruskal Reconstruction Tree, section Tutorial

questions.prompt: p1 = (1, 1), p2 = (5, 3), p3 = (2, 3). What is the cross product (p2-p1) x (p3-p1)?
questions.why: (4, 2) x (1, 2) = 4*2-2*1 = 6. It is positive, so p3 is to the left of the line from p1 to p2.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Geometry Primitives, section Location of a Point

questions.prompt: What is the area of the polygon (0,0), (4,0), (4,3), (2,5), (0,3)?
questions.why: The shoelace sum is 32, and half of it is 16.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Geometry Primitives, section Polygon Area

questions.prompt: State Pick's theorem.
questions.back: For a simple polygon with integer vertices, A = i+b/2-1, where i counts interior lattice points and b counts boundary lattice points.
questions.why: b sums gcd(|dx|, |dy|) over the edges, so i = A-b/2+1 follows from the area.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Geometry Primitives, section Lattice points in polygon

questions.prompt: How do you test whether two segments AB and CD intersect with cross products?
questions.back: They intersect if C and D lie on opposite sides of line AB and A and B lie on opposite sides of line CD. If a cross product is 0, check whether that point lies on the other segment's bounding box.
questions.why: Integer cross products avoid floating point error for integer inputs.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Geometry Primitives, section Segment Intersection

questions.prompt: Point Location Test: p1 = (1, 1), p2 = (5, 3), p3 = (4, 1). Looking from p1 to p2, where is p3?
questions.why: (p2-p1) x (p3-p1) = (4, 2) x (3, 0) = 4*0-2*3 = -6. A negative cross product means a clockwise turn, so p3 is on the right.

ref.label: CSES 2189: Point Location Test

questions.prompt: Points (0,0), (5,5), (2,7), (6,3), (1,6), (9,9). What is the smallest squared distance between two of them?
questions.why: (1,6) and (2,7) are 1 apart in x and in y, so the squared distance is 2.

ref.label: CSES 2194: Minimum Euclidean Distance

questions.prompt: How does the set-based sweep find the closest pair in O(N log N)?
questions.back: Sort by x. Keep points with x in [x-d, x] in a set ordered by y. For each new point check only set points with y in [y-d, y+d], at most a constant number, then update d.
questions.why: Each point enters and leaves the set once.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Sweep Line, section Closest Pair

questions.prompt: Restaurant Customers: how does the sweep find the most customers present at once?
questions.back: Make an arrival event +1 and a departure event -1 for each customer. Sort events, with departures before arrivals at equal times, and track the running count's maximum. O(N log N).
questions.why: Sorting the 2N events is the only non-linear step.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Sweep Line, section Restaurant Customers

questions.prompt: Points (0,0), (2,0), (4,0), (1,1), (3,1), (2,2), (4,4), (0,4), (1,3). How many vertices does the convex hull have, not counting points in the middle of a hull edge?
questions.why: The hull is the square (0,0), (4,0), (4,4), (0,4). (2,0) lies on an edge and the rest are inside.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Convex Hull, section With Monotone Chain

questions.prompt: Describe the monotone chain convex hull and its cost.
questions.back: Sort points by x, then y. Build the lower hull left to right and the upper hull right to left, popping the last point while it does not make a strict left turn. O(N log N) for the sort.
questions.why: To keep collinear boundary points, as CSES Convex Hull asks, pop only on a strict right turn.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Convex Hull, section With Monotone Chain

questions.prompt: After building a convex hull, you need the farthest pair of points. Which technique finds it in O(N)?
questions.why: The farthest pair lies on the hull. Two pointers advance around it as antipodal pairs.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Convex Hull, section Rotating Calipers

questions.prompt: Lines y = 2x+1, y = -x+7, y = 4, y = x+2. What is the minimum value at x = 3?
questions.why: The values are 7, 4, 4, and 5, so the minimum is 4.

ref.label: USACO Guide Platinum, Convex Hull Trick, section Tutorial

questions.prompt: When does the convex hull trick answer each query in amortized O(1)?
questions.back: When lines arrive in sorted slope order and queries come in sorted x order. A deque keeps the useful lines and pops from the front as x grows.
questions.why: With arbitrary query order, binary search over the hull gives O(log N). A Li Chao tree handles arbitrary insertion order.

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Convex hull trick and Li Chao tree

questions.prompt: Lines are inserted in arbitrary slope order and queries come at arbitrary x. What handles both in O(log C)?
questions.why: A Li Chao tree keeps in each node the line that wins at the midpoint and pushes the other line to one child.

ref.label: cp-algorithms, Convex hull trick and Li Chao tree, section Li Chao tree

questions.prompt: Polygon Lattice Points: how many lattice points lie strictly inside (0,0), (4,0), (4,3), (2,5), (0,3)?

questions.prompt: Same polygon. How many lattice points lie on its boundary?

questions.prompt: Maximum Manhattan Distances: points (1,1), (3,2), (2,4), (2,1), (4,5). What is the largest Manhattan distance between two of them?

ref.label: CSES 3410: Maximum Manhattan Distances

questions.prompt: Polygon Area: read n and n vertices in order. Print twice the area as an integer. Coordinates go up to 10^9 in absolute value.
questions.why: The shoelace formula sums x_i y_(i+1)-x_(i+1) y_i. Use 64-bit integers, and take the absolute value since the order may be clockwise.

ref.label: CSES 2191: Polygon Area

questions.prompt: State the inclusion-exclusion principle for the union of sets A_1, ..., A_n.

questions.why: With n sets there are 2^n-1 terms, so it suits small n or terms that group by size.

questions.prompt: What is F(90) mod (10^9+7), with F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1?

questions.prompt: a(n) = a(n-1)+a(n-2)+a(n-3). What is the side length of the smallest square matrix M with M (a(n-1), a(n-2), a(n-3)) = (a(n), a(n-1), a(n-2))?

questions.prompt: What does the (i, j) entry of A^K count when A is a graph's adjacency matrix?

questions.why: Matrix exponentiation computes A^K in O(N^3 log K).

questions.prompt: Fibonacci Numbers: read n (0 <= n <= 10^18) and print F(n) modulo 10^9+7.
questions.why: Raise [[1,1],[1,0]] to the n-th power by squaring. The entry at row 0, column 1 is F(n).
